lessons.title: What an Embedded System Is: The Computer Hidden Inside Things
lessons.content:
Look around your home right now and count the computers. You will probably say one laptop and a couple of phones. Now count again, honestly. The rice cooker that switches from cook to warm by itself has a tiny computer. The washing machine that runs a 40-minute program has one. The TV remote, the microwave, the digital scale at the bazar, the IPS that kicks in during load shedding, the inverter AC, the electricity prepaid meter on the wall, even a modern ceiling fan regulator may have one. Most homes in Dhaka have far more hidden computers than visible ones. Those hidden computers are embedded systems, and this course is about how to build them.

What an embedded system is: An embedded system is a computer built into a bigger product to do one specific job, usually without the user ever thinking of it as a computer. The word embedded means planted inside. A rice cooker is a cooking pot first; the computer inside is just a part, like the heating plate or the lid. The user presses a button and expects rice, not an operating system update. A general definition you can write in an exam: an embedded system is a combination of hardware and software, designed for a dedicated function, built into a larger mechanical or electrical system, often with real-time and resource constraints.

The two halves, hardware and firmware: Every embedded system has hardware, usually a microcontroller plus sensors, actuators, power circuits and connectors, and software, which in this world we call firmware. Firmware is the program stored permanently in the chip's flash memory. It starts running the moment power comes on and normally runs until power goes off. There is no desktop, no app store, no double-click. The firmware is written once by engineers, tested, and then burned into thousands or millions of identical units. The word firm sits between hard and soft: it can be changed, but not casually.

Embedded versus general-purpose computers: Your laptop is a general-purpose computer. Today it plays a cricket stream, tomorrow it compiles C code, next week it edits a video. You install new programs whenever you like. An embedded system is the opposite: it is designed for one job, or a small fixed set of jobs, and the program rarely changes after it leaves the factory. Because the job is known in advance, engineers can choose exactly enough hardware for it and nothing more. A laptop has gigabytes of RAM; a microcontroller in a TV remote may have a few hundred bytes. That is not a weakness. It is the whole point: smaller, cheaper, lower power, more reliable.

A small comparison with numbers: A typical laptop CPU runs at a few gigahertz, has 8 GB or more of RAM, draws tens of watts, and costs hundreds of dollars. The ATmega328P microcontroller on an Arduino Uno runs at 16 MHz, has 2 KB of SRAM and 32 KB of flash, draws a few milliamps, and costs a couple of dollars. That is roughly a million times less RAM. Yet it can read a temperature sensor, run a motor, blink a display and talk over a serial line all at once, because its job is small and well defined.

Reactive systems: Most embedded systems are reactive. They sit in a loop, watching inputs and reacting to changes. A door alarm waits for the magnetic switch to open, then sounds the buzzer. An electronic water pump controller waits for the tank sensor to say empty, then switches the motor on, and waits again for full. Compare this with a classic program that reads input, computes, prints output and ends. An embedded program usually never ends. Its main function contains a loop that runs forever, and the interesting part is how it responds to events from the outside world.

Real-time behaviour: Many embedded systems are also real-time systems. Real-time does not mean very fast. It means the answer must come within a deadline, and a late answer is a wrong answer. A car airbag controller must decide to fire within a few tens of milliseconds of a crash; firing one second later is useless. A washing machine motor controller must update the motor drive many times a second or the drum shakes. A digital clock must tick exactly once per second, not roughly. We will study hard and soft real-time properly in lesson 23; for now remember: in embedded work, when something happens matters as much as what happens.

The constraints that shape everything: Embedded designers fight with limits all day. Cost: if a product sells a million units, saving 10 taka per unit saves one crore taka. Power: many devices run on batteries for months or years. Size: a fitness band has no room for a big board. Memory: kilobytes, not gigabytes. Reliability: a pacemaker or a brake controller must not crash, and there is often nobody nearby to press reset. Environment: heat, dust, humidity and voltage fluctuations, all very familiar in Bangladesh. Lesson 2 turns these into proper design metrics.

Examples across the world: Consumer: rice cooker, microwave, washing machine, TV, smartwatch, digital camera. Home and building: IPS controller, solar charge controller, lift controller, fire alarm panel. Transport: a modern car has many electronic control units (ECUs) for the engine, brakes, airbags and windows; trains and metro rail use embedded signalling and door controllers. Medical: pacemaker, glucose meter, digital BP machine, infusion pump. Industry: garment factory sewing machines with servo motors, PLCs in a pharma plant, energy meters. Finance: the POS card machine in a shop, an ATM's card reader and cash dispenser, a bKash agent's fingerprint scanner. Agriculture: smart irrigation and pond aerator controllers, which we will build in the capstone.

Is a smartphone embedded? This is a good exam discussion. A phone has embedded systems inside it: the modem chip, the camera controller, the battery management chip, the touch controller each run their own firmware. But the phone as a whole runs a full operating system and lets you install any app, so it behaves like a general-purpose computer in your pocket. The safe answer is: a smartphone contains many embedded systems, but the phone as a whole is usually treated as a general-purpose computing device. The line between the two is blurry and keeps moving.

A little history: In 1971 Intel released the 4004, often called the first commercial microprocessor. It was designed for a calculator made by the Japanese company Busicom, a dedicated product, which makes it an embedded story from day one. Soon after came single-chip microcontrollers that put the CPU, memory and I/O on one chip, such as Intel's 8048 and later the famous 8051. Through the 1980s and 1990s, microcontrollers spread into cars, appliances and toys. Today, billions of microcontrollers are shipped every year, far more than PC and phone processors combined.

How it connects to what you learned before: In Microprocessors you programmed the 8086 and attached the 8255, 8253 and 8259 chips to it. That was a microprocessor system: the CPU alone needed several helper chips for ports, timers and interrupts. In Peripherals and Interfacing you met sensors, relays, ADCs, UART, SPI and I2C. In Operating Systems you learned scheduling and semaphores. This course stitches all of that into one product. Here the timer, ports, ADC and interrupt controller usually live inside one microcontroller chip, and you program them with C instead of assembly.

A tiny walk-through, the rice cooker: Power on. The firmware sets up the pins and timers, then enters its main loop. It reads the lid switch and the buttons. When you press Cook, it switches on the heater through a relay or a triac driver. It keeps reading a temperature sensor under the pot. While water remains, the temperature stays near 100 degrees Celsius. Once the water is absorbed, the pot temperature climbs above that. The firmware sees the rise, switches to Warm mode, and beeps. Inputs: buttons, lid switch, temperature. Outputs: heater, LEDs, buzzer. Logic: a small state machine with states Idle, Cooking, Warm. That is a complete embedded system.

In pseudo-code it looks like this: setup(); loop forever { read buttons; read temperature; if state is COOKING and temperature > threshold then state = WARM, heater = low, beep; update LEDs; }. Notice there is no exit. Notice also that the threshold is a number someone had to measure and calibrate on real pots. Real embedded work always involves the physical world, and the physical world never behaves exactly like the textbook.

Real life example 1, the prepaid electricity meter: Many homes in Bangladesh now have prepaid meters. Inside is a microcontroller connected to a metering chip that measures voltage and current, a small display, a keypad for typing the recharge token, and a relay that can cut the supply. The firmware keeps adding up energy used, subtracts it from the credit, checks that a typed token is valid, and opens the relay when credit runs out. It must never lose the balance during a power cut, so it saves important values in non-volatile memory. It must also resist tampering. Cost, reliability, security and real-time measurement all meet in one small box.

Real life example 2, a garment factory sewing machine: Modern industrial sewing machines in Gazipur and Ashulia factories use a servo motor with an embedded controller instead of an old clutch motor. The controller reads the foot pedal position, drives the motor at the requested speed, stops the needle in the up or down position precisely, and can trim thread automatically. Because the motor is driven only when needed, these machines save a lot of electricity compared with old motors that spun all day. Thousands of identical controllers, each doing one job well, all day, for years: that is embedded engineering.

What jobs and courses need this: Embedded engineers work at companies making consumer electronics, appliances, telecom equipment, medical devices, cars, drones and IoT products. In Bangladesh, local electronics manufacturers, IoT startups, power and energy companies and research labs need people who can write firmware and debug boards. The skills also feed into robotics, IoT, computer architecture research and even operating system work, because device drivers are embedded thinking applied inside a big OS.

The course map: We start with constraints and design metrics, then compare microprocessors, microcontrollers and SoCs, look inside a microcontroller, and meet the common families: AVR, ARM Cortex-M and ESP32. Then embedded C: types, bit manipulation, registers and volatile. Then the peripherals one by one: GPIO and debouncing, timers, PWM, ADC, interrupts, UART, SPI and I2C, sensors and actuators. Then the system concerns: power and sleep, watchdogs, memory and bootloaders. Then software structure: super-loop, RTOS, synchronization and real-time scheduling analysis. We finish with debugging and testing, IoT connectivity with safety and security, and a full smart irrigation capstone.

Common mistakes: Thinking embedded means small and simple. Some embedded systems, like a car's driver-assistance computer, are very complex. Thinking real-time means fast. It means predictable and on time. Thinking an Arduino board is the microcontroller. The board carries a microcontroller chip plus a USB interface, regulator and connectors. Thinking embedded software is just normal software on a small chip. It has to deal with timing, electrical noise, limited memory and the fact that it can never simply crash and show an error dialog.

What exams ask: Define an embedded system and give its characteristics. Differentiate embedded and general-purpose computers in a table. List application areas with examples. Explain what real-time and reactive mean. Draw a block diagram of a simple embedded system showing sensors, microcontroller, actuators, power supply and user interface, and explain each block. Short notes on firmware are also common.

Recap: An embedded system is a computer with a dedicated job, built inside a bigger product. It has hardware and firmware, it is usually reactive and often real-time, and it lives under tight limits on cost, power, size, memory and reliability. It is everywhere, from rice cookers to prepaid meters to factory machines. Next lesson we turn those limits into numbers engineers can actually compare.
key_points: An embedded system is hardware plus firmware built into a larger product to perform a dedicated function.
Firmware is the program stored in the chip's non-volatile memory; it starts at power-on and usually runs in an endless loop.
Embedded systems differ from general-purpose computers: fixed job, just-enough hardware, rarely changed software.
Most embedded systems are reactive (respond to events) and many are real-time (a late answer is a wrong answer).
Main constraints are cost, power, size, memory, reliability and harsh environments.
The Intel 4004 (1971) was designed for a Busicom calculator; single-chip microcontrollers like the 8048 and 8051 followed.
A smartphone contains many embedded systems but as a whole behaves like a general-purpose computer.
Typical blocks: sensors and inputs, microcontroller, actuators and outputs, power supply, user interface, communication.
lessons.tip: Every time you see an electronic product this week, ask three questions: what are its inputs, what are its outputs, and what decision does the hidden computer make in between? This habit is the core of embedded thinking.
lessons.task: Walk through your home and list at least ten devices that contain an embedded system. For two of them, draw a block diagram on paper with inputs, the microcontroller, outputs and power, and write the main loop in three or four lines of pseudo-code.

quiz.q: Which statement best defines an embedded system?
options: A computer built into a larger product to do a dedicated function
Any computer smaller than a laptop
A computer that can run any app the user installs
A server inside a data center
quiz.explain: An embedded system is hardware plus firmware dedicated to one function inside a bigger product.

quiz.q: What does real-time mean in embedded systems?
options: The device shows the current time
The result must be produced within a deadline, or it is wrong
quiz.explain: Real-time is about meeting deadlines predictably, not about raw speed.

quiz.q: What is firmware?
options: The plastic case of the device
The program stored permanently in the device's non-volatile memory
quiz.explain: Firmware is the software burned into flash that runs from power-on.

quiz.q: The Intel 4004 microprocessor was originally designed for what product?
quiz.explain: Intel designed the 4004 (1971) for a calculator made by Busicom.

quiz.q: Why is an Arduino Uno not the same thing as a microcontroller?
options: It is a board carrying a microcontroller plus USB interface, regulator and connectors
quiz.explain: The Uno is a development board; the microcontroller is the ATmega328P chip on it.

lessons.title: Characteristics, Constraints and Design Metrics
lessons.content:
Imagine two friends both want to sell a smart water pump controller to rooftop tank owners in Dhaka. Rafi designs a beautiful board with a big color touchscreen, Wi-Fi and a powerful 32-bit chip. Nadia designs a plain box with three LEDs, one button and a cheap 8-bit microcontroller. Rafi's box costs 4,000 taka to make, Nadia's costs 900. Both pump water. Which one wins? It depends on what the customer values, how many units will be sold, how long the design took, and how often each box fails. Embedded engineering is the art of answering that question with numbers instead of feelings. Those numbers are called design metrics.

What a design metric is: A design metric is a measurable feature of a system's implementation. For a sorting algorithm you measured time and memory. For an embedded system the list is longer, because you are designing a physical product that people buy, carry, power and trust. The common metrics are unit cost, NRE cost, size, performance, power and energy, flexibility, time-to-prototype, time-to-market, maintainability, correctness, reliability and safety. You cannot maximise all of them at once, which is why the design challenge is really an optimisation and trade-off problem.

Unit cost: Unit cost is the money spent to manufacture each copy of the product, not counting the one-time design work. It includes the microcontroller, sensors, passive parts, the printed circuit board, the enclosure, assembly, testing and packaging. If a product sells in large numbers, even 5 taka saved per unit matters a lot. This is why mass-market products use the smallest microcontroller that can do the job, and why engineers argue over removing a single resistor.

NRE cost: NRE stands for non-recurring engineering. It is the one-time cost of designing the system: engineer salaries, prototype boards, development tools, test equipment, certification and, for custom chips, mask costs. You pay NRE once, no matter how many units you sell afterwards. Once the design is finished, making another unit costs only the unit cost. So the real cost per product depends on volume: cost per product = NRE / N + unit cost, where N is the number of units sold.

Worked break-even example: Suppose Design A has NRE 50,000 dollars and unit cost 5 dollars, perhaps because it uses a custom, highly integrated board that took long to design. Design B has NRE 10,000 dollars and unit cost 9 dollars, perhaps because it uses an off-the-shelf module that is quick to design with but more expensive per piece. Total cost A = 50,000 + 5N, total cost B = 10,000 + 9N. They are equal when 50,000 + 5N = 10,000 + 9N, so 40,000 = 4N, and N = 10,000 units. At exactly 10,000 units both cost 100,000 dollars.

Reading the break-even: Below 10,000 units, Design B is cheaper. At 1,000 units, A costs 50 + 5 = 55 dollars per product while B costs 10 + 9 = 19 dollars per product. Above 10,000 units, Design A wins. At 20,000 units, A totals 50,000 + 100,000 = 150,000 dollars while B totals 10,000 + 180,000 = 190,000 dollars. The lesson is simple and very important: for small volumes, spend little on design and accept a higher unit price; for huge volumes, it pays to invest heavily in design to shave the unit cost. That is why a startup building 500 irrigation controllers uses ready-made modules, while a company making a million rice cookers designs a custom board.

Size and weight: Size is measured in physical space, and also in software as bytes of code and data, or in hardware as gates or board area. A hearing aid, a fitness band or a drone has strict size and weight limits. Smaller size often means more expensive parts, tighter PCB design and harder heat removal. On the software side, if your firmware grows from 30 KB to 40 KB, it no longer fits on a 32 KB chip and you must move to a bigger, more expensive one. Memory size directly turns into money.

Performance: Performance in embedded systems usually means two things. Latency, or response time, is how long from an input event to the output reaction, such as from pressing the brake pedal to the brake actuating. Throughput is how much work is done per unit time, such as samples processed per second or frames shown per second. A heart monitor may need modest throughput but strict latency on alarms. A camera needs high throughput. More performance usually costs more power and money, so engineers aim for enough performance, not maximum performance.

Power and energy: Power is the rate of using energy, measured in watts. Energy is power multiplied by time, measured in joules or, for batteries, in milliamp-hours at a given voltage. A device running at 3.3 V and drawing 10 mA uses 3.3 x 0.010 = 0.033 W, or 33 mW. A 2,000 mAh battery at a steady 10 mA would last 2,000 / 10 = 200 hours, a little over 8 days. Power matters for heat, because a sealed box in a Bangladesh summer cannot get rid of much heat, and energy matters for battery life. Lesson 18 shows how sleep modes stretch that 8 days into months.

Flexibility: Flexibility is the ability to change the functionality without a large NRE cost. A design built around a programmable microcontroller is flexible: you change the firmware, maybe even over the air. A design built around a custom chip or fixed logic is not. Flexibility protects you when customers ask for new features or when a bug is found after shipping. It usually costs some unit price and some performance, which is the classic trade-off between software and dedicated hardware.

Time-to-prototype and time-to-market: Time-to-prototype is how long it takes to build a working version you can test and show. Time-to-market is how long until the product is actually on the shelf. Markets have windows. A product for Eid, for the summer fan season or before a competitor launches must arrive on time. Arriving months late can lose a large share of the possible revenue, even if the product is excellent. This is a big reason why companies use development boards, ready-made modules and existing libraries: they buy speed with a higher unit cost.

Maintainability: Maintainability is how easy it is to modify and fix the system after its first release, especially by engineers who were not the original designers. Clean code, comments, version control, modular design, and the ability to update firmware in the field all improve it. A product that sells for ten years will probably be maintained by several different people. Cheap shortcuts in the first version become expensive later.

Correctness, reliability and safety: Correctness means the system does what the specification says. Reliability means it keeps doing it over time, under real conditions, without failures. A common measure is MTBF, mean time between failures. Another is availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), where MTTR is the mean time to repair. If MTBF is 999 hours and MTTR is 1 hour, availability is 999 / 1,000 = 99.9 percent. Safety means the system does not cause harm, even when something goes wrong. A toy can be allowed to fail; a pacemaker, a lift controller or a train brake cannot. Safety-critical products need extra design effort, testing and often formal certification.

The environment as a constraint: Embedded products live outside air-conditioned offices. In Bangladesh they face 40 degree heat, very high humidity in the monsoon, dust, salt air near the coast, voltage that sags and spikes, frequent power cuts and lightning in the rainy season. A solar charge controller on a tin roof in Rajshahi or a sensor in a shrimp farm in Khulna must survive that. Designers pick components rated for the temperature range, add surge protection, coat boards against moisture, and write firmware that handles brown-outs and sudden resets gracefully.

Why metrics compete: Improving one metric often hurts another. Adding Wi-Fi improves flexibility and features but raises cost and power. Using a faster processor improves performance but uses more power and costs more. Squeezing the size raises unit cost and NRE. Choosing a custom chip cuts unit cost and power but raises NRE and time-to-market and kills flexibility. Think of the metrics as a set of connected springs: push one down and others pop up. Good design is picking the balance that fits the product, the customer and the volume.

Real life example 1, Rafi versus Nadia again: The customers are flat owners who want the pump to switch on when the tank is low and off when full, cheaply and reliably. Nadia's 900 taka box with an 8-bit microcontroller does exactly that, uses little power and has few parts that can fail. Rafi's 4,000 taka box adds a touchscreen and Wi-Fi that most customers do not need, more parts to break, more firmware bugs and a longer development time. For this market Nadia's design scores better on unit cost, reliability and time-to-market. If later customers ask for phone alerts, a version with an ESP32 can be added at a higher price.

Scoring the trade-off with a weighted table: When several metrics matter, engineers often build a simple decision matrix. Give each metric a weight that adds up to 1, for example cost 0.4, reliability 0.3, power 0.2 and features 0.1. Then score each design from 1 to 10 on every metric. Nadia scores 9, 8, 8 and 4, so her total is 0.4 x 9 + 0.3 x 8 + 0.2 x 8 + 0.1 x 4 = 3.6 + 2.4 + 1.6 + 0.4 = 8.0. Rafi scores 4, 6, 5 and 9, giving 1.6 + 1.8 + 1.0 + 0.9 = 5.3. The table does not make the decision magically, because the weights are a judgement, but it forces the team to say out loud what matters and makes the discussion honest.

Real life example 2, a digital weighing scale for the bazar: A fish seller in Karwan Bazar needs a scale that is accurate, survives water splashes, runs all day on a rechargeable battery during load shedding, and costs little. The design team chooses a low-power microcontroller with a built-in ADC or a dedicated weighing ADC, a simple segment display, and a sealed keypad. They skip Bluetooth because it adds cost and power that the seller will not pay for. Each choice is a trade-off guided by metrics: unit cost, energy, reliability in a wet environment, and correctness of the reading.

Common mistakes: Mixing up NRE and unit cost. NRE is paid once, unit cost is paid for every unit. Forgetting that the right choice depends on volume. Confusing power and energy: a device can have low power but drain a lot of energy if it runs for a long time. Thinking more performance is always better. Ignoring time-to-market: a perfect design that arrives a year late can lose to a decent one that arrives now. Treating reliability as an afterthought rather than a design goal from the first day.

What exams ask: List and define common design metrics. Explain the design metric competition or trade-off with examples. Solve a break-even problem: given NRE and unit costs of two designs, find the volume at which they cost the same and say which to choose for a given volume. Explain time-to-market and why it matters. Compute power or battery life from voltage, current and capacity. Write short notes on reliability, MTBF and availability.

Recap: Design metrics turn vague goals into numbers. Unit cost is per piece, NRE is one-time, and total cost is NRE + unit cost x N, which gives a break-even volume, 10,000 units in our example. Size, performance, power and energy, flexibility, time-to-market, maintainability, reliability and safety all compete. Good embedded design chooses the right balance for the product and its volume. Next lesson we look at the brains we can choose: microprocessors, microcontrollers and SoCs.
key_points: A design metric is a measurable feature of an implementation: unit cost, NRE, size, performance, power, flexibility, time-to-market, maintainability, reliability, safety.
Unit cost is paid for every unit; NRE (non-recurring engineering) is the one-time design cost.
Total cost = NRE + unit cost x N; cost per product = NRE / N + unit cost.
Worked break-even: NRE 50,000 + 5N equals NRE 10,000 + 9N at N = 10,000 units; low volume favours low NRE, high volume favours low unit cost.
Performance means latency (response time) and throughput; aim for enough, not maximum.
Power is a rate (W); energy is power x time; a 2,000 mAh battery at 10 mA lasts about 200 hours.
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR); 999 h and 1 h give 99.9 percent.
Metrics compete: improving one usually worsens another, so design is a trade-off.
lessons.tip: Whenever you solve a break-even problem, also sketch the two straight lines (total cost against N) on graph paper. Seeing where they cross makes the answer obvious and helps you explain it in the exam.
lessons.task: Pick any gadget you own, such as a power bank or a remote. Estimate its unit cost from its shop price, list three design metrics that probably mattered most to its designers, and write one trade-off they made (for example: no display to save cost and power).

quiz.q: What is NRE cost?
options: The cost paid again for each unit
The yearly electricity bill of the factory
The one-time cost of designing the system
quiz.explain: Non-recurring engineering cost is paid once for design, tools and prototypes.

quiz.q: Design A: NRE 50,000, unit 5. Design B: NRE 10,000, unit 9. At what volume do they cost the same?
Using the same two designs, which is cheaper for 1,000 units?
quiz.explain: Below the 10,000-unit break-even, the low-NRE Design B is cheaper (19 vs 55 per product).

quiz.q: A device at 3.3 V draws 10 mA continuously from a 2,000 mAh battery. Roughly how long does it last?
quiz.explain: Battery life is about 2,000 mAh / 10 mA = 200 hours.

quiz.q: Which pair of metrics usually conflicts when you add Wi-Fi to a product?
options: Correctness and size of the label
NRE and the colour of the case
quiz.explain: Wi-Fi adds features but raises unit cost and power consumption.

lessons.title: Microprocessor vs Microcontroller vs SoC (and DSP, FPGA, ASIC)
lessons.content:
Think about three ways to get lunch. You can buy raw rice, dal, vegetables, spices and gas, and cook everything yourself in your own kitchen: total freedom, but you need many separate things and a lot of space. You can buy a ready meal box from a shop: rice, dal and a piece of chicken in one packet, cheap and quick, but you get what is in the box. Or you can go to a big restaurant that has many cooks, ovens and a full menu under one roof. A microprocessor system is the first way, a microcontroller is the meal box, and a system-on-chip is the restaurant. Choosing the brain of an embedded product starts with knowing which kind of lunch you need.

What a microprocessor is, a quick recap: A microprocessor (MPU) is a CPU on a single chip: registers, ALU, control unit and bus interface. You met the 8086 in the Microprocessors course. On its own it cannot do anything useful. It needs external memory chips for program and data, a clock generator (the 8284 for the 8086), and separate chips for I/O ports (8255), timers (8253) and interrupt control (8259). All of these sit on a board, wired together through the address, data and control buses. The result is powerful and flexible, but it uses many chips, a big board, more power and more money.

What a microcontroller is: A microcontroller (MCU) puts a complete small computer on one chip: a CPU core, flash memory for the program, SRAM for data, often EEPROM for settings, a clock source, and a set of peripherals such as GPIO pins, timers, PWM, an ADC, UART, SPI, I2C and an interrupt controller. You give it power, maybe a crystal and a few capacitors, and it runs. The ATmega328P on an Arduino Uno is a classic example: 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM and 1 KB EEPROM on one chip, running at 16 MHz on the Uno board. Everything the 8086 needed five or six extra chips for is already inside.

Why microcontrollers dominate embedded: One chip means a small board, fewer connections that can fail, low cost, and low power. Peripherals are designed to work with the core, so a timer can trigger the ADC, or the UART can raise an interrupt, without any external glue logic. Many MCUs run on a few milliamps and sleep on microamps. They start running code within milliseconds of power-on, with no operating system to boot. For a rice cooker, a remote control, a prepaid meter or a pump controller, that is exactly what you want.

The price of integration: The MCU's memory is fixed at manufacture. If your program needs 40 KB and the chip has 32 KB, you cannot add a memory chip to the bus the way you could with an 8086 system; you choose a bigger MCU instead. MCU CPUs are also modest: tens to a few hundred megahertz, usually without the memory management unit needed by full operating systems like Linux. Most MCUs therefore run bare-metal firmware or a small real-time operating system, not Linux or Windows.

What a system-on-chip is: A system-on-chip (SoC) integrates a whole complex system on one die: often several powerful CPU cores, a GPU, memory controllers for external DRAM, video and image processors, USB, display and camera interfaces, and sometimes radios like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or a cellular modem. The chip in your smartphone is an SoC. The Broadcom chip on a Raspberry Pi is an SoC, which is why a Pi can run full Linux with a desktop. Strictly, a microcontroller is also a small system on a chip, and Espressif describes the ESP32 as an SoC because it adds Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios to the MCU. In practice, when people say SoC they usually mean the larger, application-class chips.

MCU versus Linux-class SoC in practice: An MCU board starts in milliseconds and draws milliamps; a Linux board typically takes seconds to boot and draws hundreds of milliamps or more. The MCU gives precise, predictable timing because your code controls everything. Linux gives networking stacks, file systems, Python, cameras and displays, but its timing is less predictable because the OS decides when your program runs. A common modern design uses both: a Linux SoC for the user interface and cloud connection, and a small MCU beside it for the motor, sensors and anything with tight timing.

Counting chips, a worked comparison: Suppose you build a traffic light controller with an 8086, as students did in many old lab manuals. You need the 8086 itself, the 8284 clock generator, address latches, an EPROM for the program, a RAM chip, an address decoder such as the 74LS138, an 8255 for the lamp outputs, an 8253 for timing and perhaps an 8259 for the pedestrian button interrupt. That is around ten chips, a large board and hundreds of wires. With an ATmega328P the same job needs one chip, a crystal, a few capacitors and the lamp drivers. The firmware does the timing with an on-chip timer and reads the button with a pin-change interrupt. Same function, a fraction of the parts, cost and power.

Some real numbers side by side: The ATmega328P runs at up to 20 MHz (16 MHz on the Uno) with 2 KB of SRAM. A typical STM32 microcontroller with a Cortex-M core runs at tens to a few hundred megahertz with tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM. The ESP32 runs at up to 240 MHz with about 520 KB of on-chip SRAM plus Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The Raspberry Pi 4 SoC has four Cortex-A72 cores at 1.5 GHz and uses external RAM of 1 to 8 GB depending on the model. Each step up the list adds speed, memory and software richness, and also cost, power and boot time.

Harvard versus von Neumann, a recap: In Computer Architecture you learned that a von Neumann machine uses one memory and one bus for both instructions and data, while a Harvard machine has separate memories or buses for instructions and data. Many microcontrollers use Harvard-style designs. The AVR in the Arduino Uno keeps program code in flash and data in SRAM in separate address spaces, so it can fetch the next instruction while reading data. Many ARM Cortex-M chips have separate instruction and data buses internally while still showing one unified address map to the programmer. The benefit is speed without a big cache.

DSP, the maths specialist: A digital signal processor is a processor optimised for signal processing maths, such as filters and transforms. Its key trick is the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation, which computes a = a + b x c, typically in one cycle, along with special addressing for circular buffers. Audio equipment, modems, hearing aids and motor control often use DSPs. Today the line is blurry: ARM Cortex-M4 and M7 cores include DSP instructions, and many MCUs are sold as digital signal controllers, mixing MCU peripherals with DSP abilities.

FPGA, hardware you can rewire: A field-programmable gate array is a chip full of configurable logic blocks and programmable connections. Instead of writing instructions for a CPU, you describe a digital circuit in a hardware description language like Verilog or VHDL, and the tools configure the chip to become that circuit. Because the logic runs in true parallel, an FPGA can process very fast signals, such as video or high-speed communication, with exact timing. FPGAs cost more per unit and use more power than MCUs, and designing for them is harder, but they are great for prototyping custom hardware and for low-volume high-performance products.

ASIC, the custom chip: An application-specific integrated circuit is a chip designed for one product. Once made, it gives the lowest unit cost, the lowest power and the highest performance for that job. But it has enormous NRE: design, verification and mask costs can be very high, and a bug in the silicon means a new manufacturing run. Remember the break-even lesson: ASICs make sense only at very high volumes or when nothing else can meet the performance or power target. The chips inside cheap calculators, digital watches and many toys are often ASICs.

Placing them on a map: Think of two axes, flexibility and efficiency. A general-purpose MPU or SoC running software is the most flexible and the least efficient per job. An MCU is flexible in software and efficient in cost and power for control tasks. A DSP is efficient at signal maths. An FPGA lets you rebuild the hardware itself, with good performance but higher unit cost. An ASIC is the most efficient and the least flexible. Each step towards efficiency usually means higher NRE and longer time-to-market, which links directly back to the design metrics of lesson 2.

How to choose, step by step: First ask what the product must do and how fast. Simple control with sensors, buttons and motors: an MCU. Needs Wi-Fi or Bluetooth cheaply: an MCU with built-in radio, like the ESP32. Needs a camera, a touchscreen with rich graphics, or full Linux software: an SoC board or module. Needs heavy real-time signal maths: a DSP or an MCU with DSP instructions. Needs custom high-speed parallel logic: an FPGA. Millions of identical units where every cent and microwatt counts: consider an ASIC. Then check volume, power budget, cost target, available tools and your team's skills.

Real life example 1, a ceiling fan regulator versus a smart TV: A remote-controlled fan regulator only needs to read an infrared receiver, drive a triac or motor driver at a few speed levels, and remember the last setting. A cheap 8-bit MCU does it with plenty of room left. A smart TV must decode high-definition video, run apps like YouTube, draw a menu with smooth graphics and connect to Wi-Fi. That needs an SoC with multiple cores, a GPU and video decoders, running a full operating system. Both are embedded systems, but their brains are worlds apart.

Real life example 2, a bKash agent's point-of-sale terminal: A modern Android POS terminal used in shops runs an SoC, because it shows apps, talks over 4G or Wi-Fi and prints receipts. Inside, the card reader and the secure payment parts are often handled by a separate secure microcontroller that guards keys and handles card data. The receipt printer may have its own small controller too. One device, three kinds of brains: an SoC for the rich interface, a secure MCU for trust, and simple controllers for mechanical parts. This mix is very common in real products.

Common mistakes: Calling an Arduino or a Raspberry Pi a microcontroller without thinking. The Uno is a board with an MCU; the Raspberry Pi is a board with a Linux-capable SoC; the Raspberry Pi Pico, confusingly, is a board with an MCU, the RP2040. Thinking a microprocessor is always better because it is faster: for controlling a pump, it is wasteful. Thinking an FPGA is a processor: it is configurable hardware, although you can build a soft processor inside it. Forgetting that the right choice depends on volume, power and time-to-market, not just speed.

What exams ask: Differentiate microprocessor and microcontroller in a table (on-chip memory and peripherals, cost, power, board size, typical applications, examples). Define SoC with examples. Explain Harvard versus von Neumann and why MCUs often use Harvard designs. Write short notes on DSP, FPGA and ASIC, and compare them on flexibility, NRE, unit cost, performance and power. Choose a suitable processor type for a given application and justify the choice.

Recap: A microprocessor is a CPU chip that needs many helper chips. A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip, cheap, low power and perfect for control. An SoC integrates a complex system with powerful cores, graphics and often radios, and usually runs a full OS. DSPs specialise in signal maths, FPGAs let you build custom hardware, and ASICs give the best efficiency at the cost of huge NRE. Next lesson we open up a microcontroller and look at every block inside.
key_points: A microprocessor (like the 8086) is a CPU chip that needs external memory, clock, I/O, timer and interrupt chips.
A microcontroller puts CPU, flash, SRAM, often EEPROM, clock and peripherals on one chip: small, cheap, low power.
An SoC integrates a complex system (multiple cores, GPU, memory controller, often radios) and usually runs a full OS like Linux.
MCUs boot in milliseconds and give predictable timing; Linux SoCs give rich software but less predictable timing.
Many MCUs use Harvard-style separate instruction and data paths; the AVR keeps code in flash and data in SRAM.
A DSP is optimised for multiply-accumulate signal maths; Cortex-M4/M7 include DSP instructions.
FPGAs are reconfigurable hardware described in Verilog/VHDL; ASICs are custom chips with high NRE and the lowest unit cost at volume.
Choose by job, timing, power, volume and time-to-market, not by raw speed.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page comparison table with columns MPU, MCU, SoC, DSP, FPGA, ASIC and rows flexibility, NRE, unit cost, power, typical example. Filling it from memory is one of the best revision exercises for this topic.
lessons.task: Search the model number of any two devices you own (for example your phone and your Wi-Fi router) and find out what main chip they use. Decide whether each is an MCU or an SoC, and write one sentence explaining why.

quiz.q: Which statement about a microcontroller is correct?
options: It always needs external RAM and ROM chips
It contains CPU, memory and peripherals on one chip
It is the same as an FPGA
quiz.explain: An MCU integrates the CPU core, flash, SRAM and peripherals such as timers and ADC on a single chip.

quiz.q: Which device is best described as a Linux-capable SoC board?
quiz.explain: The Raspberry Pi uses a Broadcom SoC and runs Linux; the Uno and Pico carry microcontrollers.

quiz.q: What operation is a DSP especially optimised for?
quiz.explain: DSPs execute multiply-accumulate quickly, the core of filters and transforms.

quiz.q: Why does an ASIC make sense only at very high volume?
options: Because it has the highest unit cost
Because its NRE is very high and must be spread over many units
Because it cannot be manufactured in small numbers
Because it is slower than an MCU
quiz.explain: ASICs have huge design and mask costs; only large volumes bring cost per unit down.

quiz.q: A product needs a touchscreen with rich graphics, a camera and Linux software. Which brain fits best?
quiz.explain: Rich graphics, cameras and Linux need the cores, GPU and memory controllers of an application SoC.

lessons.title: Inside a Microcontroller: Core, Memories, Clock, Reset and Peripherals
lessons.content:
Imagine a small but complete village packed onto one tiny island. There is a headman who makes decisions, a library that keeps the permanent rules, a notice board where people scribble today's work, a locker that remembers a few things even through storms, a clock tower that keeps everyone in rhythm, a bell that restarts the village day, and many workshops: a blacksmith, a post office, a measuring station. A microcontroller is exactly such a village on a chip a few millimetres wide. In this lesson we walk around the island block by block, using the ATmega328P from the Arduino Uno as our guide and the STM32 and ESP32 as neighbours.

The big picture: Every microcontroller has the same main blocks. A CPU core that executes instructions. Non-volatile program memory, almost always flash. Volatile data memory, SRAM. Often a small EEPROM for settings. A clock system that creates the timing heartbeat. A reset system that starts everything in a known state. Internal buses that connect the core to memories and peripherals. And a set of peripherals: GPIO ports, timers, PWM, ADC, serial interfaces, an interrupt controller and a watchdog. All of them reach the outside world through a limited number of pins.

The CPU core: The core fetches instructions from flash, decodes them, and executes them using registers and an ALU, just like the CPUs you studied in Architecture. The ATmega328P has an 8-bit AVR core with 32 general-purpose 8-bit registers, and most of its instructions execute in a single clock cycle, so at 16 MHz it performs close to 16 million simple instructions per second. An STM32 uses a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M core, which handles 32-bit numbers in one step and usually runs faster. The core also has a program counter, a stack pointer and a status register with flags such as zero and carry, similar to the 8086 flags you met earlier.

Flash memory, the library: Flash holds your program and constant data. It keeps its contents without power, which is why the device works the moment it is switched on. The ATmega328P has 32 KB of flash. On an Arduino Uno a small bootloader occupies the top 512 bytes, so about 31.5 KB is left for your sketch. Flash is read quickly but written slowly, and only in blocks, and it wears out after many erase cycles, around 10,000 for this chip. So flash is for code and rarely changed data, not for values that change every second.

SRAM, the notice board: SRAM holds variables, the stack and any buffers while the program runs. It is fast and can be written as often as you like, but it forgets everything when power goes off. The ATmega328P has only 2 KB, which is 2,048 bytes. That is tiny: an array of 500 float values at 4 bytes each already needs 2,000 bytes and leaves almost nothing for the stack. Running out of SRAM is one of the most common reasons an Arduino program behaves strangely, because the stack silently grows into the variables. Embedded programmers count bytes the way a careful student counts pocket money.

EEPROM, the locker: EEPROM is non-volatile like flash, but it can be written one byte at a time and has higher endurance, about 100,000 write cycles per cell on the ATmega328P, which has 1 KB of it. It is used for settings that must survive a power cut: a calibration factor, a user's chosen pump threshold, a device ID, a counter of how many times the machine ran. Many 32-bit chips like the STM32 and ESP32 do not have true EEPROM and instead emulate it in a reserved part of flash, using wear levelling tricks you will meet in lesson 20.

The memory map: The CPU sees memories and peripheral registers as addresses. On the ATmega328P, the data address space starts with the 32 general registers, then 64 I/O registers, then 160 extended I/O registers, and SRAM begins at address 0x0100 and ends at 0x08FF. Flash lives in a separate program address space, the Harvard idea from the last lesson. On Cortex-M chips everything shares one 4 GB address map: flash near address 0x0000 0000 or 0x0800 0000 on STM32, SRAM at 0x2000 0000, and peripheral registers starting at 0x4000 0000. Knowing the map is the key to lesson 8, where we touch registers directly.

The clock system, the clock tower: Every action inside the chip happens on clock edges, so the clock decides speed and also power. There are several sources. An external quartz crystal, or a cheaper ceramic resonator, gives an accurate frequency; the Uno runs its ATmega328P at 16 MHz this way. An internal RC oscillator needs no external parts but is less accurate; the ATmega328P has an 8 MHz internal oscillator, and it ships from the factory with a divide-by-8 setting, so a brand-new chip runs at 1 MHz until you change its fuses. Many 32-bit MCUs add a PLL, phase-locked loop, which multiplies a slow clock up; a classic STM32F103 setup multiplies an 8 MHz crystal by 9 to get 72 MHz. Prescalers then divide the main clock for each peripheral.

Why clock accuracy matters: A UART at 9,600 baud expects each bit to last a precise time. If your internal oscillator is off by several percent, serial data turns into garbage, which is why serial links and real-time clocks usually rely on crystals. Timing loops, PWM frequency and ADC sampling all scale with the clock too. Many chips also have a separate 32.768 kHz crystal input for a low-power real-time clock, because 32,768 is 2 to the power 15, so a 15-stage binary counter produces exactly one tick per second.

Voltage and speed: The ATmega328P can run from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, but the maximum safe clock depends on the voltage: up to 4 MHz at 1.8 V, up to 10 MHz at 2.7 V, and up to 20 MHz at 4.5 V and above. This is why a 3.3 V Arduino-style board often runs the same chip at 8 MHz while the 5 V Uno runs it at 16 MHz. Lower voltage also saves power, a link to lesson 18.

Reset, the village bell: Reset forces the chip into a known starting state: registers cleared, peripherals off, the program counter pointing to the reset vector. The ATmega328P has four reset sources. Power-on reset happens when the supply first rises. External reset happens when the RESET pin is pulled low, the button on the Uno. Watchdog reset happens when the firmware fails to feed the watchdog timer in time. Brown-out reset happens when the supply voltage falls below a safe level, so the CPU does not run with corrupted logic. A register called MCUSR records which source caused the last reset, which is very useful when debugging a device that restarts mysteriously in the field.

Peripherals, the workshops: The ATmega328P in its 28-pin package has 23 general-purpose I/O lines in three ports (B, C and D). It has two 8-bit timers and one 16-bit timer, which together can generate six PWM outputs. It has a 10-bit ADC with six input channels on the 28-pin package, an analog comparator, one USART for serial, an SPI port, a two-wire interface (TWI, compatible with I2C), a watchdog timer and an interrupt system with 26 vectors. An STM32 or ESP32 has many more of each, plus DMA controllers and, on the ESP32, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios.

Pins and alternate functions: There are never enough pins for every peripheral, so pins are shared. A pin is plain GPIO by default, and when you enable a peripheral it takes over the pin. On the ATmega328P, pin PD0 is also the UART receive line RXD and PD1 is the transmit line TXD, which is why using digital pins 0 and 1 on an Uno interferes with uploading and Serial. PB3 is also MOSI for SPI and a PWM output. PC0 to PC5 are also ADC inputs 0 to 5. On STM32 a multiplexer lets you choose among many alternate functions per pin. Planning which peripheral uses which pin is one of the first design steps for any board.

Reading a datasheet: The datasheet is the microcontroller's bible, often hundreds of pages. Do not read it front to back. Start with the features summary on the first page: memory sizes, peripherals, voltage and speed. Then the pin configuration and block diagram. Then the electrical characteristics, especially absolute maximum ratings; for the ATmega328P the absolute maximum DC current per I/O pin is 40 mA, and you should design well below that. Finally, for each peripheral you use, read its chapter and its register description. ARM-based chips split this into a datasheet for the specific part and a long reference manual for the whole family.

Real life example 1, choosing an MCU for a classroom attendance device: A university in Dhaka wants a card-tap attendance box. Requirements: read an RFID card over SPI, show the name on a small LCD over I2C, store up to 2,000 records when the internet is down, and send records over Wi-Fi. Walk through the blocks: SPI and I2C are needed, so check peripherals. 2,000 records of 16 bytes each are 32,000 bytes, far more than 2 KB of SRAM, and they must survive power cuts, so they go to flash or an external memory. Wi-Fi is needed, so an ESP32 with its built-in radio and megabytes of external flash fits far better than an ATmega328P.

Real life example 2, the remote of an air conditioner: The remote needs a keypad, an infrared LED driven at a carrier frequency by a timer, a small segment LCD, and two AAA cells that should last a year or more. A tiny low-power 8-bit or 32-bit MCU with a timer, a few GPIO pins and an LCD driver is ideal. The chip spends almost all its time in deep sleep, wakes on a key press interrupt, sends the code, and sleeps again. Here the important blocks are the low-power clock, sleep modes and wake-up interrupts, not raw speed.

Common mistakes: Mixing up flash, SRAM and EEPROM, especially thinking variables live in flash. Forgetting that a new ATmega328P runs at 1 MHz from the internal oscillator until its fuses are changed. Using pins 0 and 1 on an Uno for buttons and then wondering why Serial breaks. Ignoring the voltage and speed limits, or the per-pin current limit, and damaging a chip. Assuming every MCU has true EEPROM. Reading the datasheet only after the board is built, when the pin plan is already wrong.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the block diagram of a microcontroller. Compare flash, SRAM and EEPROM in a table (volatility, write method, endurance, use). List clock sources and compare crystal and RC oscillator. Explain reset sources and the role of brown-out reset. Describe the ATmega328P features: memory sizes, timers, ADC, serial interfaces. Explain why pins have alternate functions and what that means for design.

Recap: A microcontroller is a village on a chip. The core executes instructions; flash stores the program; SRAM holds variables and the stack; EEPROM keeps settings through power cuts; the clock system sets speed through crystals, RC oscillators, PLLs and prescalers; reset puts everything in a known state from four sources; and peripherals do the real-world work through shared pins. The ATmega328P gives 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM and 1 KB EEPROM at 16 MHz on the Uno. Next we meet the major microcontroller families and how to pick one.
key_points: Main MCU blocks: CPU core, flash (program), SRAM (data and stack), EEPROM (settings), clock, reset, internal buses, peripherals and pins.
ATmega328P: 8-bit AVR core with 32 registers, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 16 MHz on the Uno; most instructions take one cycle.
Flash is non-volatile and block-written (about 10,000 cycles); SRAM is fast and volatile; EEPROM is byte-writable with about 100,000 cycles.
Clock sources: crystal or resonator (accurate), internal RC (no parts, less accurate), PLL to multiply (8 MHz x 9 = 72 MHz on STM32F103), prescalers to divide.
A new ATmega328P runs at 1 MHz (8 MHz internal RC divided by 8) until its fuses are changed.
Reset sources: power-on, external pin, watchdog and brown-out; MCUSR records the cause.
Pins are shared between GPIO and alternate functions (e.g. PD0/PD1 are UART RX/TX), so pin planning is an early design step.
Read datasheets selectively: features, pinout, block diagram, absolute maximum ratings, then each peripheral's chapter.
lessons.tip: When you start with any new microcontroller, make a one-page cheat sheet: memory sizes, clock source and speed, voltage range, maximum pin current, and a pin table with alternate functions. You will use that page more than the whole datasheet.
lessons.task: Find the ATmega328P datasheet online (or the pinout diagram of an Arduino Uno) and, on paper, draw the chip's block diagram with core, flash, SRAM, EEPROM, clock, reset and at least six peripherals. Then mark which Uno pins are shared with UART, SPI and the ADC.

quiz.q: Where are local variables and the stack stored while an AVR program runs?
quiz.explain: SRAM is the volatile working memory for variables, buffers and the stack.

quiz.q: How much SRAM does the ATmega328P have?
quiz.explain: The ATmega328P has 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM and 1 KB EEPROM.

quiz.q: Which memory is best for a calibration value that changes rarely and must survive power cuts, written byte by byte?
quiz.explain: EEPROM is non-volatile, byte-writable and has higher endurance than flash.

quiz.q: What is the role of a brown-out reset?
options: Reset the chip when the supply voltage drops below a safe level
quiz.explain: Brown-out detection holds the CPU in reset when voltage is too low to run reliably.

quiz.q: A classic STM32F103 uses an 8 MHz crystal and a PLL multiplier of 9. What is the system clock?
quiz.explain: The PLL multiplies the input: 8 MHz x 9 = 72 MHz.

lessons.title: Microcontroller Families: 8051, PIC, AVR, ARM Cortex-M and ESP32
lessons.content:
Walk into any electronics market in Dhaka, say Patuatuli or the shops around Elephant Road and the Stadium market, and ask for a microcontroller board. The shopkeeper will ask you back: Arduino Uno? Nano? ESP32? Blue Pill? Each of these names hides a different chip family, made by a different company, with a different CPU inside. For a beginner this zoo of names is confusing. In this lesson we sort the zoo into a few families, see what makes each one special, and learn a simple way to choose. We stay at the concept level: you do not need to memorise every part number, only understand the big differences.

What a family is: A microcontroller family is a group of chips that share the same CPU core and the same style of peripherals, but differ in memory size, pin count, speed and price. A company designs one core and then sells dozens of variants: one with 8 KB flash and 20 pins for a toy, one with 256 KB flash and 100 pins for an industrial controller. Code written for one member usually moves to another member with small changes. So when you learn one family well, you have really learned a whole shelf of chips.

The two big axes: Two questions separate most families. First, the word size of the CPU: 8-bit, 16-bit or 32-bit. An 8-bit CPU works on 8 bits at a time in its registers and ALU; adding two 32-bit numbers takes it several instructions. A 32-bit CPU does that in one. Second, who owns the core design: some companies design their own core (for example AVR by Atmel, now part of Microchip), while many others license a ready-made core, mostly from ARM, and add their own peripherals around it. Keep these two axes in mind and every family below falls into place.

The 8051, the grandfather: Intel introduced the 8051 in 1980. It is an 8-bit microcontroller with a Harvard style memory layout: separate program memory and data memory. The original had 4 KB of on-chip ROM, 128 bytes of RAM, four 8-bit I/O ports, two 16-bit timers and a serial port. Intel stopped making it long ago, but the design was so popular that many other companies still make 8051-compatible chips, and many universities, including several in Bangladesh, still teach it in labs. Its assembly language feels close to the 8085 and 8086 style you met in the Microprocessors course. Today it is mainly found inside cheap appliances and as a small core hidden inside bigger chips.

PIC, the workhorse from Microchip: Microchip's PIC family is another long-lived 8-bit line, with 16-bit and 32-bit members added later. PICs are known for being cheap, robust and available in very small packages, even with only 6 or 8 pins. You will find them in remote controls, chargers and small industrial boards. They come with Microchip's own tools (MPLAB IDE and the XC compilers). For a student the main lesson from PIC is that a tiny chip with a few hundred bytes of RAM can still run a complete product.

AVR and the Arduino world: AVR is an 8-bit RISC family designed by Atmel, which Microchip bought in 2016. Most AVR instructions run in a single clock cycle, and it has 32 general-purpose registers, which made it friendly to C compilers. The most famous member is the ATmega328P, the chip on the Arduino Uno and Nano: 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, running at 16 MHz on those boards. Smaller ATtiny chips have as few as 8 pins.

Board vs chip vs IDE: Students often mix up three different things called Arduino. The chip is the ATmega328P, made by Microchip. The board is the Arduino Uno: a PCB with the chip, a 16 MHz crystal, a voltage regulator, a USB-to-serial converter and header pins. The software is the Arduino IDE plus the Arduino core library, which gives you easy functions like pinMode, digitalWrite and delay, and hides the register details. Arduino is not a chip family at all; it is an ecosystem. Today the same Arduino functions also run on ARM boards and on ESP32, because people wrote Arduino cores for them. Under the friendly functions, the compiler still produces normal machine code for whichever chip is on the board.

Why 8-bit is still alive: If 32-bit chips exist, why would anyone use 8-bit? Because many jobs are tiny. A rice cooker that reads one temperature sensor and switches one heater needs no fast maths. An 8-bit chip is simple, tolerates 5 V supplies on many models, has a clean and well understood datasheet, and is cheap in large volumes. Millions of 8-bit MCUs still ship every year. But the price gap has shrunk so much that for new designs many engineers now start with a small 32-bit chip anyway.

ARM Cortex-M, the 32-bit standard: ARM is a British company that does not manufacture chips itself. It designs CPU cores and licenses them to companies such as STMicroelectronics, NXP, Texas Instruments, Nordic, Microchip and Raspberry Pi. Its microcontroller cores are called Cortex-M. Cortex-M0 and M0+ are the smallest and cheapest, for simple low-power jobs. Cortex-M3 is the classic mid-range core. Cortex-M4 adds DSP instructions and, in most chips, a single-precision floating-point unit, useful for audio, motor control and filters. Cortex-M7 is the high-performance member. All of them are 32-bit, and all share one interrupt controller design called the NVIC and one programming style called CMSIS, which we will meet when we discuss registers and interrupts.

STM32 as an example: STMicroelectronics sells the STM32 family, a huge range of Cortex-M chips. The STM32F103, found on the cheap Blue Pill board, uses a Cortex-M3 running up to 72 MHz, with 64 KB flash and 20 KB SRAM on the common version. Compare that with the ATmega328P: about four and a half times the clock, a 32-bit core instead of 8-bit, and ten times the RAM, often for a similar board price. That is why many university projects in Bangladesh move from Arduino Uno to STM32 once they need more speed or more pins.

ESP32, the connected one: The ESP32 from Espressif Systems is a system-on-chip with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth built in. The original ESP32 has a dual-core Tensilica Xtensa LX6 CPU running up to 240 MHz and 520 KB of SRAM, with program code kept in an external flash chip that sits in the same module. It has many peripherals: ADC, DAC, PWM, UART, SPI, I2C, touch sensing. Because Wi-Fi is on the chip, an ESP32 board can send sensor data to the internet without any extra module, which makes it the favourite of IoT hobbyists. Newer members like the ESP32-C3 use a RISC-V core instead of Xtensa, which shows that families can change cores over time.

RP2040, a newer student favourite: Raspberry Pi, famous for its Linux single-board computers, also makes a microcontroller called the RP2040, used on the Raspberry Pi Pico board. It has two Cortex-M0+ cores running at 133 MHz and 264 KB of SRAM, but no internal flash: the program lives in an external flash chip on the board. It is popular because it is cheap, well documented and can be programmed in C, C++ or MicroPython. Do not confuse the Pico (a microcontroller board) with a Raspberry Pi 4 (a full computer that runs Linux).

8-bit vs 32-bit side by side: Take the job of adding two 32-bit numbers. On an AVR it takes four 8-bit add instructions, one per byte, carrying from byte to byte, exactly like the ADC chain you saw in 8086 assembly. On a Cortex-M3 it is one instruction. Pointers on AVR are 16 bits, so the address space is small; on Cortex-M they are 32 bits, so the chip can address up to 4 GB of address space, with flash, RAM and peripherals placed at fixed regions. 32-bit chips usually also have more timers, DMA controllers and faster buses. The cost is more complex peripherals: setting up a timer on STM32 means writing more registers than on AVR.

How to choose, step by step: Start from the job, not from the chip you already like. One, list the I/O you need: how many pins, how many ADC channels, which buses like UART, SPI or I2C, any USB. Two, estimate memory: how big is the program, how much RAM for buffers. Three, decide on connectivity: if the device must talk to Wi-Fi, an ESP32 saves you a whole extra chip. Four, check power: battery devices need good sleep modes. Five, check the ecosystem: free compiler, debugger, examples, community, and whether you can actually buy the part in Bangladesh or import it easily. Six, think about volume and price: for 10 units, pick what is easiest; for 100,000 units, a few taka per chip matters.

A quick worked choice: Suppose you want a classroom attendance device that reads an RFID card over SPI, shows a name on a small display over I2C, and uploads the record to a server over Wi-Fi. An ATmega328P could read the card, but it has only 2 KB of RAM and no Wi-Fi, so you would need an extra Wi-Fi module and careful memory use. An ESP32 has SPI, I2C, plenty of RAM and Wi-Fi on one chip. The ESP32 is the clear choice. Now suppose instead you build a simple battery-powered water tank level alarm with one float switch and a buzzer: an 8-bit ATtiny or PIC is more than enough and sleeps on microamps.

Real life example 1, a garment factory counter: Many garment factories around Gazipur and Savar use simple production counters on sewing lines. Each counter reads a button or sensor every time a piece is finished and shows the count. This job needs a few inputs, a display and maybe a serial link to a central PC. An 8-bit AVR or PIC handles it easily, costs little and runs for years. If the factory later wants the counts on a live dashboard over Wi-Fi, the designers can switch to an ESP32 without rewriting the whole idea.

Real life example 2, a motor controller for an e-rickshaw: Battery-driven easy-bikes and e-rickshaws on our roads have a motor controller box. Driving a brushless motor smoothly means measuring currents with the ADC, running control maths thousands of times per second and generating several PWM signals in sync. That is exactly the kind of job where a Cortex-M4 with DSP instructions and an FPU shines. An 8-bit chip would struggle with the maths at that speed.

Common mistakes: Calling Arduino a microcontroller; it is a board and software ecosystem around a microcontroller. Thinking ARM makes the STM32 chip; ARM designs the core, ST makes the chip. Thinking 32-bit always means more power hungry; many Cortex-M0+ parts sleep at very low currents. Comparing chips only by clock speed: a 16 MHz AVR and a 16 MHz Cortex-M0+ do different amounts of work per cycle, and peripherals, RAM and tools often matter more. And believing that ESP32 is an ARM chip: the original ESP32 uses Xtensa cores.

What exams ask: Short notes on the 8051 architecture and its features. Differences between 8-bit and 32-bit microcontrollers. What ARM Cortex-M profiles are and how they differ (M0, M3, M4). Why ESP32 is popular for IoT. Given a project description, choose a suitable microcontroller and justify. Explain board versus chip using the Arduino Uno as the example.

Recap: Families share a core and a peripheral style. The 8051 and PIC are long-lived 8-bit lines; AVR powers the Arduino Uno with its ATmega328P. ARM licenses Cortex-M cores to many chip makers, from tiny M0+ to fast M7, with STM32 as a common example. ESP32 adds Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on chip, and RP2040 is a cheap dual-core M0+ chip. Choose by I/O, memory, connectivity, power, ecosystem and volume, never by clock speed alone. Next we start writing real embedded C for these chips.
key_points: A microcontroller family shares one CPU core and peripheral style but varies in memory, pins, speed and price.
The 8051 (Intel, 1980) and PIC (Microchip) are long-lived 8-bit families still found in cheap products and labs.
AVR is an 8-bit RISC family; the ATmega328P on the Arduino Uno has 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM at 16 MHz.
Arduino is a board plus IDE plus library ecosystem, not a chip family.
ARM designs Cortex-M cores (M0/M0+, M3, M4 with DSP and usually an FPU, M7) and licenses them to companies like ST (STM32).
The original ESP32 has dual Xtensa LX6 cores up to 240 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
8-bit chips need several instructions for 32-bit maths; 32-bit chips do it in one and have larger address spaces.
Choose by I/O, memory, connectivity, power, tools and volume, not by clock speed alone.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page comparison table for ATmega328P, STM32F103, ESP32 and RP2040 with core, clock, flash, RAM and special features. Filling it in yourself fixes the families in memory far better than reading.
lessons.task: Pick three gadgets at home (for example a remote, a digital scale and a Wi-Fi router). For each, write which family you would choose to build it (8-bit, Cortex-M or ESP32) and give two reasons based on pins, memory, connectivity and power.

quiz.q: What is the Arduino Uno?
options: A board built around the ATmega328P with USB, regulator and crystal
quiz.explain: Arduino Uno is a board; the microcontroller on it is the ATmega328P, and Arduino also means the IDE and library ecosystem.

quiz.q: Which company designs the Cortex-M cores used in STM32 chips?
quiz.explain: ARM designs and licenses the cores; STMicroelectronics builds the STM32 chips around them.

quiz.q: Which feature makes the ESP32 especially popular for IoT projects?
options: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are built into the chip
quiz.explain: With radio on chip, an ESP32 can connect to the internet without an extra module.

quiz.q: How many 8-bit add instructions does an AVR need to add two 32-bit numbers?
quiz.explain: Four bytes, one add per byte, with the carry passed along, like an ADD followed by ADC instructions.

quiz.q: Which Cortex-M core adds DSP instructions and usually a floating-point unit?
quiz.explain: Cortex-M4 adds DSP instructions and in most chips a single-precision FPU.

lessons.title: Embedded C Part 1: Toolchain, Fixed-Width Types and Memory Sections
lessons.content:
Imagine you write a letter in Bangla for your grandmother in a village near Rangpur, but you write it on your laptop in Dhaka. The letter is born in one place and lives in another. Embedded code is exactly like that. You write and compile it on a big PC, but it must run on a tiny chip with 2 KB of RAM that has no screen, no keyboard and no operating system. This lesson explains how C code travels from your laptop into a microcontroller, why the size of a simple int suddenly becomes a serious question, and where every variable actually lives inside the chip.

Why C for embedded work: Most microcontroller firmware in the world is written in C, with C++ growing and assembly used only in small hot spots. C is close to the hardware: you can take an address and treat it as a register, you control every byte, and there is no hidden garbage collector or virtual machine. At the same time it is much easier to read and maintain than assembly, and one C program can be moved from one chip to another. Chip makers ship their libraries and examples in C, so C is the common language of the whole industry. Rust and MicroPython exist and are growing, but C is what you must know first.

The cross-compiler: On your PC, gcc normally produces machine code for the PC's own x86 or ARM processor. A microcontroller has a different instruction set, so we need a cross-compiler: a compiler that runs on one machine (the host) and produces code for another machine (the target). For AVR chips this is avr-gcc. For ARM Cortex-M chips it is usually arm-none-eabi-gcc. The Arduino IDE quietly calls these compilers for you. Chip makers also offer full IDEs such as STM32CubeIDE or MPLAB X, which bundle the compiler, a code editor and a debugger.

From source to chip, step by step: First the preprocessor handles #include and #define. Then the compiler turns each .c file into an object file of machine code with unresolved names. Then the linker joins all object files and libraries, and, using a linker script that describes the chip's memory map, decides the exact address of every function and variable: code to flash starting at a fixed address, variables to SRAM. The output is an ELF file with debug information. A small tool then converts it into a plain image, usually an Intel HEX file (.hex, text lines of addresses and bytes) or a raw .bin. Finally a programmer tool such as avrdude for AVR, or a debug probe for ARM, writes that image into the chip's flash. This last step is called flashing or burning.

The host is not the target: This sounds obvious but causes real bugs. On your 64-bit laptop, sizeof(int) is 4 bytes. On an AVR compiled with avr-gcc, sizeof(int) is 2 bytes. On a Cortex-M it is 4 bytes again. The C standard only promises that int is at least 16 bits. So code like int count = 40000; works on your laptop but overflows on an Arduino Uno, because a 16-bit signed int only reaches 32767. Overflowing a signed int is undefined behaviour in C, so the result is not even guaranteed to be a predictable wrong number. Many students meet this bug when they multiply milliseconds, for example 60 * 1000 for one minute, which equals 60000 and does not fit in a 16-bit int.

Fixed-width types: The cure is the header stdint.h, part of C99. It gives types whose size is the same on every compiler: uint8_t (unsigned 8-bit, 0 to 255), int8_t (-128 to 127), uint16_t (0 to 65535), int16_t (-32768 to 32767), uint32_t (0 to 4294967295) and int32_t. Embedded code uses these everywhere. A register that is 8 bits wide is read into a uint8_t. A millisecond counter that must run for weeks goes into a uint32_t. When you see a variable declared as plain int in good embedded code, it usually means the author truly did not care about its size.

Choosing the smallest safe type: On an 8-bit AVR, every 16-bit or 32-bit operation costs extra instructions, and every byte of RAM is precious when you have only 2,048 of them. So we pick the smallest type that safely holds the value. A loop over 10 LEDs fits in uint8_t. An ADC reading from a 10-bit converter, 0 to 1023, needs uint16_t. A count of milliseconds since power-on needs uint32_t: a uint16_t would wrap after 65,535 ms, which is just over a minute. On a 32-bit Cortex-M, using uint8_t for a loop counter can actually be slightly slower because the CPU works naturally on 32 bits, which is why stdint.h also offers uint_fast8_t and similar types. For a beginner, the safe rule is: correct size first, speed tricks later.

Unsigned overflow wraps around: For unsigned types, C defines overflow exactly: the value wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit count. A uint8_t holding 255, plus 1, becomes 0. A uint8_t holding 0, minus 1, becomes 255. This is useful: a timer tick counter that wraps is still fine if you compute elapsed time as now minus start using unsigned maths. For example, with uint8_t, if start = 250 and now = 4 after wrapping, then now - start = 4 - 250, which wraps to 10. That is the correct number of ticks. This trick is how the Arduino millis() comparison keeps working when its 32-bit counter wraps after about 49.7 days.

Signed vs unsigned mixing: When you compare a signed and an unsigned value of the same size, C converts the signed one to unsigned. So the test if (-1 < 1u) is false, because -1 becomes a huge unsigned number. In firmware this shows up when a function returns -1 for error but the result is stored in an unsigned variable. The fix is simple discipline: use unsigned types for bit patterns, registers, sizes and counters, signed types only for values that can really be negative, like a temperature of -5 degrees, and turn on compiler warnings.

Where things live, the memory sections: After linking, your program is split into sections. .text holds the machine code and stays in flash. .rodata holds constant data such as lookup tables and string literals; on ARM it stays in flash. .data holds global and static variables that have a non-zero starting value, like int speed = 100; their values are stored in flash and copied into SRAM at startup. .bss holds global and static variables that start at zero, like int counter; they need no stored copy, the startup code just fills that SRAM area with zeros. The stack grows from the top of SRAM downwards and holds local variables and return addresses. The heap, if used, holds memory from malloc.

A tiny worked map: Suppose a program has 6 KB of code, a 200-byte constant table, global variables totalling 300 bytes of which 120 bytes have starting values, and you expect at most 500 bytes of stack. Flash use is about 6 KB plus 200 bytes plus 120 bytes for the stored .data values. SRAM use is 300 bytes for .data and .bss plus 500 bytes of stack, so 800 bytes, leaving about 1.2 KB free on an ATmega328P. The compiler prints similar numbers after every build: on Arduino it says how much program storage and how many bytes of dynamic memory are used. Watch that second number closely.

const and the Harvard twist: On ARM Cortex-M, flash and RAM share one address space, so a const table is simply read from flash by a normal pointer, and it costs no RAM. On AVR, flash and RAM are separate address spaces (Harvard). A normal const array in avr-gcc is still copied into SRAM at startup, because normal pointers point into RAM. To keep it only in flash you must mark it with PROGMEM and read it with special functions like pgm_read_byte. Arduino's F() macro for strings in Serial.print does the same job. Many Arduino projects run out of RAM simply because they print lots of string literals without F().

Why we avoid malloc: On a PC, malloc and free are everyday tools. On a small MCU they are risky. With only 2 KB of SRAM, the heap and the stack grow towards each other and can silently collide. Repeated malloc and free of different sizes leaves the heap full of small holes, called fragmentation, until one day a request fails even though enough total memory is free. And a device that must run for years without a reboot cannot afford a once-a-month failure. So most embedded code uses static allocation: fixed-size global buffers decided at compile time. Many safety coding standards, MISRA C being the famous one, restrict or forbid dynamic allocation after startup.

The stack is also limited: Each function call pushes its return address, saved registers and local variables onto the stack. A local array like char buf[256]; inside a function costs 256 bytes of stack while that function runs. Deep recursion or large local arrays can overflow a small stack, overwriting .bss variables below it, and the symptom is random strange behaviour, not a clean error message. Good habits: avoid recursion, keep big buffers global or static, and on bigger chips use stack painting, filling the stack with a known pattern and checking later how much was touched.

Real life example 1, a digital weighing scale in a kacha bazar: A shop scale reads a load cell through a 24-bit ADC chip and shows the weight in grams. The raw reading needs a 32-bit variable, because 24 bits do not fit in uint16_t. The price per kilogram multiplied by grams can exceed 65,535 too: 1,200 taka per kg for beef times 2,500 grams is 3,000,000, so the programmer uses uint32_t and divides by 1,000 at the end. A designer who used plain int on an 8-bit chip would print nonsense prices for big purchases.
