Real life example 2, a bus ticket printer: Handheld ticket machines used by some city bus companies store route names and fares as constant tables. On an 8-bit chip these tables must be placed in flash, not copied to RAM, or the 2 KB RAM fills up before the program even starts. The firmware also counts tickets in a uint16_t or uint32_t stored in EEPROM so the count survives a power cut. Every line of that firmware is shaped by the questions in this lesson: how big, where stored, how long it lives.

Common mistakes: Assuming int is 32 bits everywhere. Writing 60 * 1000 and expecting 60000 on an AVR; write 60000UL or cast to uint32_t. Forgetting that const arrays still use RAM on AVR without PROGMEM. Using malloc in a loop. Putting a 1 KB local array in a function on a 2 KB chip. Mixing signed and unsigned in comparisons. Ignoring the memory usage line printed after every build.

What exams ask: Define cross-compiler and explain host versus target. Describe the build steps from .c to .hex and flashing. Explain why stdint.h types are used in embedded C, with an example of int overflow. Explain .text, .data, .bss, stack and heap and where each lives. Why is dynamic allocation discouraged in embedded systems? Calculate flash and RAM use for a small program.

Recap: Embedded C is written on a host and cross-compiled for a target. The build goes preprocess, compile, link with a linker script, convert to hex or bin, then flash. Int size changes between chips, so use uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t and friends. Unsigned overflow wraps, which makes elapsed-time maths safe. Code and constants live in flash, .data is copied to SRAM, .bss is zeroed, and the stack sits at the top of SRAM. Avoid malloc and big local arrays on small chips. Next lesson: the bit manipulation tricks that let C talk to individual register bits.
key_points: A cross-compiler (avr-gcc, arm-none-eabi-gcc) runs on the host PC and produces machine code for the target MCU.
Build flow: preprocess, compile, link with a linker script, convert ELF to HEX or BIN, then flash the chip.
sizeof(int) is 2 on AVR but 4 on Cortex-M and PCs, so use stdint.h types like uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t.
Unsigned overflow wraps modulo 2^n, so elapsed time computed as now minus start stays correct across wraps.
.text and constants live in flash, .data is copied to SRAM at startup, .bss is zeroed, the stack grows down from the top of SRAM.
On AVR (Harvard), const tables need PROGMEM to stay out of SRAM; on Cortex-M const data is read straight from flash.
Embedded code avoids malloc because of tiny heaps, stack collisions and fragmentation; static buffers are preferred.
lessons.tip: After every build, read the memory usage lines the compiler prints and write them in your notebook. Watching flash and RAM numbers change as you add code teaches you more about memory sections than any diagram.
lessons.task: On paper, write a list of 8 variables for a simple fan controller (temperature reading, fan speed percent, seconds since start, error flag and so on). For each, choose the smallest safe stdint type and say whether it goes to .data, .bss, stack or flash.

quiz.q: On an AVR compiled with avr-gcc, what is sizeof(int)?
quiz.explain: avr-gcc uses a 16-bit int, which is why int count = 40000 overflows on an Arduino Uno.

quiz.q: What does a cross-compiler do?
options: Runs on the host and produces code for a different target processor
quiz.explain: It runs on your PC but emits machine code for the microcontroller's instruction set.

quiz.q: A uint8_t holds 250 at start and 4 later after wrapping. What is now minus start in uint8_t maths?
quiz.explain: 4 - 250 = -246, which wraps modulo 256 to 10, the correct number of ticks.

quiz.q: Where does a global variable declared as int counter; (no initial value) live?
quiz.explain: Zero-initialised globals go to .bss; startup code fills that SRAM area with zeros.

quiz.q: Why is malloc usually avoided in small microcontroller firmware?
options: Tiny heap, fragmentation and possible stack collision can cause rare failures
quiz.explain: With a few KB of SRAM, fragmentation and heap/stack collisions can make a long-running device fail unpredictably.

lessons.title: Embedded C Part 2: Bit Manipulation, Masks and Shifts
lessons.content:
Think of the light switch board in a typical Bangladeshi bedroom: one panel with eight switches in a row, for the fan, the tube light, the bulb, the socket and so on. If someone tells you to turn on the fan without touching any other switch, you reach for exactly one switch. A microcontroller register is that switch board. It is one 8-bit or 32-bit number, and each bit controls one thing: one pin, one feature, one flag. Bit manipulation is the skill of flipping exactly the switches you want and leaving the rest alone. Almost every line of low-level firmware uses it, so this lesson is worth practising until it feels automatic.

Why bits and not whole numbers: A register such as the output port of an MCU holds 8 pins in one byte. Bit 0 might be pin 0, bit 5 might be the pin with the LED. If you write the whole byte, say PORTB = 32;, you turn the LED on but you also force the other seven pins to 0, maybe switching off a motor someone else turned on. So we need operations that touch only selected bits. C gives us six bitwise operators for this: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), left shift (<<) and right shift (>>). They work on each bit position separately, unlike the logical operators && and ||, which treat the whole number as true or false.

Binary and hex recap: One hex digit is exactly four bits, which is why embedded people love hex. 0xA0 is 1010 0000 in binary, which is 160 in decimal. Bits are numbered from the right starting at 0, so in 1010 0000, bit 7 is 1, bit 6 is 0, bit 5 is 1, and bits 4 to 0 are 0. Learn the sixteen patterns 0x0 to 0xF by heart; reading a register in hex becomes as easy as reading a clock.

The mask idea: A mask is a number with 1s only in the positions you care about. The mask for bit 5 is 0010 0000, or 0x20. The expression (1 << 5) builds that mask: start with 1 (0000 0001) and shift it left 5 places. So (1 << n) is the mask for bit n. A mask for bits 5 and 4 together is (1 << 5) | (1 << 4) = 0011 0000 = 0x30. Masks are like stencils: they decide which bits an operation is allowed to touch.

Setting a bit with OR: x |= (1 << n); turns bit n to 1 and leaves every other bit unchanged. Why? OR with 0 keeps a bit as it was, and OR with 1 forces it to 1. Worked example: x = 1010 0000 (0xA0). Set bit 3: mask is 0000 1000. 1010 0000 OR 0000 1000 = 1010 1000, which is 0xA8. Only bit 3 changed. If bit 3 had already been 1, nothing would change, so setting is safe to repeat.

Clearing a bit with AND and NOT: x &= ~(1 << n); turns bit n to 0 and leaves the rest. The mask (1 << 5) is 0010 0000; NOT flips it to 1101 1111. AND with 1 keeps a bit, AND with 0 forces it to 0. Worked: x = 1010 0000, clear bit 5: 1010 0000 AND 1101 1111 = 1000 0000, which is 0x80. A very common beginner bug is writing x &= (1 << n); without the NOT, which clears every bit except bit n, the exact opposite of what you wanted.

Toggling a bit with XOR: x ^= (1 << n); flips bit n: a 0 becomes 1 and a 1 becomes 0. XOR with 0 keeps a bit, XOR with 1 inverts it. Worked: x = 1010 0000, toggle bit 7: 1010 0000 XOR 1000 0000 = 0010 0000, which is 0x20. Toggling is perfect for a blinking LED: each time a timer fires, toggle the LED bit, and you never need to remember whether it was on or off.

Testing a bit with AND: To ask whether bit n is 1, compute x & (1 << n). The result is either 0 (the bit is 0) or the mask value itself (the bit is 1). Worked: x = 1010 0000, test bit 5: 1010 0000 AND 0010 0000 = 0010 0000 = 32, which is non-zero, so in C it counts as true. Write it as if (x & (1 << 5)) { ... }. Do not write if ((x & (1 << 5)) == 1), because the result is 32, not 1, and that test will always fail. If you need exactly 0 or 1, shift back down: (x >> 5) & 1.

Shifts as fast maths: Shifting left by 1 multiplies an unsigned number by 2, and shifting right by 1 divides it by 2, dropping the remainder. 0x3C is 0011 1100, which is 60. Shift right by 2: 0000 1111 = 15, which is 60 divided by 4. Shift left by 1: 0111 1000 = 120. Compilers already turn multiplication by constants into shifts when it helps, so write clear maths and let the compiler optimise; but you must recognise the trick when you read old code or datasheets. Note that bits shifted off the end are lost: in an 8-bit variable, 1000 0000 shifted left once becomes 0000 0000.

Multi-bit fields: Many registers hold small numbers inside a few bits, for example a 2-bit field that selects a clock prescaler or a pin mode. To change such a field you cannot just OR, because OR can only add 1s, never remove them. You need read-modify-write: read the register, clear the whole field with a mask, OR in the new value shifted into place, write back. In C: x = (x & ~(0x3 << 4)) | (value << 4); for a 2-bit field at bits 5 and 4. Worked: x = 1010 0000, so the field bits 5:4 currently hold 10. Set them to 01. First x & ~(0x30) = 1010 0000 AND 1100 1111 = 1000 0000. Then OR with (01 << 4) = 0001 0000. Result 1001 0000, which is 0x90. Bit 7 was preserved; the field now holds 01.

Reading a field: To read a field out, shift it down and mask. For bits 7:6 of 1010 0000: x >> 6 gives 0000 0010, AND with 0x3 gives 2. So the field holds the value 2. Datasheets describe registers exactly this way, with tables saying bits 7:6 are CLKSEL or similar, so this pattern turns datasheet tables directly into code.

Setting and clearing many bits at once: Masks combine. To set bits 0 and 2 together: x |= (1 << 0) | (1 << 2);. To clear bits 0 to 3 (the low nibble): x &= ~0x0F;. With x = 1010 0000 the low nibble is already 0, so x stays 0xA0. To set the low nibble: x |= 0x0F; gives 1010 1111 = 0xAF. Doing several bits in one statement is also faster and, as we will see in the next lesson, can avoid glitches where pins change one by one.

Named bits and macros: Raw numbers like (1 << 5) are hard to read. Chip headers give names to bit positions, for example on AVR the bit PB5 is defined as 5, so you write PORTB |= (1 << PB5);. avr-libc also provides the macro _BV(n), defined as (1 << (n)), so you may see PORTB |= _BV(PB5);. Many projects define their own helpers like #define SET_BIT(reg, n) ((reg) |= (1U << (n))). Note the parentheses around every macro argument; without them, passing an expression like a + 1 can expand into the wrong order of operations.

Pitfall 1, operator precedence: In C, the comparison operators bind tighter than the bitwise &, ^ and |. So if (x & 0x20 == 0) is parsed as if (x & (0x20 == 0)), which is x & 0, which is always false. Always add parentheses: if ((x & 0x20) == 0). The same applies to shifts mixed with + and -: 1 << n + 1 means 1 << (n + 1), because + binds tighter than <<.

Pitfall 2, int width and signed shifts: The literal 1 has type int. On AVR, int is 16 bits, so (1 << 15) sets the sign bit of a signed int, and (1 << 20) is undefined behaviour. When you build masks for bits above 14 on an 8-bit or 16-bit target, or for 32-bit registers in general, write 1UL << 20 or 1U for safety; on Cortex-M, use 1U << 31 rather than 1 << 31. Also avoid right-shifting negative signed numbers: whether the sign bit is copied in is implementation-defined. Keep bit work on unsigned types such as uint8_t and uint32_t.

Pitfall 3, bit-fields in structs: C allows struct { unsigned mode : 2; } to name bits. It looks tidy, but the C standard leaves the order of bits inside the storage unit to the compiler. So using bit-fields to map hardware registers can break when you change compilers. Vendor headers mostly use masks and shifts for this reason, though some do use bit-field structs for a specific compiler. For portable code, prefer masks.

Real life example 1, a load-shedding indicator panel: Imagine a small panel in a market in Mymensingh with 8 LEDs on one port, one for each shop, showing which shops are running on the IPS during load shedding. The firmware keeps one uint8_t status. When shop 3's IPS switches on, it runs status |= (1 << 3); when it switches off, status &= ~(1 << 3);. Writing status to the port updates all LEDs at once. A single byte represents eight shops, and no shop's LED disturbs another.

Real life example 2, reading a status register in a GSM module: Many devices report several conditions in one status byte: bit 0 data ready, bit 1 error, bit 2 busy. A smart water meter that sends readings over GSM might read such a byte and check if (status & (1 << 1)) to detect an error before sending. Checking each flag with a mask, instead of comparing the whole byte to fixed numbers, keeps the code correct even when other flags are set at the same time.

Common mistakes: Writing x & (1 << n) == 1. Forgetting the ~ when clearing. Using = instead of |= and wiping other bits. Using OR to change a multi-bit field. Shifting 1 beyond int width on AVR. Confusing & with && and | with ||. Counting bits from the left instead of from bit 0 on the right.

What exams ask: Write C statements to set, clear, toggle and test bit n. Given a register value, compute the result after a sequence of operations. Write code to change a 2-bit field without disturbing others. Explain why read-modify-write is needed. Explain why if (x & 0x20 == 0) is wrong. Convert between hex and binary and count set bits.

Recap: A mask picks the bits you care about, built with 1 << n. Set with |=, clear with &= ~, toggle with ^=, test with &. Fields need read-modify-write: clear the field, then OR in the shifted value. Shifts multiply and divide by powers of two. Mind precedence, use unsigned types and wide literals, and prefer masks over bit-fields for registers. Next lesson: how these bits actually reach the hardware through memory-mapped registers and why volatile matters.
key_points: A register is a row of switches; bit manipulation changes only the bits you choose.
(1 << n) is the mask for bit n; combine masks with |.
Set: x |= mask. Clear: x &= ~mask. Toggle: x ^= mask. Test: if (x & mask).
Worked on 0xA0: set bit 3 gives 0xA8, clear bit 5 gives 0x80, toggle bit 7 gives 0x20.
Multi-bit fields need read-modify-write: x = (x & ~(0x3 << 4)) | (v << 4); 0xA0 with v = 1 gives 0x90.
Read a field by shifting down and masking: (x >> 6) & 0x3.
Comparison binds tighter than &, so parenthesise; use unsigned types and 1U/1UL for high bits.
Prefer masks to struct bit-fields for hardware registers because bit order is compiler-defined.
lessons.tip: Keep a small card with the four lines set, clear, toggle and test on it, and practise each on random hex values by hand until you can do them in your head. Speed here pays off in every later lesson.
lessons.task: Start with x = 0x5A on paper. Apply in order: set bit 0, clear bit 6, toggle bit 3, then set bits 5:4 to 10 using read-modify-write. Write the binary and hex after each step, then check your answers with a calculator app in programmer mode.

quiz.q: Which statement clears bit 4 of x without changing other bits?
quiz.explain: AND with the inverted mask forces bit 4 to 0 and keeps all others.

quiz.q: x = 0xA0. What is x after x |= (1 << 3)?
x = 0xA0. What does (x & (1 << 5)) evaluate to?
quiz.explain: The AND keeps bit 5 in place, giving 0010 0000 = 32, so comparing it with 1 would be wrong.

quiz.q: Why is if (x & 0x20 == 0) a bug?
options: 0x20 is not a valid hex number
== binds tighter than &, so it becomes x & (0x20 == 0), which is always 0
quiz.explain: Precedence makes it x & 0; write if ((x & 0x20) == 0).

quiz.q: x = 0xA0. After x = (x & ~(0x3 << 4)) | (0x1 << 4), what is x?
quiz.explain: Clearing bits 5:4 gives 1000 0000, ORing 0001 0000 gives 1001 0000 = 0x90.

lessons.title: Registers, Memory-Mapped I/O and the volatile Keyword
lessons.content:
Think of the letter boxes at the entrance of an apartment building in Dhanmondi. Each flat has a numbered box. If you drop a note in box 5A, the people of flat 5A get it. Now imagine a strange building where some boxes are not boxes at all: putting a note in box G2 rings the guard's bell, and opening box G3 shows you whether the gate is open right now. A microcontroller's address space is that strange building. Most addresses are ordinary memory, but some addresses are wired straight to hardware. Writing to them changes pins and starts timers; reading them tells you what the hardware is doing at that moment. This lesson is about those special addresses and the one C keyword, volatile, that keeps the compiler from misunderstanding them.

What a peripheral register is: Every peripheral inside an MCU, whether GPIO, timer, UART or ADC, is controlled through a few registers: small storage cells inside the peripheral, usually 8, 16 or 32 bits wide. There are typically three kinds. Control or configuration registers say how the peripheral should behave, such as which pins are outputs or what the baud rate is. Status registers report what is happening, such as data received or conversion finished. Data registers carry the actual data in or out, such as the byte to send or the ADC result. You met this control-status-data trio for device controllers in the Peripherals course; here we write the C that talks to them.

Memory-mapped I/O recap: In the 8086 you saw two styles: isolated I/O, where ports live in a separate space reached only by IN and OUT instructions, and memory-mapped I/O, where device registers sit at ordinary memory addresses. Almost all modern microcontrollers use memory-mapped I/O. The CPU uses the same load and store instructions for RAM and for registers; the bus decides by the address whether the access goes to SRAM or to a peripheral. So in C, a register is just a variable at a fixed address that you reach through a pointer.

The memory map: Each chip's datasheet or reference manual has a memory map, a table of which address ranges belong to what. On ARM Cortex-M, ARM defines a standard layout: code and flash in the lowest region, SRAM from 0x20000000, and peripherals from 0x40000000. On STM32 chips, flash typically starts at 0x08000000. Each peripheral gets a base address, and its registers sit at fixed offsets from that base. On the 8-bit ATmega328P, the I/O registers sit in the low part of the data address space, just after the 32 CPU registers.

A concrete AVR example: Each AVR port has three registers. DDRx is the data direction register: a 1 in a bit makes that pin an output, a 0 makes it an input. PORTx is the output register: for an output pin it sets the pin high or low. PINx is the input register: reading it gives the actual voltage level on each pin. On the ATmega328P, PINB is at data address 0x23, DDRB at 0x24 and PORTB at 0x25. The Arduino Uno's built-in LED on pin 13 is wired to PB5, bit 5 of port B. So to light it: DDRB |= (1 << 5); makes PB5 an output, and PORTB |= (1 << 5); drives it high. You now see why the previous lesson's bit tricks matter: these are exactly those statements.

Reaching an address from C: How does PORTB become a usable name? By casting a number into a pointer and dereferencing it. You could write #define PORTB (*(volatile uint8_t *)0x25). Read it from inside out: 0x25 is just a number; (volatile uint8_t *) tells the compiler to treat it as the address of an 8-bit volatile value; the leading * dereferences it, so PORTB behaves like a normal variable living at address 0x25. Now PORTB = 0xFF; stores a byte at 0x25, which the hardware sees as all port B pins high. avr-libc's real headers do the same thing through helper macros, so you never type the address yourself, but it is good to know nothing magic is happening.

The Cortex-M way, structs: A 32-bit peripheral may have ten or twenty registers. Defining each one by hand is tedious, so vendor headers following ARM's CMSIS convention describe a whole peripheral as a struct whose members are laid out in the same order and size as the hardware registers, each marked volatile. Then a pointer to that struct is placed at the peripheral's base address. For a GPIO port you write things like GPIOA->ODR to reach the output data register, GPIOA->IDR for the input data register, and GPIOA->MODER for the mode register. The struct layout simply does the offset arithmetic for you: if MODER is at offset 0 and ODR at offset 0x14, then GPIOA->ODR is at base plus 0x14.

The optimiser problem: Compilers are clever. If you write a loop that reads the same variable again and again without changing it, the optimiser concludes the value cannot change and reads it once, keeping it in a CPU register. For normal memory that is a perfect optimisation. For a hardware register it is a disaster. Consider waiting for a UART byte: while ((STATUS & READY) == 0) { } . If STATUS is not marked volatile, the compiler may read it once before the loop, see 0, and turn the loop into an infinite loop that never looks at the hardware again. Or consider writing a register twice in a row to pulse a pin: the compiler may delete the first write as useless, since the second overwrites it.

What volatile means: volatile tells the compiler: this object can change, or be observed, outside the code you can see, so every read in the source must really read it from memory, every write must really be written, and they must not be removed or merged. With volatile, each pass of the wait loop performs a fresh load from the status register, and each of two writes really reaches the hardware. That is exactly why vendor headers declare every register volatile.

The three classic uses of volatile: One, memory-mapped hardware registers, as above. Two, global variables shared between an interrupt service routine and the main code. If an ISR sets a flag and main waits in a loop for it, the flag must be volatile, or the compiler may hoist the read out of the loop in main, because from main's point of view nothing changes the flag. Three, variables shared between tasks in a multitasking system, though there you will also need proper locks, which the RTOS lessons cover. A short example: volatile uint8_t button_pressed = 0; set to 1 in the ISR, checked and cleared in main.

What volatile does not do: volatile is not a lock and does not make operations atomic. On an 8-bit AVR, a volatile uint16_t is still read with two separate byte loads. If an interrupt fires between them and updates the variable, main can read the low byte of the old value and the high byte of the new value, a torn read. And count++ on a volatile is still three steps: read, add, write. volatile only promises that the accesses happen; it does not stop them being interrupted. Lesson 14 on interrupts shows how to protect such accesses with short critical sections.

Read-modify-write on shared registers: The statement PORTB |= (1 << 5); looks like one action, but in general it is three: read PORTB, OR in the bit, write PORTB back. Suppose main reads PORTB, then an interrupt fires and the ISR sets bit 2 of PORTB to switch on a buzzer, then main resumes and writes back its old copy with bit 5 set. Bit 2's change is lost: the buzzer goes silent. This is the read-modify-write hazard. On AVR, the compiler can often turn a single-bit change on low I/O addresses into one sbi or cbi instruction, which cannot be split, but you should not rely on that for multi-bit changes or other registers.

Hardware help against read-modify-write: Chip designers know this problem, so many MCUs provide registers that change bits without a read. On STM32 GPIO, the BSRR register lets you write 1s to its lower 16 bits to set pins and to its upper 16 bits to reset pins; bits written as 0 change nothing, so no read is needed and the operation is a single store. On the ATmega328P, writing a 1 to a bit of PINx toggles the corresponding PORTx bit, again with no read-modify-write. When such registers exist, prefer them in code that runs alongside interrupts.

Registers with side effects: Some registers behave strangely compared with memory. Reading a UART data register removes the byte from the receive buffer, so reading it twice loses data. Some status flags are cleared by writing a 1 to them, not a 0, so a careless |= on the register can clear flags you did not mean to touch. Some bits are read-only, and writing them does nothing. This is why you must read each register's description in the datasheet before using it, and why vendors mark read-only registers as const volatile: you may read it, and it may change underneath you, but your code must not write it.

Arduino functions vs registers: digitalWrite(13, HIGH) does the same job as PORTB |= (1 << 5);, but it first looks up which port and bit pin 13 maps to, checks whether a PWM timer is attached to it and turns that off, and then writes the register. That generality costs time: commonly measured at a few microseconds per call on a 16 MHz Uno, compared with a single instruction of 2 clock cycles, about 0.125 microseconds, for the direct register write. For blinking an LED nobody cares. For generating a fast signal or bit-banging a protocol, direct register access can be dozens of times faster.

Real life example 1, an automatic school bell: Many schools in Bangladesh now use automatic bell controllers that ring at set times. The controller's firmware configures a GPIO pin as output via its direction register, then at each period sets the bit in the output register to energise a relay, and clears it a few seconds later. A real-time clock chip tells the time, and a small LCD shows the next bell. If a timer interrupt also toggles a status LED on the same port, the programmer must avoid the read-modify-write hazard, or once in a long while the bell relay could switch at the wrong moment.

Real life example 2, a fuel dispenser display: A petrol pump's display board reads pulses from a flow meter and shows litres and taka. An interrupt counts pulses into a volatile counter, and main converts the count into litres for the display. Without volatile, an optimising compiler could keep showing a stale value in some loop. Without protecting the multi-byte read, the display could flash a wildly wrong number for a moment when the count crosses a byte boundary, say from 255 to 256. Both bugs are the subject of this lesson.

Common mistakes: Forgetting volatile on a flag shared with an ISR, so the program works with optimisation off and freezes with it on. Thinking volatile makes code thread-safe. Using |= on registers whose flags clear on writing 1. Reading a data register twice in a debug print and losing a byte. Writing PORTB = value; when you meant to change just one pin. Mixing up PORTx and PINx on AVR: reading PORTx gives what you last wrote, not the real pin level.

What exams ask: Explain memory-mapped versus isolated I/O. Write C to access a register at a given address. What does volatile do, and give three situations where it is required. Explain why volatile does not guarantee atomicity. Explain the read-modify-write hazard with an interrupt and how a set/reset register avoids it. Given DDRB, PORTB and PINB, write code to make a pin an output and turn it on.

Recap: Peripheral registers are control, status and data cells at fixed addresses in the memory map. In C we reach them through a casted volatile pointer, or through CMSIS-style structs on Cortex-M. volatile forces every access to really happen, which is needed for registers, ISR-shared variables and task-shared data, but it is not a lock and not atomic. Read-modify-write can lose updates when interrupts touch the same register; set/reset registers such as BSRR avoid it. Next we use all this to drive and read real pins: GPIO.
key_points: Peripherals are controlled through control, status and data registers at fixed addresses (memory-mapped I/O).
On ATmega328P, PINB is at 0x23, DDRB at 0x24, PORTB at 0x25; the Uno LED on pin 13 is PB5.
In C a register is a dereferenced volatile pointer, e.g. (*(volatile uint8_t *)0x25); Cortex-M uses CMSIS structs like GPIOA->ODR.
volatile makes every read and write in the source really happen, stopping the optimiser from caching or deleting accesses.
Use volatile for hardware registers, variables shared with ISRs, and data shared between tasks.
volatile is not atomic: a 16-bit read on an 8-bit MCU and count++ can still be interrupted midway.
Read-modify-write can lose an ISR's change; set/reset registers like STM32 BSRR avoid the read.
Some registers have side effects (reading UART data removes it, some flags clear on writing 1), so read the datasheet.
lessons.tip: Open the ATmega328P datasheet's register summary table and find PORTB, DDRB and PINB yourself. Seeing the real addresses and bit names once makes every register macro in code feel concrete instead of magic.
lessons.task: Write, on paper, three versions of turning on the Uno LED: the Arduino digitalWrite call, the named-register version with DDRB and PORTB, and a raw version using a volatile pointer to the address 0x25. Then write a two-line wait loop on a status bit and mark which variable must be volatile and why.

quiz.q: On an AVR, which register sets whether a pin is an input or an output?
quiz.explain: DDRx is the data direction register: 1 = output, 0 = input.

quiz.q: What does volatile tell the compiler?
options: Every access in the source must really happen because the value can change outside the visible code
Make all operations on it atomic
quiz.explain: volatile forbids caching, merging or removing accesses; it says nothing about atomicity.

quiz.q: A flag is set inside an ISR and polled in main. What must it be declared as?
quiz.explain: Without volatile, the compiler may read the flag once and loop forever.

quiz.q: Why can PORTB |= (1 << 5); lose a change made by an interrupt?
options: It is a read-modify-write: an ISR can change PORTB between the read and the write-back
quiz.explain: Main writes back its stale copy, overwriting the ISR's update.

quiz.q: How does the STM32 BSRR register avoid the read-modify-write hazard?
options: Writing 1s sets or resets chosen pins and 0s change nothing, so no read is needed
quiz.explain: Lower 16 bits set pins, upper 16 bits reset pins, and zeros are ignored, so a single store does the job.

lessons.title: GPIO: Pins, Pull-ups and Driving the Outside World
lessons.content:
Think about the doorbell of a flat in Mirpur. Someone presses the button, a wire goes from 0 volts to 5 volts, and inside a small box a chip notices it and starts the ding-dong tune. Now think about the light on a phone charger that turns from red to green. A chip decided to change a wire from one level to another, and the LED changed colour. Both jobs, noticing a wire and controlling a wire, are done by the most basic peripheral of every microcontroller: the GPIO pin. Before timers, ADCs or Wi-Fi, this is where every embedded programmer starts, usually by blinking one LED.

What GPIO means: GPIO stands for General Purpose Input/Output. A GPIO pin is a physical leg of the chip that your program can use in one of two ways. As an output, the program decides the voltage on the pin: logic 1 puts it near the supply voltage (for example 5 V or 3.3 V), logic 0 puts it near 0 V (ground). As an input, the program reads the voltage that something outside puts on the pin and gets back a 1 or a 0. "General purpose" means the chip does not decide the meaning. The same pin can drive an LED in one product and read a door sensor in another.

Ports and pins: Pins are grouped into ports, usually 8, 16 or 32 pins per port, because each port is controlled by registers of that width. On the ATmega328P of the Arduino Uno, there are ports B, C and D. Arduino digital pin 13, the one with the on-board LED, is really PB5, bit 5 of port B. On an STM32 you see names like PA5 or PC13. When you read a schematic or datasheet, always translate the board's friendly name into port and bit, because that is what the registers use.

The three AVR registers per port: In the previous lesson we met memory-mapped registers and volatile. Each AVR port has three of them. DDRx, the Data Direction Register, chooses direction: bit = 1 makes the pin an output, bit = 0 makes it an input. PORTx holds the output value when the pin is an output. PINx is where you read the actual voltage level of the pin. So to make PB5 an output and turn it on, you write DDRB |= (1 << 5); then PORTB |= (1 << 5);. To read PD2 you test PIND & (1 << 2). STM32 chips use different names (MODER for mode, ODR for output data, IDR for input data, BSRR for atomic set and reset), but the idea is the same: one register chooses the role, one holds what you drive, one shows what is really there.

What a pin looks like inside, push-pull output: A normal output is built with two transistors, one connecting the pin to the supply and one connecting it to ground. When you write 1, the top transistor turns on and pushes current out. When you write 0, the bottom one turns on and pulls current in. Only one is on at a time. This is called a push-pull output, and it is the default on almost every MCU. It can actively drive the line both high and low, which gives clean, fast edges.

Open-drain output: Some pins can be set to open-drain (open-collector in older bipolar language). Here only the bottom transistor is used. Writing 0 pulls the line to ground; writing 1 simply lets go, so the pin floats unless an external resistor pulls it up. Why would anyone want a weaker output? Because several open-drain outputs can share one wire safely: if any device pulls low, the line is low, and nobody fights. This is exactly how I2C works, which we will see in lesson 16. Open-drain is also handy for level shifting, because the pull-up resistor can go to a different voltage than the chip's own supply, as long as the pin can tolerate it.

Inputs and the floating problem: An input pin has a very high input resistance, so it draws almost no current. That is good, but it also means an unconnected input is like a door that is neither open nor locked. Its voltage drifts with electrical noise, your hand nearby, or a neighbouring wire. Reading it gives random 1s and 0s. This is called a floating input. Beginners often connect a button between the pin and 5 V and nothing else. When the button is pressed the pin reads 1, but when it is released the pin is floating, not 0. The program then sees ghost presses.

Pull-up and pull-down resistors: The fix is to give the pin a default level through a resistor. A pull-up resistor (often 10 kilo-ohm) connects the pin to the supply, so with nothing else connected it reads 1. The button then connects the pin to ground; pressing it forces the pin to 0. A pull-down resistor does the opposite: it connects the pin to ground, so the default is 0, and the button connects it to the supply. The resistor is large enough that when the button is pressed only a tiny current flows, for example 5 V / 10,000 ohm = 0.5 mA, which is harmless.

Internal pull-ups: Most MCUs have pull-up resistors built in, which saves parts on the board. On the AVR, if a pin is an input (DDR bit 0) and you write 1 to its PORT bit, the internal pull-up switches on. The datasheet gives a range of about 20 to 50 kilo-ohm, so do not depend on an exact value. STM32 and ESP32 pins have both internal pull-ups and pull-downs that you choose in the configuration register. In Arduino code, pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP) does this for you.

Active low, the usual button wiring: With a pull-up, the button reads 0 when pressed and 1 when released. This is called active low. It feels backwards at first, but it is the most common wiring in industry, because the pull-up comes free inside the chip and the button only needs a wire to ground, which is everywhere on a board. In code you just invert the test: if ((PIND & (1 << 2)) == 0) means "button pressed". Many signals in datasheets are active low too, and their names carry a bar or a slash, like RESET with a bar on top or nCS.

How much current a pin can give: A GPIO pin is a signal, not a power supply. The ATmega328P datasheet lists an absolute maximum of 40 mA per pin and 200 mA through the VCC and GND pins of the whole chip. Absolute maximum means "beyond this the chip may be damaged", not "safe to use all day". Designers usually keep a pin below about 20 mA, and many 3.3 V chips are weaker, often only a few mA to around 20 mA depending on settings. So an LED is fine, a small buzzer may be fine, but a motor, a relay coil or a pump is never driven directly. For those you use a transistor or driver, which we saw in Peripherals & Interfacing and will recap in lesson 17.

LED resistor recap: An LED needs a series resistor to limit current. With a 5 V pin, a red LED that drops about 2 V, and a target of 15 mA, the resistor is R = (5 - 2) / 0.015 = 200 ohm. The nearest standard value, 220 ohm, gives a little less current, which is fine. Without the resistor, current is limited only by the pin's internal transistor, the pin gets hot, and the LED or pin may be damaged.

3.3 V versus 5 V: Older AVR boards run at 5 V; most modern 32-bit chips such as STM32 and ESP32 run at 3.3 V. Mixing them needs care. A 5 V output into an ESP32 input can damage it, because ESP32 pins are not 5 V tolerant. Many STM32 pins are marked FT, five-volt tolerant, in the datasheet, and those can accept 5 V as inputs, but not every pin. The other direction is about thresholds: an ATmega328P at 5 V treats an input as high when it is at least 0.6 x VCC, which is 3.0 V. A 3.3 V output just passes that, with little margin. For anything important, use a proper level shifter or a resistor divider for a 5 V to 3.3 V input.

Reading a button, step by step: Wire a push button from PD2 to ground. In setup, make PD2 an input (DDRD &= ~(1 << 2)) and enable its pull-up (PORTD |= (1 << 2)). In the loop, read the bit. When not pressed, the pull-up holds the pin at 5 V and you read 1. When pressed, the switch connects the pin to ground and you read 0. If the button controls the LED on PB5, the whole program is: if the bit is 0, set PB5; else clear PB5. That is a complete embedded system with one input, one output and no operating system.

Toggling and atomic writes: To toggle the LED, you can write PORTB ^= (1 << 5), which reads, flips and writes back. On the ATmega328P there is a neat trick: writing a 1 to a bit of PINx toggles the matching PORTx bit in hardware, in one step. On STM32, the BSRR register lets you set or reset single pins with one write, without touching the others. Why care? Because a read-modify-write can be interrupted halfway, and if an interrupt changes another bit of the same port in between, your write puts the old value back. Single-write set/reset registers avoid that.

Arduino functions versus direct registers: pinMode, digitalWrite and digitalRead are friendly and portable: the same sketch works on Uno, Mega or an ESP32. But each call looks up tables to translate pin numbers into ports and bits and checks things like PWM settings, so it takes a few microseconds on a 16 MHz Uno. A direct register write such as PORTB |= (1 << 5) compiles to a single SBI instruction that takes 2 clock cycles, about 0.125 microseconds. For blinking an LED, nobody cares. For generating a fast signal or bit-banging a protocol, the difference matters. Learn the registers so you know what the friendly functions hide.

Alternate functions: Most pins have a second job. PD0 and PD1 on the Uno are also the UART RX and TX pins, PB3 is also an SPI line and a PWM output, and many port C pins are ADC inputs. When you enable a peripheral such as the UART, it takes over the pin and your GPIO settings may be ignored. On STM32 you choose the alternate function explicitly with a register. Planning which pin does what, before drawing the PCB, is called pin mapping, and getting it wrong means rewiring boards later.

Real life example 1, a rice cooker: A typical electric rice cooker has a button, a couple of LEDs (cook and warm) and a heating element switched through a relay or triac. The microcontroller reads the button with a pull-up, lights the cook LED with a 220 ohm resistor, and drives a transistor that switches the relay coil. None of these loads is driven straight from a pin except the small LEDs. Each GPIO pin does one clear job.

Real life example 2, a shop's token display: A small shop in Gulistan might use a token board with two buttons, next and reset, and a few seven-segment digits. The buttons are active low inputs with internal pull-ups. The segments are driven through transistors, multiplexed so a few pins can drive many digits. Reading and driving pins, plus correct current limits, is all the hardware needs.

Common mistakes: Leaving an input floating and wondering why it reads random values. Forgetting the LED resistor. Driving a motor or relay coil directly from a pin. Connecting a 5 V signal to a 3.3 V-only pin. Writing to PORTx when you meant PINx, or reading PORTx when you wanted the real pin level (PORTx shows what you wrote, PINx shows what is there). Forgetting that the button is active low and inverting the logic by accident.

What exams ask: Explain the role of DDR, PORT and PIN registers and write the code to make a pin an output and set it. Compare push-pull and open-drain outputs. Explain floating inputs and why pull-up or pull-down resistors are needed; draw both circuits. Calculate an LED series resistor. Discuss 3.3 V and 5 V interfacing. Explain why GPIO pins cannot drive motors directly.

Recap: A GPIO pin is either an output that the program drives or an input that the program reads. Direction, output value and input value each live in a register. Push-pull drives both ways, open-drain only pulls low and lets lines be shared. Inputs need a defined level, given by pull-up or pull-down resistors, often built in. Pins have current limits and voltage limits, so loads go through drivers and mixed voltages need care. Next lesson: why a simple button is not as simple as it looks, and how to debounce it.
key_points: GPIO pins are grouped in ports; each pin can be an output the program drives or an input the program reads.
On AVR, DDRx sets direction, PORTx holds the output value (or enables pull-up on inputs), PINx reads the real pin level.
Push-pull outputs drive high and low; open-drain outputs only pull low and let several devices share one line.
An unconnected input floats and reads random values; pull-up or pull-down resistors give it a default level.
With a pull-up and a button to ground, the input is active low: 0 means pressed.
Pins have current limits (ATmega328P absolute max 40 mA per pin); motors and relays need transistor drivers.
3.3 V chips like ESP32 are not 5 V tolerant; mixed voltages need level shifting or dividers.
Direct register writes are much faster than Arduino digitalWrite, and set/reset or toggle registers avoid read-modify-write races.
lessons.tip: For every pin you use, write one line in a pin table: port and bit, direction, pull-up or not, active high or low, and what it connects to. This small table prevents most beginner wiring bugs.
lessons.task: Draw on paper a button connected to a microcontroller pin with an internal pull-up, and an LED with a series resistor on another pin. Write the four lines of register code (direction, pull-up, read, write) and calculate the resistor for a 3.3 V pin, a 2 V LED and 10 mA.

quiz.q: On an AVR, which register reads the actual voltage level on a pin?
quiz.explain: PINx shows the real level on the pins; PORTx only shows what you wrote.

quiz.q: Why does an unconnected input pin give random readings?
options: It is floating, with no defined voltage, so noise decides its level
quiz.explain: A floating input has very high resistance and no driver, so noise and stray fields set its level.

quiz.q: A button connects a pin to ground and the internal pull-up is on. What does the pin read when the button is pressed?
options: 0, because the button is active low
quiz.explain: Pressing connects the pin to ground, so it reads 0: active low.

quiz.q: What is the series resistor for a 5 V pin, a 2 V LED and 15 mA?
Why is open-drain used for shared lines like I2C?
options: Any device can pull the line low without fighting, and a resistor pulls it high
quiz.explain: Open-drain only pulls low, so several devices can share one line safely.

lessons.title: Debouncing and Input Handling: Taming Noisy Buttons
lessons.content:
Imagine you build a simple counter for a cricket scorer at a school match in Rajshahi. Every time a run is scored, the scorer presses a button and the display adds one. You test it: press once, and the display jumps from 0 to 4. Press again, it jumps to 9. Nothing is wrong with your code's addition. The problem is the button itself. A mechanical switch does not close cleanly. For a few milliseconds its metal contacts bounce against each other like a dropped cricket ball bouncing on the pitch, and your fast microcontroller faithfully counts every bounce. This lesson is about taming that bounce, which is called debouncing, and about handling inputs properly in general.

What switch bounce is: Inside a push button or toggle switch, two metal pieces are pushed together by a spring or lever. When they hit, they are springy, so they touch, separate, touch again, and only settle after a short time. Electrically, instead of one clean step from 1 to 0, the pin sees a burst of fast pulses: 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, and finally a steady 0. Releasing the button can bounce too. The bounce time depends on the switch; typical small buttons settle within a few milliseconds, while poor or worn switches can chatter for 10 to 20 milliseconds or more. That sounds tiny, but a 16 MHz microcontroller can run a loop thousands of times in one millisecond.

Why it matters: In the GPIO lesson we read a button by checking one bit. If the program only cares whether the button is held right now, for example "pump runs while the button is held", bounce causes a tiny flicker and nobody notices. But many programs care about events: count presses, toggle a light on each press, move to the next menu item. An event-based program that sees ten edges instead of one does ten things instead of one. The same problem appears with reed switches, limit switches on machines, rotary encoders and relay contacts.

Two places to fix it: You can remove bounce in hardware, before the signal reaches the pin, or in software, after the pin is read. Both are used in real products. Hardware costs parts and board space but frees the CPU; software costs a little code and timing but is free in parts. Most low-cost products today debounce in software, but it is important to understand both.

Hardware debounce with an RC filter: Put a resistor and capacitor so that the capacitor voltage follows the switch slowly. When the switch closes, the capacitor discharges through a resistor; short bounces cannot change its voltage much, because a capacitor needs time to charge and discharge. The time constant tau = R x C sets how slow it is. For example, 10 kilo-ohm with 1 microfarad gives tau = 10 ms, longer than most bounce. The problem is that the capacitor voltage moves slowly through the middle zone, between clear 0 and clear 1, and a normal input may read it as 0 and 1 several times while it passes.

Adding a Schmitt trigger: A Schmitt trigger input has two thresholds: it switches to 1 only when the voltage rises above an upper threshold, and back to 0 only when it falls below a lower threshold. The gap between them is called hysteresis. A slow, slightly noisy RC voltage then produces one clean edge. Chips like the 74HC14 are Schmitt trigger inverters made for this. Many MCU input pins already have some Schmitt trigger behaviour built in; the datasheet tells you. So the classic hardware recipe is RC filter plus Schmitt trigger. Hysteresis is a big idea that comes back later, for example in the irrigation controller of lesson 26, where the pump starts at one moisture level and stops at a different one.

Software debounce, method 1, wait and check again: The simplest code: when you see the pin change, wait about 20 to 50 milliseconds, then read again. If it is still pressed, accept it as a press. In Arduino style: if (digitalRead(2) == LOW) { delay(30); if (digitalRead(2) == LOW) { count++; while (digitalRead(2) == LOW) {} } }. The last line waits for release so one long press does not count many times. This works for a beginner project, but delay() and the while loop block the whole CPU. While it waits, it cannot refresh a display, read a sensor or answer the UART. In a real product, blocking code is a smell.

Software debounce, method 2, sample at a steady rate: A better way: read the button at a fixed interval, for example every 5 ms, from a timer tick or a non-blocking check in the main loop. Keep a counter. If the reading equals the current accepted state, reset the counter. If it differs, increase the counter, and when it reaches 4 accept the new state. Four equal samples, 5 ms apart, means the input must be stable for about 20 ms before you believe it. Bounces shorter than that never reach a count of 4, because any bounce back resets the counter. The CPU spends only a few microseconds every 5 ms on this, and never blocks.

Walking through the counter method: Suppose the accepted state is released (1), the counter is 0, and samples arrive every 5 ms. The user presses, and the samples read 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. First sample 0 differs, counter goes to 1. Next sample 1 equals the accepted state, counter resets to 0. Then four 0s: counter 1, 2, 3, 4. At 4 the program changes the accepted state to pressed and reports one press event. The bounce produced exactly one event, about 20 ms after the contacts settled. That small delay is not noticeable to a human, who perceives anything under roughly 50 to 100 ms as instant.

Software debounce, method 3, the shift register trick: Another popular form keeps the last 8 samples in a byte. Every 5 ms: history = (history << 1) | reading. If history becomes 0x00, the button has been low for 8 samples (40 ms) and is surely pressed; if it is 0xFF, surely released. Anything mixed means bouncing, so do nothing. This needs one byte per button and almost no code, which is why it is common on small 8-bit chips.

Software debounce, method 4, a state machine: For buttons with more behaviour, write an explicit state machine with states like IDLE, DEBOUNCE_PRESS, PRESSED, DEBOUNCE_RELEASE. Each 5 ms tick looks at the current state and the pin, and moves to the next state when the timing rule is met. State machines take more lines but make complicated behaviour clear and testable. You will meet them again when we build the super-loop and the capstone.

Edge detection: Once you have a clean, debounced state, you usually want events, not levels. Keep the previous debounced state. If previous was released and current is pressed, that is a press event (a falling edge for an active low button). If previous was pressed and current is released, that is a release event (a rising edge). In code: pressed_event = (prev == 1 && now == 0); prev = now;. Toggle logic, counters and menus should react only to these edges.

Long press and double press: With a timer and edges you can build richer buttons. Record the time of the press edge. If the button is still held after, say, 1,000 ms, report a long press, perhaps to enter a settings menu. If it is released earlier, report a short press. For a double press, after a release start a short window, about 300 ms, and see if another press arrives. Many products, from wristwatches to wall clocks sold in Dhaka markets, set the time using just two buttons this way, with long press to enter settings and short press to change digits.

Interrupts and bounce: You might think: let the pin trigger an interrupt on a falling edge, then I never miss a press. But bounce produces many edges, so the interrupt fires many times. If you use pin-change interrupts for buttons, use them only to wake the chip or to note that something happened, and still debounce with time inside the main logic. Some designers disable the pin interrupt for 20 to 50 ms after the first edge. For a human button, a 5 ms polling tick is simpler and plenty fast. Lesson 14 covers interrupt rules in depth.

Keypads, a quick recap: A 4 x 4 keypad, like the one on a door lock or a vending machine, has 16 keys but only 8 wires, arranged as 4 rows and 4 columns. The firmware drives one row low at a time and reads the 4 columns with pull-ups; a 0 on a column means the key at that row and column is pressed. You met keypad scanning and ghosting in Peripherals & Interfacing. The new point here: every key in the matrix bounces, so debounce each key's state the same way, usually scanning all rows every 5 to 10 ms and running the counter or shift method per key.

Other noisy inputs: Debounce ideas apply beyond buttons. A float switch in a water tank can wobble with ripples, so the reading flips around the threshold. A cheap PIR motion sensor can glitch. Long wires running past a motor pick up spikes. In all these, the rule is the same: do not believe one sample; require a stable reading for a time, or add hysteresis, or both.

Real life example 1, a road crossing button: Imagine a pedestrian crossing button at a busy road in Chattogram. People press it many times, hard, with dirty hands; the switch is outdoors, wet in monsoon and old. The controller samples it every 10 ms, accepts a press after 3 stable samples, records the request, and ignores further presses until the walk light has been served. Debouncing plus "latch the request" makes the system calm no matter how many times people hit the button.

Real life example 2, a rice mill counter: A small rice mill in Dinajpur wants to count sacks passing on a conveyor using a mechanical limit switch that each sack pushes. A sack wobbles as it passes, so the switch can chatter for longer than a finger press. The engineer measures the chatter with a logic analyzer, sees up to about 30 ms, and sets the debounce to require 50 ms of stable signal. The count matches the hand tally at the end of the day.

Common mistakes: Using delay()-based debouncing in a program that must do other things at the same time. Debouncing the press but forgetting the release, so one press counts twice. Triggering interrupts on a bouncing switch and counting every bounce. Setting the debounce time so long that fast, real presses are missed. Applying the same timing to every input without measuring: a hand button and a machine switch can behave very differently.

What exams ask: Explain switch bounce and draw the waveform. Draw an RC debounce circuit with a Schmitt trigger and explain hysteresis. Write pseudo-code for software debouncing using sampling and a counter, and calculate the total delay (sample period x required count, here 5 ms x 4 = 20 ms). Distinguish level and edge, and write edge detection code. Explain why interrupts on raw buttons are problematic.

Recap: Mechanical contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, creating many edges for one press. Hardware fixes use an RC filter and a Schmitt trigger with hysteresis. Software fixes require a stable reading over time: wait-and-recheck (simple but blocking), periodic sampling with a counter, a shift-register history, or a state machine. After debouncing, turn levels into edge events and build features like long press on top. Next lesson we meet the hardware that makes all this periodic sampling easy: timers and counters.
key_points: Mechanical switches bounce: for a few milliseconds (sometimes 10-20 ms or more) the pin toggles many times for one press.
Bounce matters whenever the program counts or reacts to events instead of just reading a level.
Hardware debounce uses an RC filter (tau = R x C) plus a Schmitt trigger whose hysteresis gives one clean edge.
Delay-and-recheck debouncing works but blocks the CPU.
Sampling every 5 ms and requiring 4 equal samples accepts a change after about 20 ms of stable input, without blocking.
A shift-register history (0x00 or 0xFF) and explicit state machines are other common software methods.
After debouncing, detect edges (press and release events) and build long press or double press on top.
Raw buttons on edge interrupts fire many times; use interrupts to wake, and debounce with time.
lessons.tip: When an input misbehaves, measure before you guess: a cheap logic analyzer or even an oscilloscope app shows you how long the bounce really lasts, and then you can choose a debounce time with a reason behind it.
lessons.task: On paper, simulate the counter method: start with accepted state 1 and counter 0, and process the samples 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0 (5 ms apart, need 4 equal). Write the counter after each sample and mark when the press is accepted and how many milliseconds after the first sample that happens.

quiz.q: Why does a single button press sometimes count as several presses?
options: The contacts bounce and create several edges
quiz.explain: Contact bounce makes the pin toggle several times before it settles.

quiz.q: Samples are taken every 5 ms and 4 equal samples are needed. About how long must the input be stable?
quiz.explain: 5 ms x 4 = 20 ms of stable input.

quiz.q: What does a Schmitt trigger add to an RC debounce circuit?
options: Hysteresis, so a slow noisy voltage gives one clean edge
quiz.explain: Two thresholds with a gap (hysteresis) stop the slow RC voltage from toggling the input many times.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with debouncing using delay() and a while loop?
options: It blocks the CPU from doing anything else while waiting
quiz.explain: Blocking code stops the CPU from refreshing displays, reading sensors or handling other tasks.

quiz.q: In the shift-register method, history = (history << 1) | reading every 5 ms. What does history == 0x00 mean for an active low button?
options: Pressed steadily for 8 samples, about 40 ms
quiz.explain: Eight 0 samples in a row means the active low button has been pressed and stable for 8 x 5 = 40 ms.

lessons.title: Timers and Counters: The Heartbeat of Firmware
lessons.content:
Think of the call to prayer, the school bell, the alarm on your phone, the traffic light at Bijoy Sarani. All of them depend on knowing time precisely and acting at the right moment. A microcontroller faces the same need all day: blink this LED every 500 ms, sample that sensor every 5 ms, measure how long an echo took, count how many pulses a water meter sent. You could try to do all this with delay loops, counting how many instructions burn a millisecond, but that wastes the CPU and breaks the moment your code changes. Every MCU instead has dedicated hardware for time: timers and counters. They are the heartbeat of almost every embedded program.

What a timer is: At its core, a timer is just a binary counter register, say 8 or 16 bits wide, that adds 1 on every pulse of some clock. That is all. If the clock is the CPU clock (or a divided version of it), the count tells you how much time has passed, and we call it a timer. If the pulses come from an external pin, for example from a sensor, the count tells you how many events happened, and we call it a counter. Same hardware, two uses. The magic is that it counts in hardware, in parallel with your program, without the CPU doing anything.

The ATmega328P timers: The Uno's chip has three: Timer0 (8-bit), Timer1 (16-bit) and Timer2 (8-bit). An 8-bit timer counts 0 to 255 and then wraps to 0; a 16-bit timer counts 0 to 65,535. STM32 chips have many more timers, mostly 16-bit with some 32-bit ones, with richer features, and ESP32 has general-purpose 64-bit timers. You met the 8253/8254 programmable timer chip in the Microprocessors course, with its counters and modes. In a modern MCU those same ideas live inside the chip, next to the CPU.

The prescaler: A 16 MHz clock ticks every 62.5 ns. An 8-bit timer counting that fast overflows after only 256 x 62.5 ns = 16 microseconds, too short for most jobs. So timers have a prescaler, a divider in front of the counter. On the ATmega328P, Timer0 and Timer1 can divide the clock by 1, 8, 64, 256 or 1024. The timer's tick time is N / f_clk. With N = 64 and f_clk = 16 MHz, tick = 64 / 16,000,000 = 4 microseconds. So 1 ms corresponds to 1 ms / 4 us = 250 counts. Remember this formula: counts = desired time / tick time.

Overflow: When the counter reaches its maximum and wraps to 0, the timer sets an overflow flag, and if you enabled it, raises an overflow interrupt. The overflow period is (max + 1) x tick. For Timer0 with N = 64: 256 x 4 us = 1,024 us = 1.024 ms. For the 16-bit Timer1 with N = 256: tick = 16 us, and 65,536 x 16 us = 1.048576 s. Notice that neither is a round number. Overflow is fine for "roughly every millisecond", but if you need exactly 1 ms or exactly 1 s, you need another trick.

Compare match and CTC mode: Each timer has one or more output compare registers, OCR. The hardware constantly compares the counter with OCR. When they are equal, a compare match happens: a flag is set, an interrupt can fire, and an output pin can be set, cleared or toggled. In CTC mode (Clear Timer on Compare match), the counter resets to 0 right after the match. So the counter now counts 0, 1, ..., OCR, 0, 1, ... and the period becomes (OCR + 1) x tick. This lets you choose any period you like, as long as it fits in the counter width.

Worked example, a 1 ms tick: We want an interrupt every 1 ms. With N = 64, tick = 4 us, so we need 250 counts. Because the count includes 0, OCR = 250 - 1 = 249. That fits easily in 8 bits. The general CTC formula is f_interrupt = f_clk / (N x (OCR + 1)) = 16,000,000 / (64 x 250) = 1,000 Hz. Exactly 1 ms, as long as the crystal is exact. That 1 ms tick is perfect for debouncing, scheduling tasks and timekeeping.

Worked example, 1 Hz from a 16-bit timer: For a once-per-second interrupt, try N = 256: tick = 16 us, and we need 1 s / 16 us = 62,500 counts, so OCR = 62,499. That fits in 16 bits (max 65,535). With N = 64 we would need 250,000 counts, which does not fit, so the method is: pick the smallest prescaler that makes the count fit, because a smaller prescaler gives finer resolution. Check: 16,000,000 / (256 x 62,500) = 1 Hz.

Setting up a timer, the shape of the code: You do not need to memorise register bits, but the steps are always the same. One, choose the mode (normal, CTC, PWM) in control registers. Two, write the compare value into OCR. Three, enable the interrupt you want in the interrupt mask register. Four, set the prescaler bits, which also starts the timer. Five, enable global interrupts. Then write a short ISR that does the periodic job, such as incrementing a millisecond counter or setting a flag for the main loop. On STM32 the names differ (prescaler register PSC, auto-reload register ARR, compare registers CCR), but the steps are the same, and the period is (PSC + 1) x (ARR + 1) / f_clk.

Input capture, measuring time of external events: Sometimes you want to know when something happened, not make something happen. Timer1 on the ATmega328P has an input capture unit: when a chosen edge arrives on the ICP1 pin, the hardware copies the current count into the ICR1 register at that exact instant. Your ISR then reads the stored value at leisure. Because the hardware did the copying, the timestamp is accurate even if the ISR runs a little late.

Worked input capture: Set Timer1 to N = 8, so tick = 8 / 16 MHz = 0.5 us. A signal of unknown frequency arrives. One rising edge is captured at count 1,000 and the next at 3,000. The period is 3,000 - 1,000 = 2,000 ticks = 2,000 x 0.5 us = 1 ms, so the frequency is 1 kHz. If the counter wrapped between the two edges, unsigned 16-bit subtraction still gives the right answer as long as less than one full wrap passed. The same method measures pulse widths, such as the echo pulse from an ultrasonic sensor or the pulses from an RC receiver.

Counter mode, counting events: If you select the external clock source, the timer counts pulses on a pin (T0 or T1 on the ATmega328P) instead of clock ticks. A water flow sensor in a farm pipe gives a pulse for every small volume of water; an anemometer gives pulses as it spins; an energy meter gives an LED pulse per watt-hour unit. The timer counts them in hardware while the CPU sleeps or does other work. Every second, the program reads the count, computes the rate, and resets it. No pulse is missed, even very short ones, because no software is involved in the counting.

The millis() idea: Arduino's millis() is a perfect case study. On the Uno, Timer0 runs with N = 64 and overflows every 1.024 ms. Its overflow ISR adds to a 32-bit millisecond count and keeps a fractional part, so every so often it adds an extra millisecond to stay correct on average. millis() simply returns that count. Because it is a 32-bit unsigned value, it wraps after 2^32 ms, about 49.7 days. If your device is meant to run for months, your time comparisons must survive that wrap.

Non-blocking delays: Here is the most useful pattern in embedded programming: if (millis() - last >= 500) { last += 500; toggleLed(); }. The loop runs freely, doing other things, and only toggles the LED when 500 ms have passed. Because the subtraction is done with unsigned integers, it gives the correct elapsed time even across the 49.7-day wrap. Writing if (millis() >= last + 500) instead is a bug that appears after about 49.7 days, when last + 500 wraps around. Using last += 500 instead of last = millis() also keeps the average rate exact even if a check happens a little late.

Why not delay()? delay(500) makes the CPU spin doing nothing for 500 ms. Two jobs with different periods, say an LED every 500 ms and a sensor every 200 ms, become impossible to combine cleanly with delays. With timers and non-blocking checks, you can run dozens of periodic jobs in one loop. This is the foundation of the super-loop design in lesson 21 and of an RTOS tick in the lessons after it.

Timer resolution and accuracy: A timer is only as accurate as its clock. A crystal is typically accurate to tens of parts per million; an internal RC oscillator can be off by a percent or more, and it drifts with temperature. One percent of a day is about 14 minutes, which is why clocks and data loggers use a crystal or a separate real-time clock chip with a 32.768 kHz watch crystal (2^15 Hz, so a 15-bit counter overflows exactly once per second). Resolution is the tick time: with N = 64 you cannot measure better than 4 us. Pick the prescaler for the job: small N for fine resolution, large N for long periods.

Real life example 1, a mosque prayer clock: Digital prayer-time clocks seen in many mosques in Bangladesh show the time and the next prayer, and some beep before the jamaat. Inside, a crystal or RTC chip keeps time, a timer tick of a few milliseconds scans the multiplexed seven-segment display fast enough to look steady, and a one-second event updates the clock. The same few timers handle display refresh, button debouncing and the beep.

Real life example 2, a bicycle speedometer: A small magnet on the wheel passes a sensor once per revolution. Using input capture, the MCU measures the time between pulses. If the wheel circumference is 2 m and the time between pulses is 0.5 s, the speed is 4 m/s, which is 14.4 km/h. When the bike stops, no new pulse arrives, so the firmware also uses a timeout: if no pulse in 3 s, show 0. Timers measure, and timers also decide when to give up waiting.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the minus 1 in OCR = counts - 1. Choosing a prescaler where the count does not fit in the register (above 255 or 65,535). Using two different libraries that both reconfigure the same timer, for example a servo library and a tone library fighting over Timer1, so one of them breaks. Comparing times with >= on raw values instead of unsigned subtraction. Doing heavy work inside a timer ISR so that it runs longer than its own period.

What exams ask: Define timer and counter and the role of the prescaler. Compute the tick time, overflow time and OCR value for a given clock, prescaler and period (16 MHz, N = 64, 1 ms gives OCR = 249; 1 s with N = 256 gives OCR = 62,499). Explain normal, CTC and input capture modes. Compute frequency from two capture values. Explain why non-blocking delays are preferred.

Recap: A timer is a hardware counter clocked by a prescaled system clock; a counter counts external pulses. Tick = N / f_clk; overflow period = (max + 1) x tick; CTC period = (OCR + 1) x tick. Compare match gives exact periodic interrupts, input capture timestamps external edges, and counter mode counts events with no CPU effort. millis() and unsigned subtraction give non-blocking timing that survives wraparound. Next lesson: the timer's most visible trick, PWM.
key_points: A timer is a hardware counter clocked by the (prescaled) system clock; in counter mode it counts external pulses instead.
Tick time = N / f_clk; at 16 MHz with prescaler 64 the tick is 4 us, so 1 ms = 250 counts.
Overflow period = (max + 1) x tick: an 8-bit timer with N = 64 overflows every 1.024 ms.
In CTC mode the period is (OCR + 1) x tick: 1 ms needs OCR = 249 (N = 64); 1 s needs OCR = 62,499 (N = 256, 16-bit).
Input capture copies the count at the instant of an edge; the difference of two captures gives period or pulse width.
Arduino millis() comes from Timer0 overflow and wraps after about 49.7 days.
Non-blocking timing uses unsigned subtraction: if (millis() - last >= interval), which survives wraparound.
Timer accuracy depends on the clock source: crystals are far better than internal RC oscillators.
lessons.tip: Keep one line on your desk: tick = N / f_clk, counts = time / tick, OCR = counts - 1. Almost every timer question, in exams and in real projects, is these three steps plus checking that the count fits in 8 or 16 bits.
lessons.task: For a 16 MHz MCU, find a prescaler (1, 8, 64, 256 or 1024) and OCR value for a 16-bit timer in CTC mode to give interrupts every 10 ms and every 250 ms. Check each answer with f = 16,000,000 / (N x (OCR + 1)) on a phone calculator.

quiz.q: At 16 MHz with a prescaler of 64, what is one timer tick?
What OCR value gives a 1 ms period in CTC mode at 16 MHz with N = 64?
quiz.explain: 1 ms / 4 us = 250 counts, and OCR = counts - 1 = 249.

quiz.q: An 8-bit timer runs with a 4 us tick. How often does it overflow?
Input capture with a 0.5 us tick records 1,000 and then 3,000 on two rising edges. What is the signal frequency?
quiz.explain: 2,000 ticks x 0.5 us = 1 ms period, so 1 kHz.

quiz.q: Which check keeps working after millis() wraps around?
quiz.explain: Unsigned subtraction gives the correct elapsed time even across the wrap.

lessons.title: PWM: Making Analog-like Control from a Digital Pin
lessons.content:
Picture a ceiling fan regulator in a Dhaka home during a hot June afternoon. You turn the knob and the fan slows down or speeds up. Now picture a phone screen dimming at night, or an LED strip in a wedding gate fading in and out. In each case something is being run at "partly on". But a microcontroller pin only knows two states: fully on at the supply voltage, or fully off at 0 V. So how does a digital chip produce "40% brightness" or "half speed"? The trick is to switch fully on and fully off very fast, and control what fraction of the time it stays on. This is Pulse Width Modulation, PWM, and it is the timer's most visible job.

The core idea: Turn a light on for 1 second and off for 1 second, and you see blinking. Do the same 1,000 times per second and your eye cannot follow; it sees a light at about half brightness. A motor is similar: its rotor and load have inertia, so it cannot speed up and slow down a thousand times a second; it settles at a speed set by the average power. PWM uses this averaging done by eyes, motors, heaters and simple filters. The output is purely digital, but the effect on the load is analog-like.

Period, frequency and duty cycle: A PWM signal repeats with a fixed period T; the frequency is f = 1 / T. In each period the signal is high for a time t_on and low for the rest. The duty cycle is D = t_on / T, written as a percentage. A 1 kHz signal has T = 1 ms; if it is high for 0.25 ms, D = 25%. Duty 0% means always off, 100% always on, 50% a square wave. Frequency and duty are independent: frequency says how fast the pattern repeats, duty says how much of each repeat is on.

Average voltage: For an ideal PWM between 0 and V_high, the average voltage is V_avg = D x V_high. On a 5 V pin, 25% duty gives 0.25 x 5 = 1.25 V on average, and 50% gives 2.5 V. Be careful with words: the pin never actually sits at 1.25 V. It is at 5 V a quarter of the time and 0 V the rest. Only after averaging, by a filter, a motor or an eye, does it behave like 1.25 V. Power into a resistive load such as a heater is proportional to duty too, which is why PWM is efficient: the switching transistor is either fully on (low voltage drop) or fully off (no current), so it wastes little heat compared with a resistor that drops the extra voltage.

How a timer makes PWM: In the timer lesson we saw the counter and the compare register OCR. For PWM, the counter runs repeatedly from 0 up to a top value TOP. The output pin is set high when the counter restarts at 0, and cleared when the counter matches OCR. So the pin is high for counts 0 to OCR and low for the rest. The hardware does this forever, with zero CPU effort. To change brightness, your program just writes a new OCR value. This is called fast PWM, non-inverting mode, on the AVR. Inverting mode simply swaps high and low.

The fast PWM frequency formula: The counter runs through TOP + 1 counts per period, each lasting N / f_clk. So f_PWM = f_clk / (N x (TOP + 1)). On a 16 MHz ATmega328P with an 8-bit timer (TOP = 255): with N = 8, f = 16,000,000 / (8 x 256) = 7,812.5 Hz; with N = 64, f = 16,000,000 / (64 x 256) = 976.5625 Hz. That second number is exactly why Arduino's analogWrite on Uno pins 5 and 6 runs at about 980 Hz. The other PWM pins use phase-correct mode, where the counter counts up and then down, which halves the frequency to about 490 Hz (16,000,000 / (64 x 510)).

Duty cycle from OCR: In fast non-inverting mode the pin is high for OCR + 1 counts out of TOP + 1, so D = (OCR + 1) / (TOP + 1). For 25% duty with TOP = 255, we need (OCR + 1) = 64, so OCR = 63. For 50%, OCR = 127. One subtle point on the AVR: OCR = 0 does not give exactly 0%, it gives a very narrow pulse of one count each period. That is why Arduino's analogWrite(pin, 0) simply turns the pin fully off instead of using the timer. Read the datasheet for such edge cases on any chip.

Resolution versus frequency: The number of possible duty steps is TOP + 1. With TOP = 255 you have 256 steps, which is 8-bit resolution. With TOP = 1023 you get 10-bit resolution, 1,024 steps. But a larger TOP means a longer period and a lower frequency. With no prescaler (N = 1) at 16 MHz, 8-bit PWM can reach 16,000,000 / 256 = 62.5 kHz, but 10-bit PWM only 16,000,000 / 1,024 = 15.625 kHz. This trade-off is fixed by the clock: f_PWM x (number of steps) cannot exceed f_clk / N. Faster chips such as STM32 at 72 MHz or more give you both higher frequency and finer resolution.

Choosing the frequency: Different loads want different frequencies. For LEDs, the frequency must be high enough that there is no visible flicker, including when the camera of a phone films it; a few hundred hertz is often enough for the eye, while higher values help with cameras. For DC motors, low frequencies produce audible whining and jerky torque, so motor drivers often use around 20 kHz or more, just above the range most people hear. PC cooling fans with 4-pin connectors use a 25 kHz PWM control signal. For heaters, which change temperature slowly, even a period of a second or more is fine. Too high a frequency also has a cost: transistors lose more energy in every switching edge, so more edges per second means more heat.

Servo motors, a special case: A hobby servo, like the SG90 used in student projects, is not controlled by duty cycle in the usual sense. It expects a pulse about every 20 ms, a 50 Hz frame, and the width of the pulse sets the angle: roughly 1 ms for one end, 1.5 ms for the centre and 2 ms for the other end. The exact limits vary between servo models, so you calibrate. The servo has its own electronics that compare the pulse width with a position sensor inside.

Worked servo setup: On the 16-bit Timer1 at 16 MHz, choose N = 8, so one tick is 0.5 us. For 50 Hz we need a period of 20 ms = 40,000 ticks, so TOP = 39,999 (on the AVR, TOP is held in the ICR1 register in this mode). Check: 16,000,000 / (8 x 40,000) = 50 Hz. Now the pulse widths: 1 ms = 2,000 ticks, 1.5 ms = 3,000 ticks, 2 ms = 4,000 ticks. Using D = (OCR + 1) / (TOP + 1), OCR for the centre is 2,999, close enough to say "about 3,000". Between the ends we have 2,000 ticks of range, so with 0.5 us steps the angle resolution is very fine, much better than with an 8-bit timer.

Driving real loads with PWM: The PWM pin itself still has the GPIO current limits. For an LED, a pin and resistor is fine. For a motor, the pin drives a MOSFET or a motor driver chip, and for a motor that needs both directions, an H-bridge, where one input sets direction and the PWM input sets speed. The flyback diode, or the driver's built-in diodes, is essential because the motor's inductance creates voltage spikes every time PWM switches off. You met these driver circuits in Peripherals & Interfacing; the firmware side is just: set the PWM frequency once, then change OCR to change speed.

Ramping and soft start: Jumping a motor from 0% to 100% duty instantly causes a big inrush current, mechanical jerk and sometimes a reset of the MCU if the power supply dips. Good firmware ramps: increase OCR by a small step every few milliseconds using a timer tick. A water pump in an irrigation system or a conveyor belt in a factory starts much more gently this way. The same smooth ramp makes LED fades look natural.

Brightness is not linear: Our eyes are more sensitive to changes at low brightness than at high brightness. A 10% duty LED looks much brighter than one-tenth of full, and going from 80% to 100% barely looks different. So LED dimmers often use a gamma or lookup table: a slider position is mapped to a duty that grows slowly at first and faster later. The table lives in flash as a const array, a good example of the embedded C ideas from lesson 6.

PWM as a cheap DAC: If you need an actual steady analog voltage, put a low-pass RC filter after the PWM pin. Its cutoff frequency f_c = 1 / (2 x pi x R x C) must be far below the PWM frequency. For example, R = 10 kilo-ohm and C = 1 microfarad give f_c of about 15.9 Hz. With a 7,812.5 Hz PWM, the ripple is small, and the output settles at about D x 5 V. The cost is slow response: the voltage needs many milliseconds to settle after a duty change. For audio or fast signals, a real DAC is better, as we will see in the next lesson.

Real life example 1, a solar charge controller: Many homes and shops in rural Bangladesh use solar home systems with a battery. The charge controller uses PWM on a MOSFET between the panel and the battery. When the battery is low, duty is near 100% to push maximum current. As the battery approaches full, the controller lowers the duty to hold the voltage at a safe level without overcharging. It is the same OCR update loop, just with a voltage measurement deciding the duty.

Real life example 2, an LED signboard: A shop sign in Bashundhara City fades from dim to bright and back. Each colour channel of an RGB LED strip has its own PWM output driving a MOSFET.
