Three duty values mix any colour: red 100%, green 50%, blue 0% gives an orange tone. Running at a high PWM frequency keeps the sign from flickering in customers' phone videos.

Common mistakes: Confusing frequency with duty. Thinking the pin outputs a true middle voltage. Forgetting the minus 1 in TOP + 1 or OCR + 1. Choosing a PWM frequency that whines in a motor or flickers on camera. Driving a motor directly from the pin or without a flyback path. Reconfiguring a timer for PWM that is already used by millis() or another library, so delays and time stamps break.

What exams ask: Define duty cycle and compute average voltage (25% of 5 V = 1.25 V). Use f_PWM = f_clk / (N x (TOP + 1)) to find frequency or TOP (N = 8, TOP = 255 gives 7,812.5 Hz; N = 64 gives 976.56 Hz). Compute OCR for a given duty. Explain the resolution versus frequency trade-off. Design a 50 Hz servo signal and its pulse counts (TOP = 39,999; 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 ticks). Explain why PWM is efficient and how an RC filter turns it into a DAC.

Recap: PWM switches a pin fully on and off at a fixed frequency and controls the fraction of on time, the duty cycle. The load averages it, giving brightness, speed or power proportional to duty. A timer produces PWM in hardware: TOP sets the frequency, OCR sets the duty. Higher resolution costs frequency. Servos read pulse width in a 50 Hz frame. Use drivers, ramps and the right frequency for each load. Next lesson: going the other way, turning real analog voltages into numbers with the ADC.
key_points: PWM switches a pin fully on and off quickly; the duty cycle D = t_on / T sets the average effect on the load.
Average voltage = D x V_high: 25% of 5 V gives 1.25 V on average, though the pin is only ever at 0 or 5 V.
A timer makes PWM in hardware: the counter runs 0 to TOP, the pin goes high at 0 and low at the OCR match.
Fast PWM frequency = f_clk / (N x (TOP + 1)): at 16 MHz, TOP = 255 gives 7,812.5 Hz with N = 8 and 976.56 Hz with N = 64.
More duty steps (bigger TOP) means lower frequency: 8-bit at N = 1 reaches 62.5 kHz, 10-bit only 15.625 kHz.
Servos need a 50 Hz frame with 1 to 2 ms pulses: N = 8, TOP = 39,999, pulses of 2,000 to 4,000 ticks.
Motors need drivers, flyback protection, suitable frequency (often 20 kHz or more) and soft-start ramps.
An RC low-pass filter with cutoff far below the PWM frequency turns PWM into a slow, cheap DAC.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a PWM number, ask two separate questions: how often does it repeat (frequency, set by N and TOP) and how much of each cycle is on (duty, set by OCR). Keeping these two apart solves most PWM confusion.
lessons.task: With a 16 MHz clock and prescaler 64, calculate the fast PWM frequency for TOP = 255 and the OCR for 10%, 50% and 75% duty. Then with your phone's slow-motion camera, film a dimmed LED (a phone torch on low, a dimmed lamp or an LED sign) and see whether you can spot the flicker.

quiz.q: A 5 V PWM signal has 25% duty. What is its average voltage?
quiz.explain: V_avg = D x V_high = 0.25 x 5 = 1.25 V.

quiz.q: At 16 MHz, fast PWM with N = 8 and TOP = 255 has what frequency?
Which change gives finer duty resolution but lowers the PWM frequency?
quiz.explain: TOP + 1 is the number of steps; a bigger TOP gives more steps but a longer period.

quiz.q: For a 50 Hz servo frame on Timer1 at 16 MHz with N = 8, how many ticks is a 1.5 ms centre pulse?
quiz.explain: One tick is 0.5 us, so 1.5 ms / 0.5 us = 3,000 ticks.

quiz.q: Why do motor drivers often use PWM around 20 kHz or more?
options: To avoid audible whining from the motor
quiz.explain: Lower PWM frequencies make the motor whine audibly; around 20 kHz and above is mostly beyond human hearing.

lessons.title: ADC and DAC on a Microcontroller: Turning Voltages into Numbers and Back
lessons.content:
Imagine you are building a small box that tells a tea-stall owner in Sylhet how hot his kettle is. The temperature sensor gives a voltage, maybe 0.3 volts. But your microcontroller does not understand volts. Its CPU only knows numbers like 0, 1, 62 or 1023. Somebody has to stand between the smooth, analog world and the digital CPU and translate. That somebody is a peripheral inside the chip called the ADC, the analog-to-digital converter. Its partner, the DAC, does the opposite job. In this lesson we learn how to use them from firmware, with real numbers.

A quick recap first: In Computer Peripherals & Interfacing you met sampling, the Nyquist rule, step size, quantisation error, and ADC types such as flash and successive approximation (SAR). Here we will not rebuild those circuits. We will treat the ADC as a block inside the microcontroller, learn its registers and settings, and learn to turn its raw number into a useful value like 30.3 degrees Celsius. Most microcontroller ADCs, including the ones in the ATmega328P, STM32 and ESP32, are SAR converters, so the SAR idea of guessing one bit at a time is the one to remember.

What the ADC really measures: An ADC never measures a voltage on its own. It compares the input voltage with a reference voltage, called Vref. The result is a fraction: how big is the input compared to Vref? If the input equals half of Vref, the answer is about half of the full range. So the reference is the ruler. If the ruler is wrong, every reading is wrong. This one idea explains most beginner bugs with ADCs.

Resolution: Resolution is how many bits the result has. A 10-bit ADC gives 2 to the power 10 = 1024 different codes, from 0 to 1023. A 12-bit ADC gives 4096 codes, from 0 to 4095. More bits means smaller steps, which means you can notice smaller changes. The ATmega328P on an Arduino Uno has a 10-bit ADC. Many STM32 chips and the ESP32 have 12-bit ADCs.

Step size, worked: The step size is Vref divided by the number of codes. For a 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V, the step is 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. That means the ADC cannot tell apart two voltages that differ by less than about 4.88 mV. For a 12-bit ADC with Vref = 3.3 V, the step is 3.3 / 4096 = 0.806 mV, about six times finer. Step size is sometimes called 1 LSB, because it is the value of the least significant bit.

The conversion formula: For the AVR, the datasheet gives ADC = Vin x 1024 / Vref. Turning it around, the voltage is V = reading x Vref / 1024. Example: on a 5 V Uno, a reading of 512 gives 512 x 5 / 1024 = 2.5 V. For a 12-bit converter you divide by 4096 instead: a reading of 2048 with Vref = 3.3 V gives 2048 x 3.3 / 4096 = 1.65 V. Some books write 1023 or 4095 in the bottom of the fraction. The difference is less than one step, so do not fight about it in an exam, but follow the formula your datasheet or teacher uses and say which one you used.

Worked example with the LM35: The LM35 is a common temperature sensor whose output rises by 10 mV for every degree Celsius. So 0.25 V means 25 C. Suppose the Uno reads 62 on the LM35 pin. Voltage = 62 x 5 / 1024 = 0.303 V. Temperature = 0.303 V / 0.010 V per degree = 30.3 C. In C, using integers to avoid slow floating point on an 8-bit chip, you might write: uint16_t raw = adc_read(0); uint32_t mv = (uint32_t)raw * 5000 / 1024; uint16_t deci_c = mv; Here mv is millivolts, and since the LM35 gives 10 mV per degree, mv is also the temperature in tenths of a degree (303 means 30.3 C). Notice the cast to uint32_t: raw x 5000 can reach about 5 million, which overflows a 16-bit int.

The resolution problem in that example: Each step is 4.88 mV, and the LM35 gives 10 mV per degree, so our resolution is only about half a degree. If you need finer readings, change the ruler. The ATmega328P has an internal reference of about 1.1 V. With Vref = 1.1 V the step becomes 1.1 / 1024 = 1.07 mV, so each step is about 0.1 degree. The catch: now the input must stay below 1.1 V, so the LM35 can only show up to about 110 C. That is fine for a room or a tea kettle, not for an oven. Choosing Vref is choosing between range and fineness.

Where Vref comes from: On the ATmega328P you can choose AVcc (the analog supply, usually 5 V), the internal 1.1 V reference, or an external voltage on the AREF pin. If you use AVcc and your USB supply is actually 4.8 V instead of 5 V, every reading is off by 4%. A stable reference chip or the internal reference helps. On battery devices the supply drops as the battery drains, so a supply-based reference makes readings drift as weeks pass.

Channels and the multiplexer: A microcontroller usually has one ADC but many analog pins. In front of the ADC sits an analog multiplexer, a switch that picks which pin to connect. On the ATmega328P you choose the channel with the MUX bits in the ADMUX register, along with the reference bits. So reading three sensors means: select channel 0, convert, select channel 1, convert, and so on. After switching channels, the first reading can be slightly off because the internal capacitor still holds the old voltage, so many programmers throw away the first sample after a switch.

How a conversion runs, step by step: First select reference and channel. Then start the conversion by setting a start bit (ADSC on the AVR). The ADC samples the input onto a small internal capacitor, then the SAR logic tries bits from most significant to least. When done, it sets a flag and clears the start bit. Firmware either waits in a loop until the bit clears (polling) or lets the ADC-complete interrupt fire. Finally the code reads the result registers. On the AVR you read ADCL first and then ADCH, because reading the low byte locks the result until the high byte is read.

Sampling time and speed: The SAR ADC needs a clock. On the ATmega328P the ADC clock should be between 50 kHz and 200 kHz for full 10-bit accuracy. With a 16 MHz system clock and a prescaler of 128, the ADC clock is 16,000,000 / 128 = 125 kHz. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, which is 13 / 125,000 = 104 microseconds. That gives roughly 9,600 conversions per second. Enough for temperature, light and soil moisture, nowhere near enough for audio at 44.1 kHz. If you need faster sampling, you need a faster ADC, often found in 32-bit chips.

Source impedance: Inside, the ADC charges a tiny capacitor during the sample phase. If your sensor circuit has a high resistance, like a voltage divider made of two 1 megaohm resistors, the capacitor cannot charge fully in time and the reading comes out low. AVR datasheets recommend a source impedance of 10 kilohm or less. The fixes are smaller divider resistors, a small capacitor at the pin, or a slower sampling setting.

Noise and averaging: Real readings jump around by a few counts, from supply ripple, motor noise and the sensor itself. A simple cure is to take several samples and average them. If the noise is random, averaging 16 samples reduces it by about a factor of 4, the square root of 16. Other tricks: keep analog wires short, put a 100 nF capacitor near the supply pins, avoid reading while a motor is switching, and use the sleep-mode noise reduction feature some MCUs offer, where the CPU sleeps during the conversion so its own switching noise stays quiet.

Calibration: Even a perfect formula meets an imperfect sensor. A cheap sensor might read 2 degrees high. The fix is calibration: measure a known value (ice water at 0 C, a good thermometer at room temperature) and store an offset or a gain correction in EEPROM. For a sensor with a straight-line response, two known points are enough to find both gain and offset. The ESP32 is a known example: its ADC is not perfectly linear, and Espressif provides calibration functions for that reason.

The DAC, the reverse direction: A DAC takes a number and outputs a voltage: V = code x Vref / 2^n. The ESP32 has two 8-bit DAC channels. With 3.3 V full scale the step is 3.3 / 256 = 12.9 mV, and writing 128 gives about 1.65 V. Uses include generating a test voltage, simple audio tones, or a bias voltage for another circuit. Many STM32 parts also include a 12-bit DAC. The ATmega328P has no DAC at all.

The poor man's DAC: When there is no DAC, we fake one with PWM followed by an RC low-pass filter, as you saw in the previous lesson. A 25% duty cycle on a 5 V pin, smoothed by the filter, gives about 1.25 V. It is cheap and good enough for LED brightness or a slow control voltage, but it has ripple and responds slowly. This is why Arduino calls its PWM function analogWrite even though the pin is still only switching between 0 and 5 V.

Real life example 1, a cold storage monitor in Bogura: Potato cold storages must keep the room around a fixed low temperature. An engineer uses an STM32 with a 12-bit ADC and a temperature sensor. She reads every second, averages 16 samples to remove noise, converts with V = reading x 3.3 / 4096, applies the calibration offset measured with a lab thermometer, and sends an alarm if the temperature leaves the safe band. Because the supply voltage varies when the compressor starts, she uses a stable reference so the reading does not jump every time the motor kicks in.

Real life example 2, a phone battery meter: Your phone or a power bank wants to know battery voltage. A lithium cell can be above 4 V, more than a 3.3 V MCU can read directly. So designers use a voltage divider, for example two equal resistors, to halve the voltage. The ADC sees half, the firmware multiplies by two. To save battery, the divider is often switched on only during the measurement, because a divider always connected drains a little current all day.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that Vref is the ruler and assuming 5 V when the supply is really 4.8 V. Overflowing a 16-bit int in the conversion math. Feeding a voltage higher than the supply into an analog pin, which can damage the chip. Using huge divider resistors so the sample capacitor cannot charge. Reading right after switching channels. Thinking analogWrite on an Uno is a real DAC.

What exams ask: Find the step size for n bits and a given Vref. Convert a reading to voltage and then to a physical quantity, like the LM35 example. Find the minimum number of bits for a required resolution. Explain the role of the multiplexer, reference and prescaler. Compute conversion time from ADC clock and cycles. Compare a real DAC with PWM plus RC filter.

Recap: The ADC compares an input with Vref and returns a code from 0 to 2^n - 1. Step size is Vref / 2^n, and voltage is reading x Vref / 2^n. Choose Vref to trade range against fineness. Respect the ADC clock, source impedance and channel switching. Fight noise with averaging and good layout, and fix sensor error with calibration. A DAC goes the other way, and PWM plus a filter is the cheap substitute when there is no DAC. Next lesson: interrupts, so the CPU does not have to wait for every conversion.
key_points: An ADC compares the input with a reference voltage Vref; the reference is the ruler for every reading.
An n-bit ADC has 2^n codes; step size = Vref / 2^n (10-bit at 5 V = 4.88 mV, 12-bit at 3.3 V = 0.806 mV).
Voltage = reading x Vref / 2^n; on a 5 V Uno a reading of 512 is 2.5 V.
LM35 gives 10 mV per degree: reading 62 -> 0.303 V -> 30.3 C; a 1.1 V reference gives finer steps but a smaller range.
One ADC serves many pins through a multiplexer; discard the first sample after switching channels.
ATmega328P: ADC clock 50-200 kHz, 16 MHz / 128 = 125 kHz, 13 clocks = 104 us per conversion.
Averaging, good layout and low source impedance fight noise; calibration fixes sensor offset and gain.
A DAC turns a code into a voltage (ESP32 has 8-bit DACs); PWM plus an RC filter is the cheap substitute.
lessons.tip: Every time you see an ADC reading, say the sentence out loud: reading divided by full scale, times Vref. If you cannot say what Vref is, you do not yet know what the reading means.
lessons.task: On paper, make a table for a 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V: readings 0, 100, 256, 512, 800 and 1023 in one column, the voltage in the next, and the LM35 temperature in the third. Then redo the voltage column for Vref = 1.1 V and note which readings would now be impossible for a hot oven.

quiz.q: What is the step size of a 10-bit ADC with Vref = 5 V?
An Uno (10-bit, Vref = 5 V) reads 62 from an LM35. What is the temperature?
Why might you switch the ATmega328P to its internal 1.1 V reference for an LM35?
options: To get finer steps, about 1.07 mV, at the cost of a smaller input range
To make conversions twice as fast
To allow inputs up to 10 V
To turn the ADC into a DAC
quiz.explain: A smaller Vref means smaller steps (1.1 / 1024 = 1.07 mV), but inputs above 1.1 V can no longer be measured.

quiz.q: With a 16 MHz clock and prescaler 128, how long does a normal 13-cycle AVR conversion take?
quiz.explain: ADC clock = 125 kHz, so 13 / 125,000 s = 104 microseconds.

quiz.q: Which statement about analogWrite on an Arduino Uno is true?
options: It outputs PWM, which only becomes a steady voltage after an RC filter
quiz.explain: The ATmega328P has no DAC; analogWrite produces PWM, and an RC low-pass filter averages it into a voltage.

lessons.title: Interrupts on Microcontrollers: ISRs, Latency, Priorities and Shared Data
lessons.content:
Imagine a shopkeeper in Mirpur who is also cooking rice in the back room. He could walk to the front door every ten seconds to check whether a customer has come. That wastes his time and the rice may burn. Or he could hang a bell on the door. When a customer walks in, the bell rings, he stops stirring, serves the customer quickly, and goes back to the pot exactly where he left off. The bell is an interrupt. A microcontroller lives this way all day: a timer finishes, a byte arrives on the UART, a button is pressed, and the CPU must react without constantly checking.

A quick recap: In Microprocessors & Assembly you learned polling versus interrupts, the 8086 interrupt vector table of 256 entries at address 0000:0000, IRET, and the 8259 PIC that collects requests from many devices. You also saw in Operating Systems how interrupts drive the kernel. A microcontroller uses the same idea but packs everything inside one chip: the interrupt controller, the vector table and the devices that raise requests. This lesson is about using that machinery safely from C.

What an interrupt is on an MCU: An interrupt is a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause the normal program, run a special function called an interrupt service routine (ISR), and then return to exactly the instruction it was about to run. Sources inside the chip include timers (overflow, compare match), the UART (byte received, transmit buffer empty), the ADC (conversion complete), SPI and I2C, pin changes and external interrupt pins, and the watchdog. Each source has its own entry in the vector table.

The vector table: On most MCUs the vector table sits at the start of flash memory. On the AVR each entry holds a jump instruction to the ISR. On ARM Cortex-M each entry holds the address of the handler, and the very first entries hold the initial stack pointer and the reset handler address. You almost never write this table by hand. In avr-gcc you write ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) { ... } and the compiler puts the address in the right slot. On STM32 the startup file lists names like USART1_IRQHandler, and you simply define a C function with that exact name.

Three switches must be on: For an interrupt to fire, usually three things must be true. First, the peripheral's own enable bit must be set, for example the receive-complete interrupt enable bit in the UART control register. Second, the global interrupt enable must be on: on the AVR that is the I bit in the status register, set with sei() and cleared with cli(). On Cortex-M the NVIC also has a per-interrupt enable bit. Third, the event must actually happen, which sets the peripheral's interrupt flag. Forgetting one of these is the classic reason an ISR never runs.

What the CPU does, step by step: The event sets a flag. When the current instruction finishes, the CPU checks for pending enabled interrupts. If one is waiting, it saves the return address (and on Cortex-M several registers too) on the stack, disables or masks further interrupts as the architecture requires, and jumps through the vector to the ISR. The ISR runs. At the end a special return instruction (RETI on the AVR, an exception return on Cortex-M) restores everything and the main program continues as if nothing happened.

Clearing the flag: If the flag stays set after the ISR returns, the CPU sees it pending again and jumps right back in, forever, and the main program freezes. On the AVR many flags are cleared automatically when the vector is taken, and some, like the UART receive flag, clear when you read the data register. On STM32, many peripherals require you to clear the pending flag yourself inside the handler. Always check the datasheet for each source.

The golden rules of an ISR: Keep it short: grab the data, set a flag, get out. Do not call delay functions inside an ISR, because while you wait, other interrupts may be blocked and data is lost. Avoid printf and other slow library calls; sending 50 characters at 9600 baud takes about 52 ms, an eternity. Do not wait in a loop for some other event. Make variables shared with the main program volatile, so the compiler re-reads them from memory instead of keeping a stale copy in a register. And do the heavy work, like calculating, logging or updating a display, in the main loop when it sees the flag.

A tiny example: volatile uint8_t tick = 0; ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) { tick = 1; } int main(void) { setup_timer(); sei(); while (1) { if (tick) { tick = 0; read_sensor(); update_lcd(); } } } The ISR does one store. The main loop does the slow work. This pattern, a short ISR plus a flag handled in the loop, is the backbone of most bare-metal firmware.

Interrupt latency: Latency is the time from the event until the first useful instruction of the ISR runs. It has several parts: finishing the current instruction, the hardware's own response time, saving registers, and any time interrupts were disabled by other code. The ATmega328P datasheet gives a minimum response of four clock cycles, which at 16 MHz is 0.25 microseconds, plus the compiler's register saving at the start of the ISR. On Cortex-M3 and M4 the hardware entry takes 12 cycles with zero-wait-state memory, and the hardware itself saves eight registers, so C handlers need no special keywords. The biggest real-world latency source is usually your own code: a long ISR or a long cli() section delays everyone else.

The CPU cost of interrupts, worked: Suppose an ISR takes 50 microseconds and fires 1,000 times per second. It uses 50 microseconds x 1,000 = 50 ms of every second, which is 5% of the CPU. If someone changes the rate to 10,000 per second, it becomes 50%, and the main loop starts to crawl. If the rate goes to 20,000 per second, the ISR needs 100% of the time and the system collapses. Always estimate time per ISR times rate.

Priorities: What if two interrupts are pending at once? On the AVR the priority is fixed by position in the vector table: a lower vector address means higher priority, so the external interrupt INT0 beats a timer. On Cortex-M, the NVIC lets you assign a priority number to each interrupt, and a lower number means more urgent. The number of priority levels depends on the chip; many STM32 parts use 4 bits, giving 16 levels.

Nesting: Nesting means a more urgent interrupt can interrupt an ISR that is already running. On the AVR, the I bit is cleared automatically on entry, so by default ISRs do not nest. You can re-enable interrupts inside an ISR, but this is risky and rarely needed. On Cortex-M nesting is built in: a higher-priority interrupt preempts a lower-priority handler automatically. Cortex-M also has tail-chaining: if another interrupt is pending when one handler ends, the CPU jumps straight into the next handler without restoring and re-saving all registers, which saves cycles.

Shared data and the torn read: Here is a sneaky bug. On an 8-bit AVR, a 16-bit variable is read as two separate bytes. Suppose an ISR increments a uint16_t counter, and the main program reads it. The counter is 0x00FF (255). Main reads the low byte: 0xFF. Before it reads the high byte, the ISR fires and the counter becomes 0x0100 (256). Main now reads the high byte: 0x01. It assembles 0x01FF, which is 511, a value that never existed. volatile does not help here; volatile only stops caching, it does not make the read a single step.

Critical sections, the fix: Disable interrupts for the few instructions that copy the shared variable, then re-enable them: cli(); uint16_t copy = counter; sei(); avr-libc provides ATOMIC_BLOCK(ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE) { copy = counter; } which also restores the previous interrupt state correctly. Keep these sections tiny, because every microsecond with interrupts off adds to the worst-case latency of every interrupt. On 32-bit Cortex-M, a single aligned 32-bit read or write is atomic, but read-modify-write operations like counter++ are not, so the same care applies.

External and pin-change interrupts: An external interrupt pin (INT0 and INT1 on the ATmega328P) can be set to trigger on a low level, any change, a falling edge or a rising edge. Pin-change interrupts cover groups of pins but only tell you that something in the group changed, so the ISR must read the pins to find which. Mechanical buttons bounce, as you saw in the debouncing lesson, so one press can fire many interrupts. For buttons, a timer-based sampling scan is often simpler and more reliable than edge interrupts.

Interrupts and sleep: Interrupts are also the alarm clock that wakes a sleeping MCU. The firmware sets up a wake source, such as a timer, a pin change or a UART byte, and puts the CPU to sleep. When the interrupt arrives, the CPU wakes, runs the ISR, and continues. We will use this heavily in the power management lesson.

Real life example 1, an electricity prepaid meter: The meter counts energy pulses from its measuring chip. Each pulse triggers an interrupt that increments a counter, a job of a few instructions. A timer interrupt every second sets a flag. The main loop, seeing the flag, recalculates the remaining balance, updates the display and checks whether to cut supply when credit runs out. If someone made the pulse ISR also update the LCD, pulses arriving during the slow display write could be missed, and the customer would be billed wrongly.

Real life example 2, a motorbike engine controller: An engine control unit must fire the spark plug at a precise crank angle. A sensor on the crankshaft produces a pulse each time a tooth passes, and an input capture interrupt timestamps it. Missing or delaying it by even a short time means the spark comes at the wrong moment. Here interrupt priority is a design decision: the crank interrupt gets the highest priority, while diagnostics and dashboard communication run at lower priority.

Common mistakes: Forgetting sei() or the peripheral enable bit. Not clearing the flag, so the ISR runs forever. Calling delay or printf in an ISR. Shared variables without volatile. Reading multi-byte shared variables without a critical section. Leaving interrupts disabled for a long time. Assuming the ISR name is correct when a typo in a Cortex-M handler name silently sends the interrupt to the default handler, which often just loops forever.

What exams ask: Define ISR and interrupt latency and list what contributes to latency. Compare polling and interrupts for an MCU. Explain the steps the CPU takes on an interrupt. State ISR design rules. Explain the role of volatile and why it is not enough for atomicity. Compute CPU load from ISR time and rate. Describe priority and nesting on AVR versus Cortex-M NVIC.

Recap: An interrupt makes the CPU jump through the vector table to a short ISR and then return. It needs the peripheral enable, the global enable and the event. Clear flags, keep ISRs short, share data through volatile flags and copy multi-byte data inside short critical sections. Latency is the sum of instruction completion, hardware response, register saving and disabled time. AVR priorities are fixed by vector order with no nesting by default, while the Cortex-M NVIC gives programmable priorities, nesting and tail-chaining. Next we put interrupts to work in the UART.
key_points: An interrupt pauses the main program, runs an ISR through the vector table, then returns to the exact next instruction.
An interrupt fires only if the peripheral enable bit, the global enable (sei on AVR) and the event flag are all present.
Clear the interrupt flag (automatic for many AVR sources, often manual on STM32) or the ISR re-enters forever.
ISR rules: short, no delay or printf, set a volatile flag and do heavy work in the main loop.
Latency = finish current instruction + hardware response + register saving + time interrupts were disabled.
CPU load = ISR time x rate: 50 us at 1,000 per second uses 5% of the CPU.
AVR: fixed priority by vector order, no nesting by default; Cortex-M NVIC: programmable priorities, nesting, tail-chaining.
volatile is not atomic: copy multi-byte shared data inside a short critical section (cli/sei or ATOMIC_BLOCK).
lessons.tip: For every ISR you write, fill in one line in a comment: what sets the flag, who clears it, how long the ISR takes and how often it runs. If you cannot fill all four, the ISR is not finished.
lessons.task: On paper, simulate the torn read: start a 16-bit counter at 0x00FF, read the low byte, let an imaginary ISR add 1, then read the high byte. Write the value you get. Repeat with the counter starting at 0x01FF and see what wrong value appears.

quiz.q: An ISR runs again and again and the main program freezes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The global interrupt enable is off
The interrupt flag is never cleared
The vector table is in flash
quiz.explain: If the flag stays set after the ISR returns, the CPU sees the interrupt pending again and re-enters immediately.

quiz.q: An ISR takes 50 microseconds and fires 1,000 times per second. What share of CPU time does it use?
quiz.explain: 50 us x 1,000 = 50 ms per second = 5% of the CPU.

quiz.q: Why does volatile alone not protect a 16-bit counter shared with an ISR on an 8-bit AVR?
options: volatile puts the variable in flash
The 16-bit read takes two steps and the ISR can change the value in between
quiz.explain: volatile forces fresh reads, but the read still happens as two byte accesses; a critical section is needed.

quiz.q: On an ARM Cortex-M NVIC, what does a lower priority number mean?
quiz.explain: On Cortex-M, a numerically lower priority value is more urgent and can preempt higher-numbered handlers.

quiz.q: Which action is acceptable inside a typical ISR?
options: Printing a long message with printf
Storing a received byte in a buffer and setting a flag
Waiting in a loop for a button press
quiz.explain: ISRs should be short: capture data, set a flag, and leave the slow work to the main loop.

lessons.title: UART in Firmware: Frames, Baud Rate Registers and Ring Buffers
lessons.content:
Imagine two friends on opposite rooftops in Old Dhaka sending messages with a torch. They agree beforehand: a long dark means I am waiting, a quick flash means a letter is starting, then eight blinks for the eight bits, then darkness again. Both count with the same rhythm, so neither needs to shout the timing. That is exactly how a UART works. It is the oldest, simplest and still the most used way for a microcontroller to talk to a PC, a GPS module, a GSM modem or another microcontroller.

A quick recap: In Computer Peripherals & Interfacing you met serial versus parallel, bit rate and baud, the asynchronous frame with start, data, parity and stop bits, and RS-232 levels with the MAX232 level shifter. In Microprocessors you saw the 8251 USART chip. Here the UART is a peripheral inside the MCU, and our job is to program it: pick the baud rate register value, check the error, send and receive bytes, use interrupts and a ring buffer, and design a tiny command protocol on top.

What UART means: UART stands for universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter. Asynchronous means there is no shared clock wire. Each side has its own clock, and they only agree on the speed, the baud rate. The wiring is minimal: TX of one device goes to RX of the other, RX to TX, and the grounds are connected. That crossing, TX to RX, is the first thing to check when nothing works.

The frame, again in one breath: The line rests at logic 1, called idle. A frame begins with a start bit of 0, which tells the receiver to start counting. Then come the data bits, usually 8, least significant bit first. An optional parity bit follows. Then one or two stop bits of 1 return the line to idle. The common setting is written 8N1: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. So each byte costs 10 bits on the wire.

Worked frame for the letter A: In ASCII, A is 0x41, which is 01000001 in binary. Sent LSB first, the data bits go out in the order 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. So the full 8N1 frame on the wire is: idle 1, start 0, then 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0, then stop 1. Ten bits in total. At 9600 baud each bit lasts 1 / 9600 = 104.17 microseconds, so the frame lasts about 1.04 ms. If you look at the line with a logic analyzer you will see a low start bit, one high bit, five lows, one high, one low, and then the line goes high.

Throughput, worked: At 9600 baud with 8N1, 10 bits per byte means at most 9600 / 10 = 960 bytes per second. At 115200 baud you get 11,520 bytes per second, and one byte takes about 86.8 microseconds. This matters. If your code prints a 64-character debug line at 9600 baud, it takes about 64 x 1.04 = 67 ms. A control loop that must run every 10 ms will simply break if it waits for that print.

How the receiver stays in step: Since there is no clock wire, the receiver must sample each bit near its middle. Many UARTs, including the AVR's in normal mode, run an internal clock 16 times faster than the baud rate. When they see the falling edge of the start bit, they wait about half a bit, check that the line is still low, and then sample every 16 ticks, landing near the middle of each data bit. Small speed differences between the two sides are tolerated because the timing is re-synchronised at every start bit, so errors only build up over one frame of 10 bits.

The baud rate register: The UART gets its timing by dividing the CPU clock. On the AVR in normal mode the formula is UBRR = fclk / (16 x baud) - 1, and the register can only hold a whole number. For a 16 MHz Uno at 9600 baud: 16,000,000 / (16 x 9600) - 1 = 103.17, so we write 103. The actual baud is 16,000,000 / (16 x 104) = 9,615 baud, an error of about 0.16%. That is tiny and perfectly fine.

When the error is too big: Now try 115200 baud at 16 MHz: 16,000,000 / (16 x 115200) - 1 = 7.68. Round to 8, and the actual rate becomes 16,000,000 / (16 x 9) = 111,111 baud, about 3.5% slow. Because the receiver samples mid-bit and error builds up over 10 bits, a total mismatch above roughly 2% starts to cause wrong bytes. The AVR has a double-speed mode (U2X) using 8 instead of 16 in the formula; then UBRR = 16.36, rounded to 16, gives 117,647 baud, about 2.1% fast. Usable on many setups, but borderline.

Why some boards use odd crystals: This is why you see crystals like 14.7456 MHz. 14,745,600 / (16 x 115200) = 8 exactly, so UBRR = 7 with 0% error, and 9600 gives UBRR = 95 exactly. The crystal value is chosen to divide cleanly into standard baud rates. The trade-off is a slightly slower CPU clock than 16 MHz. Also remember: if one side uses an internal RC oscillator that can be off by a few percent, UART at high speed may fail even when the formula looks perfect. Real clocks drift, so measure or calibrate when it matters.

Voltage levels: The MCU's UART pins use logic levels, often called TTL serial: 0 V for 0 and the supply (5 V or 3.3 V) for 1, idle high. Classic RS-232, as in old PC COM ports, uses opposite-sign voltages, roughly -3 V to -15 V for a 1 and +3 V to +15 V for a 0. Never connect an RS-232 port directly to an MCU pin; use a level shifter. Also take care when a 5 V board talks to a 3.3 V module like an ESP8266: the 5 V TX can damage the 3.3 V RX unless you use a divider or level shifter.

USB to serial: Modern laptops have no COM port, so we use a USB-to-serial chip such as the FT232, CP2102 or CH340, which appears on the PC as a virtual COM port. The Arduino Uno has one built in: a second small chip (an ATmega16U2) handles USB and talks UART to the ATmega328P. That is how Serial.println messages reach the serial monitor on your laptop.

Sending a byte by polling: On the AVR you wait until the data register empty flag (UDRE0) is set, then write the byte into UDR0: while (!(UCSR0A & (1 << UDRE0))) { } UDR0 = c; Simple, but the CPU sits doing nothing while each byte goes out. Receiving by polling is similar: wait for the receive complete flag RXC0, then read UDR0. If your main loop is busy for longer than one byte time when data arrives, the next byte overwrites the old one and you lose data; the hardware sets an overrun flag to tell you.

Receiving with an interrupt and a ring buffer: The robust way is to let the receive-complete interrupt store each byte into a ring buffer, also called a circular buffer. It is an array, say 64 bytes, with two indices: head, where the ISR writes, and tail, where the main loop reads. ISR(USART_RX_vect) { uint8_t c = UDR0; uint8_t next = (head + 1) % 64; if (next != tail) { buf[head] = c; head = next; } } The main loop reads while tail != head. When an index reaches the end it wraps to 0, hence the name ring. If head would catch up with tail, the buffer is full and the byte is dropped, which you can count as an error. head and tail must be volatile, and with 8-bit indices on an 8-bit MCU each access is a single byte, so no critical section is needed for the index reads.

A tiny command protocol: Raw bytes are not enough; both sides must agree what the bytes mean. A simple, popular design is text lines: the PC sends LED ON followed by a newline, and the MCU collects characters until it sees the newline, then compares the line with known commands. For sensor data, you might send T=30.3 followed by a newline. Text is easy to debug in a serial monitor. For noisy links, add a start marker, a length and a checksum, so the receiver can detect corrupted messages and resynchronise.

Flow control: What if the sender is faster than the receiver can process, for example a PC pouring a file into an MCU that must write each block to slow flash? The receiver needs a way to say wait. Hardware flow control uses two extra wires, RTS and CTS, which you met with RS-232: the receiver lowers its ready signal when its buffer is nearly full. Software flow control sends special characters instead, XOFF (0x13) to pause and XON (0x11) to resume, which works on three wires but cannot be used when those byte values may appear in binary data. Many small MCU projects skip flow control and simply keep messages short and buffers large enough.

Parity and errors: The UART hardware can detect a few problems: a framing error when the stop bit is not 1 (often a baud mismatch), an overrun when a byte arrives before the last was read, and a parity error when parity is enabled and the count of 1s is wrong. Parity catches single-bit errors but not two flipped bits, so serious protocols add a checksum or CRC on top.

Real life example 1, a GPS tracker on a Dhaka bus: Many GPS modules talk UART at 9600 baud by default and send text sentences once per second, like lines starting with $GPRMC that contain time, latitude and longitude. The tracker's MCU receives them with an interrupt and a ring buffer, picks out the position when a full line arrives, and forwards it through a GSM modem, which itself is controlled over a second UART using text AT commands. Two UARTs, zero clock wires, a whole fleet-tracking product.

Real life example 2, a weighing scale at a shop in Khulna: A digital scale's MCU sends the weight to a billing PC through a USB-serial cable. The PC software reads lines like W=1.250 kg. When the shopkeeper's new laptop showed garbage characters, the cause was simple: the software was set to 115200 while the scale sent 9600. Garbage characters in a serial monitor almost always mean a baud rate mismatch.

Common mistakes: TX connected to TX instead of RX. Forgetting the common ground. Mismatched baud rate or frame format. Using a baud rate with high error for the crystal. Driving a 3.3 V RX pin with 5 V. Printing long messages inside time-critical code or ISRs. Polling the receiver too slowly and losing bytes to overrun.

What exams ask: Draw the 8N1 frame for a given character. Compute bit time, frame time and maximum bytes per second for a baud rate. Compute UBRR for a given clock and baud, the actual baud and the percentage error. Explain why the receiver oversamples and samples mid-bit. Compare polling and interrupt reception, and explain a ring buffer. Explain TTL versus RS-232 levels.

Recap: A UART sends 10-bit 8N1 frames, LSB first, with no clock wire, relying on both sides agreeing on baud. One byte at 9600 takes 1.04 ms, so the link carries at most 960 bytes per second. UBRR = fclk / (16 x baud) - 1, and the rounding error must stay small, which is why 14.7456 MHz crystals exist. Use level shifters between different voltage worlds, interrupts with a ring buffer for reliable reception, and a simple line-based or checksummed protocol on top. Next lesson: SPI and I2C, the buses that do share a clock.
key_points: UART is asynchronous: no clock wire, TX goes to RX, grounds connected, both sides agree on the baud rate.
8N1 frame = start 0, 8 data bits LSB first, stop 1: 10 bits per byte; 'A' (0x41) goes out as 0 10000010 1.
At 9600 baud a bit is 104.17 us, a byte 1.04 ms, so at most 960 bytes per second.
AVR: UBRR = fclk / (16 x baud) - 1; 16 MHz and 9600 gives 103, actual 9,615 baud, 0.16% error.
115200 at 16 MHz gives about 3.5% error; 14.7456 MHz crystals divide standard baud rates exactly.
TTL serial uses 0 V and Vcc, RS-232 uses opposite-sign voltages; use level shifters and USB-serial chips.
Receive with an interrupt into a ring buffer (head written by ISR, tail read by main loop) to avoid overruns.
Framing errors usually mean baud mismatch; add line endings, checksums or CRC for a robust protocol.
lessons.tip: When a serial link shows garbage, check in this order: baud and frame format, TX-to-RX crossing, common ground, voltage levels. Ninety percent of UART problems die at the first two steps.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the 8N1 frames for the characters O and K (0x4F and 0x4B), bit by bit, LSB first, with start and stop bits. Then compute how long the two-character message plus a newline takes at 9600 and at 115200 baud.

quiz.q: How many bits does one 8N1 UART frame carry on the wire?
quiz.explain: 1 start bit + 8 data bits + 1 stop bit = 10 bits.

quiz.q: For an AVR at 16 MHz and 9600 baud (normal mode), what value goes into UBRR?
Why are crystals like 14.7456 MHz used on some boards?
options: They make the CPU faster than 16 MHz
They are needed for the ADC
They remove the need for a stop bit
They divide exactly into standard baud rates, giving 0% UART error
quiz.explain: 14,745,600 / (16 x 115200) = 8 exactly, so UBRR = 7 with no rounding error.

quiz.q: At 9600 baud 8N1, what is the maximum number of bytes per second?
quiz.explain: Each byte costs 10 bits, so 9600 / 10 = 960 bytes per second.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of receiving UART data with an interrupt and a ring buffer?
options: Bytes are stored as they arrive even when the main loop is busy, avoiding overruns
It removes the need for a ground wire
It converts TTL levels to RS-232
quiz.explain: The ISR saves each byte into the buffer the moment it arrives, so a busy main loop can read it later without losing data.

lessons.title: SPI and I2C in Firmware: Clocked Buses, Worked Frames and How to Choose
lessons.content:
Think of a classroom in a Rajshahi school. In one style of class, the teacher points at one student, and the two of them talk directly while everyone else stays quiet; the teacher can talk and listen at the same time, very fast. In another style, the teacher calls out a roll number, and only the student with that number answers, politely saying yes sir before speaking. The first style is SPI, the second is I2C. Both are clocked buses that connect a microcontroller to the small chips around it on the same board: sensors, memory, displays, clocks and converters.

A quick recap: In Computer Peripherals & Interfacing you were introduced to SPI, I2C and 1-Wire as on-board chip buses, with their wires and a comparison table. In the last lesson you programmed the UART, which has no clock wire. Here we go deeper on the firmware side: SPI modes and the byte swap, chip select handling, timing numbers, the exact I2C frame bit by bit, clock stretching, how an I2C bus gets stuck and how to rescue it, and how to choose among UART, SPI and I2C.

Why a clock wire helps: UART needs both sides to agree on speed, and clock error can break it. SPI and I2C add a clock line driven by one side, the master (newer documents often say controller). The other side, the slave (or target), simply reads or changes data on the clock edges. There is no baud rate to match exactly; the master can even pause the clock. This makes both buses robust and lets them run much faster than a UART on the same board.

SPI wires: SPI, the Serial Peripheral Interface, uses four signals. SCK is the clock from the master. MOSI, master out slave in, carries data from master to slave. MISO, master in slave out, carries data back. CS (chip select, also called SS) picks which slave is active, and it is usually active low: pulling CS to 0 says you, listen now. Several slaves can share SCK, MOSI and MISO, but each needs its own CS line. So with 3 slaves you need 3 + 3 = 6 pins.

The byte swap, SPI's heart: Inside the master and the slave sits an 8-bit shift register. They are connected in a ring: master MOSI into the slave, slave MISO back into the master. On each clock pulse, one bit leaves each register and enters the other. After 8 clocks, the master's byte is in the slave and the slave's byte is in the master. That means SPI is always full duplex: every time you send a byte, you also receive one. If you only want to read, you send a dummy byte, often 0x00 or 0xFF, just to make the clock run. If you only want to write, you receive a byte you ignore.

SPI modes: Different chips expect different clock styles, described by two bits. CPOL, clock polarity, says whether the clock rests low (0) or high (1). CPHA, clock phase, says whether data is sampled on the first edge (0) or the second edge (1) of each clock pulse. That gives four modes: mode 0 (CPOL 0, CPHA 0), mode 1, mode 2 and mode 3 (CPOL 1, CPHA 1). Mode 0 is the most common. The device's datasheet tells you which mode it needs, and a wrong mode usually gives data shifted by one bit or garbage. On the AVR these are bits in the SPCR register; on STM32 they are in SPI_CR1.

A worked SPI transaction: Many SPI sensors read a register like this. Pull CS low. Send the register address with a read flag (many chips use the top bit as read, for example 0x80 | 0x0F = 0x8F). While sending this byte, the byte you receive is junk, so ignore it. Then send a dummy 0x00; the byte you receive now is the register value. Pull CS high to end. In code: cs_low(); spi_xfer(0x8F); uint8_t v = spi_xfer(0x00); cs_high(); The CS edges matter: many chips use CS going high to finish the command.

SPI speed, worked: SPI clocks are typically from 1 MHz to tens of MHz, limited by the slave and the wiring. On the AVR, the SPI clock is the CPU clock divided by 2 up to 128, so a 16 MHz Uno can reach 8 MHz. At 1 MHz, each bit takes 1 microsecond, so one byte takes 8 microseconds. Sending a full frame of 1,024 bytes to a small display takes about 1,024 x 8 = 8,192 microseconds, roughly 8 ms, at 1 MHz, and about 1 ms at 8 MHz. This is why displays, SD cards and flash memory chips use SPI: they need bulk data fast.

What SPI does not give you: SPI has no addressing, so the CS line does the selecting. It has no acknowledgement, so the master never knows whether a slave is even connected; reading a missing slave often returns 0xFF or 0x00. It has no standard frame format beyond bytes, so each chip defines its own commands. It needs more pins as you add slaves. For checking that a chip is alive, firmware often reads a known ID register at startup and compares it with the datasheet value.

I2C wires and open drain: I2C, the Inter-Integrated Circuit bus, uses only two wires: SDA for data and SCL for clock, plus ground. Every device connects to the same two wires. The lines are open drain: a device can pull a line down to 0 or let go, but it never drives it high. Pull-up resistors, often 4.7 kilohm, pull the lines up to 1 when nobody is pulling down. This allows many devices to share wires without short circuits: if one device lets go and another pulls low, the line is simply low. Forgetting the pull-ups is the classic reason an I2C bus is silent.

I2C addresses: Each slave has a 7-bit address, so in theory there are 128 values, a few of which are reserved. Common examples: many temperature sensors such as the LM75 sit at 0x48 by default, the DS3231 real-time clock at 0x68, and small OLED displays often at 0x3C. Some chips have address pins so you can put several identical ones on one bus. After the 7-bit address comes one bit for direction: 0 means write, 1 means read. So the first byte on the wire is address shifted left by one, plus the direction bit. For 0x48: 0x48 x 2 = 0x90 for write and 0x91 for read.

Start, stop and ACK: Normally SDA only changes while SCL is low. Two special patterns break this rule on purpose. START: SDA falls while SCL is high. STOP: SDA rises while SCL is high. After every 8 data bits there is a 9th clock for the acknowledge. The receiver pulls SDA low during this clock to say ACK, I got it. If SDA stays high, that is a NACK, meaning no one answered or the receiver wants no more data.

A worked I2C frame, reading a temperature register: Suppose we want to read 2 bytes from register 0x00 of a sensor at 0x48. The master sends START, then 0x90 (address plus write), and the sensor ACKs. The master sends 0x00 (register pointer), ACK. Then a repeated START, then 0x91 (address plus read), ACK. Now the sensor sends the first data byte, and the master ACKs to ask for more. The sensor sends the second byte, and the master NACKs to say that is enough. Finally STOP. Counting clocks: 5 bytes x 9 clocks = 45 clocks. At 100 kHz each clock is 10 microseconds, so this takes about 450 microseconds plus start and stop, and one byte with its ACK takes 90 microseconds.

I2C speeds: Standard mode is 100 kHz, fast mode 400 kHz, and fast mode plus 1 MHz, with faster modes existing but rarer. The real limit is often the bus capacitance: long wires and many devices slow the rising edges, because only the pull-up resistor charges the line. Smaller pull-up resistors make faster edges but use more current. That is why I2C is meant for short distances on one board, not for long cables across a factory.

Clock stretching: A slow slave can hold SCL low after a byte to say wait, I am still busy, for example while it finishes a measurement. The master must notice that SCL is not going high and wait. Most MCU hardware handles this automatically, but some software (bit-banged) I2C code does not, and then it misreads a slow sensor.

When the I2C bus hangs: Imagine the MCU resets in the middle of a read while the slave is sending a 0 bit. The slave is still holding SDA low, waiting for clocks that never come. After reboot, the master sees SDA stuck low and cannot send START, so the bus looks dead. The standard recovery: the master toggles SCL as a plain GPIO up to 9 times until the slave finishes its byte and releases SDA, then sends a STOP. Good firmware does this at startup and after timeouts. Every I2C wait loop should also have a timeout so a broken sensor cannot freeze the whole device.

Comparing the three: UART: 2 wires, point to point, no clock, both sides must agree on baud, good for modules and PC links. SPI: 4 wires plus one CS per extra slave, full duplex, fast (MHz to tens of MHz), no addressing or ACK, good for displays, SD cards and flash. I2C: 2 wires for many devices, addresses and ACK built in, slower (100 to 400 kHz typical), half duplex, good for sensors, RTCs and EEPROMs. Rule of thumb: many slow chips on few pins, choose I2C; few fast chips, choose SPI; a module or another computer, choose UART.

Real life example 1, a weather station at a school in Rangpur: A student team builds a weather station with an ESP32. A temperature and humidity sensor and a small OLED display share one I2C bus at different addresses. An SD card on SPI stores readings every minute. A GSM module on UART sends a daily summary by SMS. When the OLED showed nothing, an I2C scanner sketch, which tries every address and reports which ones ACK, quickly showed the display at 0x3C instead of the 0x3D they had typed.

Real life example 2, a digital weighing scale for a rice wholesaler in Naogaon: The load cell's tiny signal goes into a dedicated ADC chip, which sends readings to the MCU over a simple two-wire serial interface, while the price display uses SPI to update fast. A real-time clock on I2C stamps each sale with the date and time. One small board, three different buses, each chosen for its job.

Common mistakes: Mixing up MOSI and MISO, or using the wrong SPI mode. Forgetting to toggle CS, or leaving two slaves selected at once. Forgetting I2C pull-ups, or adding too many in parallel from several modules. Using the 8-bit form (0x90) where a library expects the 7-bit address (0x48), or the other way round. No timeouts on I2C waits. Running I2C over long cables.

What exams ask: Draw SPI connections for one master and three slaves. Explain full duplex shifting and the four SPI modes. Compute transfer time for a number of bytes at a given clock. Draw an I2C frame with START, address, R/W, ACK, data and STOP. Compute the address byte for read and write. Explain open drain, pull-ups and clock stretching. Compare UART, SPI and I2C in a table and choose one for a given device.

Recap: SPI uses SCK, MOSI, MISO and a CS per slave, shifts bytes in both directions at once, and has four modes set by CPOL and CPHA; at 1 MHz a byte takes 8 microseconds. I2C uses two open-drain wires with pull-ups, 7-bit addresses with a read/write bit (0x48 gives 0x90 and 0x91), START, ACK, NACK and STOP; at 100 kHz a byte with ACK takes 90 microseconds. Add timeouts and bus recovery, and choose the bus by pins, speed and number of devices. Next we use these buses to talk to real sensors and drive actuators.
key_points: SPI uses SCK, MOSI, MISO and one active-low CS per slave; there is no addressing and no acknowledge.
SPI is full duplex: two shift registers form a ring, so every byte sent also brings one byte back (send a dummy byte to read).
SPI modes 0-3 come from CPOL (clock idle level) and CPHA (sampling edge); mode 0 is the most common.
At 1 MHz an SPI byte takes 8 us; SPI suits displays, SD cards and flash memory.
I2C uses two open-drain lines, SDA and SCL, with pull-up resistors; many devices share them by 7-bit address.
Address byte = address x 2 + R/W: 0x48 becomes 0x90 to write and 0x91 to read.
START and STOP change SDA while SCL is high; each byte is followed by an ACK (low) or NACK (high) clock; a byte plus ACK at 100 kHz is 90 us.
Use timeouts and the 9-clock bus recovery for stuck I2C; choose I2C for many slow chips, SPI for fast ones, UART for modules.
lessons.tip: Keep a one-page bus sheet for every project: which pins are SDA/SCL and SCK/MOSI/MISO/CS, each device's I2C address and SPI mode, and the clock speed. Most bus bugs are a wrong line on this sheet.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the full I2C frame to write the value 0x25 into register 0x01 of a device at address 0x3C: START, address byte in hex and binary, ACK, register, ACK, data, ACK, STOP. Count the clock pulses and compute the time at 100 kHz and at 400 kHz.

quiz.q: Why does an SPI master send a dummy byte when it only wants to read?
options: Because SPI is full duplex and the clock only runs while a byte is being shifted out
quiz.explain: The master must clock the shift registers by sending something; the slave's byte comes back during that same transfer.

quiz.q: What is the I2C address byte for reading from a device at 7-bit address 0x48?
quiz.explain: Shift left by one and add R/W = 1: 0x48 x 2 + 1 = 0x91.

quiz.q: What are I2C pull-up resistors for?
options: Devices only pull lines low (open drain), so resistors pull the lines high when nobody pulls down
They limit the clock to 100 kHz
quiz.explain: Open-drain outputs can only pull to 0; the pull-ups provide the 1 level and allow many devices to share the wires.

quiz.q: How long does one SPI byte take at a 1 MHz clock?
quiz.explain: 8 bits x 1 us per bit = 8 microseconds.

quiz.q: After an MCU reset, SDA is stuck low and the I2C bus seems dead. What is the standard fix?
options: Toggle SCL up to 9 times until the slave releases SDA, then send STOP
Increase the pull-up resistor to 1 megaohm
quiz.explain: The slave is waiting mid-byte; extra clocks let it finish and release SDA, and a STOP resets the bus.

lessons.title: Sensors and Actuators from the Firmware Side
lessons.content:
Imagine a water tank on the roof of a five-storey building in Mirpur. Every morning someone climbs the stairs, opens the lid, looks inside and then runs down to switch the pump on or off. Now imagine a small box on the lid that measures the water level every few seconds and switches the pump by itself. The box has two kinds of helpers. A sensor, which tells the microcontroller what is happening in the world, and an actuator, which lets the microcontroller change the world. This lesson is about writing firmware that talks to both of them correctly.

Recap in one breath: In Computer Peripherals and Interfacing you met the hardware side: what a transducer is, how an LM35 or an LDR works, why a GPIO pin cannot drive a motor, and how a transistor, relay, optocoupler and H-bridge help. We will not redo those circuits. Here we sit on the firmware side and ask: how do I read a sensor reliably, turn raw numbers into real units, clean up noise, and drive actuators safely in code?

What a sensor gives you: A sensor converts a physical quantity, like temperature, distance, light or moisture, into an electrical signal. From the microcontroller's point of view there are three families. Digital on/off sensors give a high or low level on a GPIO pin, like a PIR motion sensor or a float switch. Analog sensors give a voltage that you read with the ADC, like an LM35 or a soil moisture probe. Bus sensors contain their own small chip and send ready-made numbers over I2C, SPI, UART or a special one-wire protocol. Each family needs a different style of code.

Digital sensors in code: A digital sensor is read like a button. You configure the pin as an input, maybe enable the pull-up, and read it. The same rules from the GPIO and debouncing lessons apply: a float switch in a tank can chatter when water ripples, so you treat it with a sample-and-confirm debounce. A PIR sensor usually holds its output high for a few seconds after motion, so you often react to the rising edge rather than to the level, otherwise your code fires the same alarm hundreds of times.

Analog sensors in code: An analog sensor is read with the ADC, exactly as in the ADC lesson. You select the channel, start a conversion, wait for it to finish, and get a number such as 0 to 1023 on a 10-bit ADC. The raw number is not a temperature or a moisture level yet. It is just a fraction of the reference voltage. Your firmware must convert it, and that conversion is where most beginner bugs live: wrong reference voltage, integer division that throws away decimals, or forgetting that the sensor itself is not perfectly accurate.

Bus sensors in code: Sensors like a digital temperature and humidity chip or an accelerometer talk over I2C or SPI. You send a register address, then read back a few bytes, and combine them into a number using the bit manipulation from the embedded C lessons, for example value = (high << 8) | low. The datasheet tells you the scale, such as how many units each count is worth. Bus sensors give cleaner numbers because the conversion happens inside the sensor, close to the measurement, but you must handle bus errors and timeouts.

The DHT-type sensors: Many student projects use cheap temperature and humidity sensors from the DHT family. They use their own single-wire protocol: the MCU pulls the line low to start, then the sensor answers with 40 bits, where the length of each high pulse tells you if the bit is 0 or 1. The timing is tight, in tens of microseconds, so libraries usually do it with interrupts disabled. These sensors are also slow: you should read them only about once every one to two seconds, otherwise you get stale or failed readings.

Ultrasonic distance, the idea: The HC-SR04 ultrasonic module is the classic way to measure a water level or a parking distance. The MCU sends a short trigger pulse of about 10 microseconds. The module then fires a burst of ultrasound at 40 kHz and raises its echo pin. When the sound bounces back from the surface, the echo pin goes low. The time the echo pin stayed high is the round-trip time of the sound, there and back.

Ultrasonic distance, worked: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air at around 20 degrees Celsius. Suppose the echo pulse is 1,160 microseconds long. Distance = speed x time / 2, because the sound goes there and comes back. So d = 343 x 0.00116 / 2 = 0.199 m, about 19.9 cm. A handy shortcut: sound needs about 58 microseconds to go 1 cm and come back, so distance in cm is roughly echo time in microseconds divided by 58. Here 1,160 / 58 = 20 cm. In firmware you measure the pulse with a timer's input capture, as in the timers lesson, rather than a busy loop.

Soil moisture sensors: A soil moisture probe gives an analog voltage that changes with how wet the soil is. Cheap resistive probes push current through two metal prongs, and the prongs corrode within weeks in wet soil. Capacitive probes have no exposed metal and last much longer, so prefer them for real farms. Either way, the raw number depends on the soil type, the probe, and even the temperature. That is why you never trust a moisture number straight out of the ADC. You calibrate.

Two-point calibration: The simplest calibration uses two known points. Put the probe in dry air and note the reading, say 850. Put it in water and note the reading, say 400. For this probe, wetter means a lower reading. Now any reading can be mapped to a percentage: moisture = (850 - reading) / (850 - 400) x 100. If the ADC gives 625, moisture = 225 / 450 x 100 = 50 percent. Store the two calibration numbers in EEPROM so each device can be calibrated in the field without changing code. The same two-point idea works for temperature, light and pressure sensors.

Noise and filtering: Real readings jump around. Electrical noise from a pump motor, a loose wire, or a single bad ADC sample can produce a spike. Suppose five readings are 512, 520, 508, 700 and 515. The 700 is clearly a glitch. A moving average adds the last five and divides by five: (512 + 520 + 508 + 700 + 515) / 5 = 551. The spike still pulled the average up from about 514 to 551. A median filter sorts the five values, 508, 512, 515, 520, 700, and takes the middle one, 515. The median ignores a single spike completely, which is why it is popular for ultrasonic and moisture readings.

Choosing a filter: A moving average is cheap and smooths steady noise, but it reacts slowly and is fooled by spikes. A median handles spikes but needs sorting, which costs a little more time. A very cheap option on small MCUs is the exponential filter: new = old + (reading - old) / 8. Dividing by 8 is just a right shift by 3, so it costs almost nothing. Whatever you pick, remember the trade-off: more smoothing means slower response. A water tank can tolerate a slow filter; a robot avoiding a wall cannot.

Sanity checks: Firmware should also reject impossible values. An HC-SR04 is specified for roughly 2 cm to 400 cm, so a reading of 0 or 900 cm means no echo or a wiring fault, not a real distance. An ADC reading stuck at 0 or 1023 often means the sensor wire is broken or shorted. Good code treats these as errors, logs them, and falls back to a safe action, such as switching the pump off, instead of acting on garbage.

Actuators from the firmware side: An actuator turns an electrical command into action: a relay clicking a pump on, a motor spinning, a servo turning to an angle, a buzzer beeping. The rule from the interfacing course stays: a GPIO pin only supplies a small current, around 20 mA as a comfortable limit on an ATmega328P, so the pin always drives a driver stage, never the load itself. In code, the pin just says on, off, or a PWM duty; the driver does the heavy lifting.

Relays and the flyback reminder: A relay coil is an inductor. When you switch it off, it produces a voltage spike that can kill the transistor and reset the MCU. The fix is a flyback diode across the coil, already on most relay modules. In firmware, two habits help: never toggle a relay rapidly, because the contacts wear out and the pump hates it, and add a minimum on-time and off-time, for example the pump must stay off at least 30 seconds before switching on again.

Motors and ramping: A DC motor driven through an H-bridge gets its speed from PWM duty, as in the PWM lesson. If you jump from 0 to 100 percent instantly, the motor draws a big starting current, the supply voltage dips, and your MCU may brown out and reset. Firmware fixes this by ramping: increase the duty by a few percent every few milliseconds until it reaches the target. The same trick makes a fan or a conveyor start smoothly and reduces mechanical stress.

Servos and steppers: A hobby servo wants a pulse every 20 ms whose width, about 1 ms to 2 ms, sets the angle, which you already calculated in the PWM lesson. A stepper motor moves in fixed steps; a very common type has 200 steps per revolution, which is 1.8 degrees per step. To spin it at 60 rpm, that is one revolution per second, you need 200 steps per second, so one step every 5 ms. A timer interrupt that issues one step per tick gives smooth, accurate motion.

Real life example 1, a rooftop tank in Dhaka: An HC-SR04 sits on the lid. Every 2 seconds the MCU triggers it, measures the echo with input capture, takes the median of five readings, and converts to water depth. If the depth falls below 30 percent, the pump relay switches on; at 90 percent it switches off. Readings outside 2 to 400 cm turn the pump off and blink an error LED. The building's caretaker no longer climbs the stairs, and the tank never overflows onto the neighbour's roof.

Real life example 2, a fish pond in Mymensingh: A waterproof temperature sensor on a one-wire bus reports pond temperature every minute. An exponential filter smooths it. If the water gets too warm on a hot afternoon, the MCU starts an aerator motor through a driver, ramping it up over a second to avoid a supply dip. The farmer sets the threshold with two buttons, and the value is saved in EEPROM.

Common mistakes: Using raw ADC numbers as if they were real units. Forgetting calibration, so two identical devices disagree. Reading slow sensors too often. Busy-waiting for an echo pulse with no timeout, so the program freezes if the sensor is unplugged. Driving a relay or motor straight from a pin. Switching a motor to full speed instantly. Trusting a single sample instead of filtering.

What exams ask: Classify sensors as digital, analog or bus type. Compute distance from an ultrasonic echo time. Convert an ADC reading to a physical value using calibration. Compare moving average and median filters on a given set of readings. Explain why a flyback diode and a driver are needed, and how ramping protects the supply. Calculate the step rate for a stepper motor at a given rpm.

Recap: Sensors come as digital, analog or bus types, and each needs its own reading style. Raw readings must be converted, calibrated with known points, filtered and sanity-checked before use. Actuators are always driven through a driver, with safe timing such as minimum on and off times and ramping. With these habits, the same small MCU can run a tank, a pond or a whole farm.
key_points: Sensors reach firmware in three ways: digital on/off pins, analog voltages via the ADC, and bus sensors over I2C, SPI, UART or one-wire.
Ultrasonic distance = speed of sound x echo time / 2; 1,160 us gives about 19.9 cm, roughly 58 us per cm.
Two-point calibration maps raw readings between two known points, e.g. dry 850 and wet 400 makes 625 equal 50 percent.
A moving average of 512, 520, 508, 700, 515 gives 551, while the median gives 515 and ignores the spike.
Reject impossible readings (stuck at 0 or 1023, out of range) and fall back to a safe action.
GPIO pins drive driver stages, never loads; relays need a flyback diode and minimum on/off times.
Ramp motor PWM to avoid big starting currents and brown-out resets; a 200-step stepper at 60 rpm needs one step every 5 ms.
lessons.tip: Whenever you add a sensor, write down three numbers before writing code: its valid range, its update speed, and the reading you will treat as an error. Those three numbers prevent most sensor bugs.
lessons.task: On paper, take these seven moisture readings: 610, 615, 980, 612, 605, 618, 611. Compute the moving average and the median of the last five, then convert both to percent using dry = 850 and wet = 400. Which one would you trust?

quiz.q: An HC-SR04 echo pulse lasts 1,160 microseconds. About how far is the object?
Five readings are 508, 512, 515, 520 and 700. What does a median filter output?
quiz.explain: Sorted, the middle value is 515; the median ignores the single spike.

quiz.q: With dry = 850 and wet = 400, what moisture percent is a reading of 625?
Why should firmware ramp a DC motor's PWM duty instead of jumping to 100 percent?
options: To limit the starting current and avoid supply dips that can reset the MCU
To make the PWM frequency higher
Because GPIO pins cannot output PWM at 100 percent
quiz.explain: A sudden full-duty start draws a large current, dipping the supply and risking a brown-out reset.

quiz.q: A stepper motor has 200 steps per revolution. What step interval gives 60 rpm?
quiz.explain: 60 rpm = 1 revolution per second = 200 steps per second, so one step every 5 ms.

lessons.title: Power Management, Sleep Modes and Battery Life
lessons.content:
Think about a mobile phone during a long load-shedding evening. You keep checking the battery percentage, turning down the brightness, closing apps, maybe switching on battery saver. Now imagine a soil sensor buried in a paddy field in Rangpur, or a flood-level sensor tied to a bridge pillar on the Jamuna. Nobody will charge them every evening. They must run for months, maybe years, from a small battery or a palm-sized solar panel. For these devices, power is not a detail. It is the main design problem. This lesson shows where the power goes and how firmware saves it.

Power versus energy: Power is how fast energy is used, measured in watts or, for small electronics, in milliwatts. Energy is the total amount used over time, and a battery stores a fixed amount of energy. Battery capacity is usually written in milliamp-hours, mAh, at a given voltage. A 2,000 mAh battery can in theory supply 2,000 mA for one hour, or 20 mA for 100 hours, or 0.2 mA for 10,000 hours. So for battery life the number that matters is the average current your device draws over a long time, not the peak.

Where the power goes inside a chip: A CMOS chip uses power in two main ways. Dynamic power is spent every time a transistor switches, charging and discharging tiny capacitances. Static or leakage power is spent even when nothing switches, because transistors are not perfect switches. For dynamic power the classic formula is P is proportional to C x V squared x f, where C is the switched capacitance, V the supply voltage and f the clock frequency. You met this as the power wall in Computer Architecture; here we use it to save battery.

What the formula tells us: Frequency enters linearly: halve the clock, halve the dynamic power. Voltage enters squared, which is much stronger. If the same chip could run at 1.8 V instead of 3.3 V at the same frequency, the power would drop to (1.8 / 3.3) squared, about 0.30, so roughly 30 percent of the original. There is a catch: a chip at lower voltage usually cannot run at its highest clock, so datasheets give a safe operating area, for example a lower maximum frequency at lower voltage. Still, the lesson is clear: lower voltage and lower clock save power.

Run fast, then sleep: Halving the clock halves the power, but the job takes twice as long, so the energy for that job can stay about the same. The bigger win comes from finishing quickly and then going to a very low-power sleep. This idea is often called race to sleep. A sensor node does not need to be awake all the time. It wakes, reads a sensor, maybe sends a message, and goes back to sleep. Most of its life is spent asleep, and that is where battery life is won or lost.

Sleep modes: Microcontrollers offer several sleep levels. The deeper the sleep, the less current, but the fewer things keep running and the longer it takes to wake. An ATmega328P has modes such as Idle, ADC Noise Reduction, Power-save, Standby and Power-down. In Idle the CPU clock stops but timers, UART and other peripherals keep running, so any of their interrupts can wake the CPU. In Power-down the main oscillator stops; only a few things can wake the chip, such as an external interrupt pin, a pin-change interrupt, an I2C address match or the watchdog timer. Cortex-M chips and the ESP32 have similar ladders, often called sleep, stop or deep sleep.

Wake sources: Before sleeping, firmware must arrange a way to wake up, or the device sleeps forever. Common wake sources are a button or sensor on an interrupt pin, a timer running from a slow low-power clock, a real-time clock alarm, and the watchdog timer used as a wake-up timer. On an ATmega328P the watchdog can be set to time out after periods up to about 8 seconds, so a node that must wake every minute can sleep in several 8-second chunks and count them. Many MCUs also keep a 32.768 kHz watch crystal running in deep sleep for accurate timekeeping.

Duty cycling, worked: Suppose a field node is active for 1 second every 60 seconds, drawing 15 mA while awake and 10 microamps, which is 0.01 mA, while asleep. The average current is (15 x 1 + 0.01 x 59) / 60 = (15 + 0.59) / 60 = 0.26 mA. With a 2,000 mAh battery, life is 2,000 / 0.26, about 7,700 hours, which is about 320 days. If the same node stayed awake all the time at 15 mA, the battery would last 2,000 / 15 = 133 hours, about 5.6 days. Sleeping turned less than a week into almost a year.

Stretching it further: Now let the node wake once every 5 minutes instead of every minute. The average becomes (15 x 1 + 0.01 x 299) / 300, about 0.06 mA, and the paper calculation gives about 1,390 days, nearly four years. Real life will be shorter: batteries lose charge by themselves over time, their capacity drops in heat and cold, and a radio burst can draw far more than 15 mA. Treat such long numbers as an upper bound and test the real device with a meter. Still, the calculation shows which knob matters: the awake time and the sleep current.

The sleep current matters a lot: In the first example the sleep part contributed 0.59 out of 15.59 in the numerator, small. But if sleep current is 1 mA instead of 10 microamps because you forgot to switch something off, the average becomes (15 + 59) / 60, about 1.23 mA, and battery life falls from about 320 days to about 68 days. Beginners often build a node that sleeps beautifully on paper but leaks a few milliamps through an LED, a voltage divider or a sensor that was never powered down.

Turning things off: Firmware should power down everything it does not need. Disable unused peripherals: the ADC, comparators, unused timers, the UART when not sending. AVR chips have a Power Reduction Register that stops the clock to individual peripherals; Cortex-M chips enable clocks per peripheral, and an unused peripheral should have its clock left off. This is called clock gating. Sensors themselves can be powered from a GPIO pin or a small transistor switch, so they are turned on only for the reading. Unused pins should not float, because a floating input can flicker between high and low and waste current; set them as outputs or enable pull-ups.

Board versus chip: A bare microcontroller in deep sleep can draw only microamps, but a development board like an Arduino Uno has a power LED, a voltage regulator and a USB-to-serial chip that keep drawing current all the time. That is why a sleep test on an Uno often disappoints. For a battery product, you design your own board with only the parts you need, or you remove the power LED and choose a regulator with low quiescent current, meaning the current the regulator itself eats even with no load.

Regulators, LDO versus buck: Batteries rarely give exactly the voltage the MCU wants, so a regulator sits in between. A linear regulator, often a low-dropout regulator or LDO, simply burns the extra voltage as heat. Its efficiency is roughly Vout / Vin, so dropping 5 V to 3.3 V is only about 66 percent efficient. A switching buck converter chops the voltage with an inductor and can reach roughly 85 to 95 percent efficiency at decent loads. But a buck converter is noisier and may waste more at tiny loads, so for a node that sleeps 99 percent of the time, an LDO with very low quiescent current can win. Always check both the efficiency and the quiescent current.

Brown-out detection: As a battery drains, its voltage sags. Below a certain voltage the MCU may run but execute instructions wrongly, corrupt EEPROM writes, or drive outputs strangely. Brown-out detection, BOD, watches the supply and holds the chip in reset while the voltage is below a threshold. On the ATmega328P the BOD level can be set by fuses to about 1.8 V, 2.7 V or 4.3 V. Pick a level just above the lowest voltage at which your chosen clock speed is safe. BOD itself draws a little current, and some chips let you disable it during sleep to save power.

Measuring power: You cannot save what you do not measure. A normal multimeter in series with the supply shows average current when the device is steady. For sleep currents in microamps you need a meter range that low, and for short wake bursts you need special tools such as a current-sense amplifier, a power profiler or an oscilloscope across a small shunt resistor. A simple trick: toggle a GPIO pin when the firmware wakes and sleeps, and watch it on a logic analyzer to measure exactly how long the device is awake.

Solar and energy harvesting: Many Bangladesh field devices run from a small solar panel and a rechargeable battery. The design question becomes: does the panel collect enough energy on a cloudy monsoon week to cover the average consumption? If the node averages 0.26 mA at 3.3 V, that is under 1 mW, which a small panel easily covers on a sunny day. The battery must carry the node through nights and cloudy days. Firmware can help by checking the battery voltage with the ADC and reducing its wake rate when the battery is low.
