Real life example 1, flood sensor on the Jamuna: An ultrasonic level sensor on a bridge wakes every 10 minutes in the dry season and every minute when the water rises fast. It measures, sends a short message, and returns to power-down sleep. The sensor and radio are powered through a transistor switch so they draw nothing in sleep. A solar panel keeps the battery topped up. This adaptive duty cycle gives fast warnings when they matter and long life when nothing is happening.

Real life example 2, a TV remote: Your TV remote can run for a year or more on two AA cells. Its microcontroller spends almost all its time in deep sleep with the keypad wired to wake it. You press a button, it wakes in microseconds, sends an infrared code for a fraction of a second, and sleeps again. The average current is tiny because the awake time is tiny. The same principle runs the field sensor and the remote.

Common mistakes: Calculating battery life from peak current instead of average. Forgetting a wake source, so the device never wakes. Leaving an LED, a voltage divider or a sensor powered during sleep. Testing sleep current on a development board and blaming the chip. Ignoring regulator quiescent current. Disabling brown-out detection to save a few microamps, then getting corrupted EEPROM when the battery dies.

What exams ask: State the dynamic power relation and explain why voltage matters more than frequency. Compute the effect of reducing voltage. Calculate average current and battery life for a duty-cycled node. List sleep modes and what remains on in each. Compare LDO and buck regulators. Explain brown-out detection and clock gating.

Recap: Battery life depends on average current, so sleep as much as possible and wake only to do useful work. Power scales with V squared times f, so lower voltage and clock help. Choose the deepest sleep that still has the wake source you need, power down peripherals and sensors, avoid floating pins, pick the right regulator, and keep brown-out detection to stay safe as the battery dies.
key_points: Battery life depends on average current over time, not peak current; capacity in mAh divided by average mA gives hours.
Dynamic power is proportional to C x V squared x f; dropping 3.3 V to 1.8 V cuts power to about 30 percent at the same clock.
Race to sleep: do the work quickly, then enter the deepest sleep mode that still has the wake source you need.
Worked: 15 mA for 1 s every 60 s with 10 uA sleep averages 0.26 mA, about 7,700 h or 320 days on 2,000 mAh; always-on gives 5.6 days.
Sleep current dominates: a forgotten 1 mA leak cuts the same node to about 68 days.
Disable unused peripherals (clock gating), power sensors from a switch, and never leave inputs floating.
LDO efficiency is about Vout/Vin; buck converters reach roughly 85-95 percent but check quiescent current at tiny loads.
Brown-out detection holds the MCU in reset when supply voltage sags, protecting EEPROM and outputs.
lessons.tip: For every low-power design, make a tiny table with two rows, awake and asleep, and three columns: current, time and what is on. If you cannot fill the asleep row with confidence, measure it before trusting your battery life.
lessons.task: Calculate the battery life of a node that is awake 2 seconds every 120 seconds at 20 mA and sleeps at 20 microamps, using a 2,500 mAh battery. Then recompute if the sleep current is 0.5 mA because an LED was left on.

quiz.q: Which change reduces dynamic power the most, according to P proportional to C V^2 f?
quiz.explain: Voltage is squared, so halving it cuts dynamic power to a quarter, while halving f only halves it.

quiz.q: A node draws 15 mA for 1 s and 0.01 mA for 59 s every minute. What is the average current?
What must firmware arrange before entering a deep sleep mode?
options: A wake source such as an interrupt pin, RTC alarm or watchdog
quiz.explain: Without a wake source the device stays asleep forever.

quiz.q: Why is an LDO dropping 5 V to 3.3 V inefficient?
options: It burns the extra voltage as heat, so efficiency is about Vout/Vin, roughly 66 percent
quiz.explain: A linear regulator wastes the voltage difference as heat; 3.3 / 5 is about 66 percent.

quiz.q: What does brown-out detection do?
options: Holds the MCU in reset when supply voltage falls below a threshold
Turns off the ADC in sleep
quiz.explain: BOD keeps the chip in reset at low voltage so it does not run wrongly or corrupt memory.

lessons.title: Watchdog Timers and Reliable Firmware
lessons.content:
Picture a night guard at a garment factory in Gazipur. The owner worries that the guard might fall asleep. So he installs a simple rule: every 15 minutes the guard must press a button on a box. If the box does not get a press in time, it rings the manager's phone. The box does not know what the guard is doing; it only knows he is still alive and active. A watchdog timer is exactly this box, placed inside a microcontroller, and the guard is your firmware.

Why devices hang: Embedded devices run for months without anyone watching them. Sooner or later something goes wrong. A loop waits for a sensor flag that never comes because the wire came loose. An I2C bus gets stuck with a slave holding the data line low. Electrical noise from a motor or a lightning strike nearby flips a bit in a register. A rare bug corrupts a pointer and the program jumps into nonsense. On a PC you would press restart. A pump controller in a field or a sensor on a tower has nobody to press anything.

What a watchdog timer is: A watchdog timer, WDT, is a hardware counter that counts down (or up) by itself from its own clock. If it reaches its limit, it resets the microcontroller, just like pressing the reset button. The firmware must regularly restart the counter before it expires. This is called kicking, feeding or petting the watchdog. As long as the firmware is healthy and keeps feeding, the watchdog never fires. If the firmware hangs and stops feeding, the watchdog resets the chip and the program starts fresh from the beginning.

Why hardware and not software: The watchdog must be independent of the thing it watches. If the CPU is stuck, any software timer that depends on the CPU is stuck too. So the watchdog runs from its own clock source and its own counter. On the ATmega328P the watchdog runs from a separate on-chip 128 kHz oscillator, and its timeout can be chosen from about 16 ms up to about 8 seconds. STM32 chips have an independent watchdog, IWDG, clocked from a separate low-speed internal oscillator, plus a window watchdog, WWDG, which we will meet below.

Using it in code, the basic pattern: At startup, the firmware enables the watchdog with a chosen timeout, for example 1 second. Then the main loop does its work and feeds the watchdog once per pass. On AVR with avr-libc this is wdt_enable(WDTO_1S) once at startup and wdt_reset() inside the loop. If one pass of the loop normally takes 50 ms, the watchdog gets fed about 20 times a second and never expires. If the loop freezes anywhere, within 1 second the chip resets.

Where to feed, the important part: The place you feed the watchdog decides what it protects. Feed it in exactly one place, in the main loop, after the important work is done. A classic mistake is feeding it inside a timer interrupt. The timer interrupt keeps firing even when the main loop is stuck in an endless while loop, so the watchdog is fed forever and never rescues you. Another mistake is sprinkling feed calls everywhere, including inside wait loops, which again lets a stuck loop keep the dog happy. The watchdog should be fed only when the program has proven it is making real progress.

Choosing the timeout: The timeout must be longer than the longest normal time between feeds, with a safety margin, but short enough that a hang is caught before damage happens. Suppose the worst-case loop pass is 200 ms, including a slow sensor read. A 1 second timeout gives a comfortable five-times margin. If the loop sometimes writes to flash or waits for a modem for 3 seconds, either pick a longer timeout like 4 or 8 seconds, or feed the watchdog at known safe points inside that long operation. Think also about the physical system: if a stuck output could overfill a tank in 10 seconds, a 30-second timeout is useless.

Watching many tasks: In a program with several jobs, or an RTOS with several tasks, one stuck task might not stop the main loop. A common pattern is a check-in scheme. Each task sets its own alive flag when it completes a cycle. A supervisor, running periodically, feeds the watchdog only if every flag is set, then clears all the flags. If any task stops checking in, the flags are never all set, the watchdog is not fed, and the system resets. This turns one watchdog into a guard for many tasks.

The window watchdog: A normal watchdog only complains if you feed it too late. But a runaway program stuck in a tiny loop that happens to call the feed function would feed it too often. A window watchdog also complains if you feed it too early. You must feed it inside a time window, for example between 60 percent and 100 percent of the timeout. A program running correctly hits that window; a program that has lost its timing does not. Safety-oriented systems like motor controllers and car electronics often use window watchdogs for this reason.

Knowing why you reset: After any reset, the firmware should ask: why did I start? Most MCUs have a reset-cause register. On AVR it is MCUSR, with flags for power-on reset, external reset, brown-out reset and watchdog reset. Read it early, save the cause, and clear it. Counting watchdog resets in EEPROM is very useful: if a field device reports 40 watchdog resets in a week, you know there is a real bug or a hardware problem, even though the device seemed to keep working.

Watchdog and sleep: In the power lesson the watchdog appeared as a wake-up timer. On the ATmega328P the watchdog can be configured to raise an interrupt instead of a reset, or an interrupt first and a reset if that is not handled. A sleeping sensor node uses interrupt mode to wake every 8 seconds and count. Be careful not to confuse the two uses in one program: if the watchdog is your wake-up alarm, decide clearly which code path also protects you against a hang while awake, for example by switching to reset mode while the node is doing its work and back to interrupt mode just before sleeping.

Testing the watchdog itself: A watchdog that has never fired in testing is an untested feature. During development, add a hidden test command or button that deliberately enters an endless loop. The device should reset within the timeout, report a watchdog reset cause, and come back with all outputs safe. Also test the opposite: run the device for hours under the heaviest normal load and confirm there are zero watchdog resets, which proves your timeout is long enough.

An AVR trap: On the ATmega328P, after a watchdog reset the watchdog stays enabled, and it may be running with the shortest timeout. If your startup code is slow, for example a bootloader or a long initialization, the watchdog can fire again before your code reaches the place where it sets things up, giving an endless reset loop. The datasheet advice is to clear the watchdog reset flag in MCUSR and disable or reconfigure the watchdog very early in startup. Similar early-startup care is needed on other chips.

Brown-out reset as a partner: Not every problem is a software hang. When the supply voltage sags, for example when a big pump starts or a battery is almost empty, the CPU may behave strangely without hanging cleanly. Brown-out reset, which you saw in the power lesson, holds the chip in reset while the voltage is too low and releases it when the voltage recovers. Watchdog and brown-out detection together cover the two big ways a device goes wrong in the field: lost logic and lost power.

Fail-safe outputs: A reset is only safe if the outputs are safe during and after it. While an AVR is in reset, its I/O pins become high-impedance inputs, so they float. If a pin drives a relay transistor, a pull-down resistor on that line keeps the relay off during reset. Then the firmware's first job after startup is to set every output to its safe state before doing anything else. For a pump, a heater or a motor, safe usually means off. Design the hardware so that a dead or resetting MCU means the dangerous thing stops.

Defensive firmware: The watchdog is the last line of defence, not the first. Good firmware avoids hangs in the first place. Every wait loop gets a timeout: instead of while (!flag); write a loop that also counts time and gives up after, say, 100 ms, reporting an error. Every sensor value gets a range check. Every array index gets a bounds check. Assertions catch impossible states during testing. Bus drivers know how to recover a stuck I2C bus by clocking SCL a few times. The watchdog then only has to catch the truly unexpected.

Electrical noise and the real world: Motors, relays, fluorescent lights and lightning create electrical noise. It can couple into long sensor wires and power lines and upset the MCU. Good layout, decoupling capacitors close to each chip, a flyback diode on every coil, and separate wiring for heavy loads reduce the problem. Firmware cannot fix bad hardware, but a watchdog plus brown-out reset turns a frozen device into one that briefly restarts and carries on.

Real life example 1, a deep tube-well pump in Rajshahi: A controller switches a borewell pump on a fixed schedule and stops it if the water flow sensor reports dry running. One day the pump starting current causes a voltage dip and noise that freezes the I2C real-time clock bus. Without a watchdog, the controller would sit frozen with the pump either stuck on, burning the motor, or stuck off, drying the crops. With a 2-second watchdog fed only after a complete loop pass, the controller resets within 2 seconds, its first action sets the relay off, it recovers the bus, reads the clock and continues the schedule. The reset counter in EEPROM tells the technician to add better filtering.

Real life example 2, an ATM or a vending machine: Unattended machines like ATMs, vending machines and digital signboards on Dhaka roads run for months. Their controllers use watchdogs so that a rare software hang ends in an automatic restart rather than a dead screen waiting for a technician. The users may notice a short reboot, but the machine comes back without anyone driving out to it.

Common mistakes: Feeding the watchdog in a timer interrupt. Feeding it inside wait loops. Choosing a timeout shorter than the slowest normal operation, causing random resets. Forgetting to check or clear the reset cause, so watchdog resets go unnoticed. Leaving outputs in an unsafe state during reset. Using the watchdog to hide bugs instead of fixing them.

What exams ask: Define a watchdog timer and explain how it recovers a hung system. Explain why it needs an independent clock. Explain where to feed it and why not in an ISR. Choose a suitable timeout for a given loop time. Describe a window watchdog. Explain fail-safe design and the role of brown-out reset.

Recap: A watchdog is an independent hardware timer that resets the MCU unless the firmware regularly proves it is alive. Feed it in one place after real work, never in an ISR; pick a timeout with margin; use check-in flags for many tasks and a window watchdog for stricter checks. Record reset causes, make outputs fail safe, and write defensive code with timeouts and range checks so the watchdog is a safety net, not a crutch.
key_points: A watchdog timer is an independent hardware counter that resets the MCU if the firmware does not feed it in time.
It runs from its own clock (e.g. the ATmega328P's 128 kHz oscillator, timeouts about 16 ms to 8 s), so a stuck CPU cannot stop it.
Feed it in one place in the main loop after real work; never in a timer ISR or inside wait loops.
Timeout must exceed the worst normal loop time with margin, but be short enough to catch a hang before damage.
For many tasks, feed only when every task's alive flag is set; a window watchdog also rejects feeds that come too early.
Read and clear the reset-cause register at startup and count watchdog resets; on AVR disable or reconfigure the WDT early.
Fail-safe design: pull-downs keep outputs off during reset and the first startup action sets every output to its safe state.
Defensive firmware uses timeouts, range checks and bus recovery; the watchdog is the last line of defence.
lessons.tip: When you add a watchdog, deliberately break your program once: put an infinite loop behind a button press and confirm the device really resets and comes back with outputs off. A watchdog you never tested is just a hope.
lessons.task: Draw the main loop of a tank-pump controller on paper: read sensor, decide, drive relay, send status. Mark the single place where you would feed the watchdog, write the worst-case time of each step, and choose a timeout with at least a 3x margin.

quiz.q: What does a watchdog timer do when the firmware stops feeding it?
options: Puts the MCU into deep sleep forever
quiz.explain: When the counter expires without a feed, the watchdog resets the chip so it restarts cleanly.

quiz.q: Why is feeding the watchdog inside a timer interrupt a bad idea?
options: The interrupt keeps running even if the main loop is stuck, so the hang is never caught
Interrupts cannot access the watchdog register
quiz.explain: A timer ISR fires regardless of a frozen main loop, so the dog is always fed and never resets.

quiz.q: Why does the watchdog run from its own clock?
options: So it keeps counting even if the CPU or main clock is stuck
quiz.explain: Independence from the thing it watches is what makes the watchdog useful.

quiz.q: What extra check does a window watchdog add?
options: It counts how many tasks exist
It also resets if the watchdog is fed too early
quiz.explain: Feeds must arrive inside a time window, catching runaway loops that feed too often.

quiz.q: A loop's worst-case pass is 200 ms. Which timeout is the most sensible?
quiz.explain: 1 s gives a 5x margin over 200 ms while still catching a hang quickly; 200 ms or less would cause false resets.

lessons.title: Memory, Boot Process, Bootloaders and Firmware Updates
lessons.content:
Your phone shows a message: a system update is available, tap to install. It downloads, restarts, and a few minutes later it works as before, maybe with a new feature. You never opened the phone or connected a cable. Now imagine 5,000 irrigation controllers spread across villages in Rangpur and Dinajpur, and you find a bug in the pump logic. Sending a technician to each one with a laptop would take months and cost a fortune. Updating firmware safely, without turning devices into bricks, is a core skill of embedded engineering. To do it, you first need to understand what memory holds your program and what happens when the chip starts.

Memory recap: A microcontroller has non-volatile memory that keeps data without power, mainly flash for the program, and often a small EEPROM for settings. It also has volatile SRAM for variables and the stack, which is lost at power-off. In the embedded C lessons you saw how the linker places code and constants in flash (.text and read-only data), initialised variables in .data, zeroed variables in .bss, and the stack in SRAM. Now we follow those sections from the moment power arrives.

What happens at reset, step one: When power comes on or the reset pin is released, the CPU does not magically jump into main(). It starts from a fixed place defined by the hardware, called the reset vector. On an AVR like the ATmega328P, the CPU starts fetching instructions at flash address 0, where the vector table holds a jump to the startup code. On an ARM Cortex-M, the vector table sits at the start of memory by default: the first word is the initial value of the stack pointer and the second word is the address of the reset handler. The hardware loads the stack pointer and jumps to the reset handler.

What happens at reset, step two, the startup code: The reset handler is a small piece of code, usually supplied by the compiler or the chip vendor, that prepares the C world. It copies the initial values of .data from flash into SRAM, because a global like int count = 5; must start as 5 but must also be changeable, so it has to live in RAM. It fills .bss with zeros, because C promises that uninitialised globals start at zero. It may set up the clock, and in C++ it runs constructors of global objects. Only then does it call main(). If main ever returns, which it should not in firmware, the startup code typically loops forever.

Why this matters: Understanding startup explains real bugs. A huge initialised array makes boot slower because it is copied from flash to RAM. A global that you expected to keep its value across a watchdog reset is zeroed again by the startup code. And if the stack pointer is set wrongly, the program crashes before main even runs. When people say the program crashes before reaching main, the startup code and the vector table are where you look.

Flash memory in more detail: Flash keeps its content without power, but it has rules. You cannot overwrite a single byte freely. Flash is erased in blocks, called pages or sectors, which sets all bits to 1, and programming can only change bits from 1 to 0. To change one byte you must erase its whole page and rewrite it. On the ATmega328P a flash page is 128 bytes. Erasing and writing take milliseconds, far slower than reading, and the CPU may stall while it happens.

Endurance, the limited life: Every erase and write cycle wears flash and EEPROM cells a little. The datasheet gives an endurance figure. For the ATmega328P, flash is rated for 10,000 write/erase cycles and EEPROM for 100,000. That sounds like a lot, until you do the arithmetic. Suppose you save a counter to the same EEPROM byte once every minute. 100,000 writes at one per minute is 100,000 minutes, which is about 69 days. Your device would wear out that cell in a little over two months, while it was supposed to last ten years.

Making memory last: The first fix is to write less. Write only when the value actually changes, keep the value in RAM and save it every hour, or save it only when the supply voltage starts to drop. The second fix is wear levelling: spread the writes across many locations. If you rotate the counter across 10 EEPROM slots, each slot is written one-tenth as often, so the same once-a-minute rate lasts about 694 days instead of 69. Flash file systems and SD cards do wear levelling internally in a much more advanced way. On a small MCU you design it yourself, often with a sequence number so you can find the newest slot after reset.

How firmware gets into the chip: There are three common ways. First, an external programmer writes flash directly through a programming interface: on AVR this is ISP, which uses the SPI pins on the 6-pin ICSP header; on ARM it is the SWD or JTAG debug port, which you will meet in the debugging lesson. Second, a bootloader already in the chip receives the new program over a normal interface like UART or USB and writes it into flash. Third, over-the-air update, where the new image arrives through Wi-Fi, cellular or another radio. The program image itself is usually a .bin file, a raw copy of the bytes, or an Intel HEX file, a text format where each line holds an address, some data bytes and a checksum.

What a bootloader is: A bootloader is a small program that runs first after reset and decides what to do next. It either jumps to the main application, or, if asked, receives a new application and writes it into flash. It lives in a protected part of flash that the application normally does not overwrite. The bootloader must be small, simple and extremely reliable, because if it breaks, the device can no longer be updated without a hardware programmer.

The Arduino bootloader: When you click Upload in the Arduino IDE for an Uno, the PC tool avrdude opens the serial port, which toggles a control line that resets the ATmega328P. The chip starts in its bootloader, called Optiboot on the Uno, which occupies 512 bytes at the top of flash. For a short moment it listens on the UART. If avrdude starts talking, the bootloader receives the new program page by page and writes it with the AVR's self-programming instruction, SPM. If nothing arrives, it jumps to the existing application. That is why the board blinks and resets when you upload, and why you can program it with only a USB cable.

Over-the-air updates: For connected devices, OTA update is the modern answer to the 5,000-controllers problem. The device downloads a new firmware image over the network and installs it itself. The danger is obvious: if power fails or the download is corrupted halfway, and you were overwriting the only copy of the firmware, the device is dead. A device that cannot boot and cannot be updated is called bricked. Good OTA design is mostly about making bricking impossible.

A/B slots: The standard safe design keeps two firmware slots in flash, often called A and B. Suppose the device is running from slot A. The new image is downloaded into slot B while A keeps working normally. Only after the whole image is in slot B and has been verified does the device mark B as the one to boot next, and restart. If anything fails during the download, slot A is untouched and the device simply continues. The ESP32's partition scheme supports this directly, with two OTA application partitions and a small data partition that records which one to boot.

Verification, CRC and signatures: Before switching to the new image, the device checks it. A CRC, such as CRC-32, is a checksum that detects accidental corruption, like a flipped bit in a weak radio link. But a CRC does not stop an attacker, who can simply compute the CRC of a malicious image. For that you need a digital signature: the manufacturer signs the image with a private key, and the device checks it with the matching public key stored inside it. If the signature does not match, the image is rejected. Secure boot extends the same idea to every boot: the chip refuses to run firmware that is not properly signed. We return to security in the IoT lesson.

Rollback: Even a perfectly downloaded and signed image can contain a bug that crashes it at startup. A robust scheme boots the new image in a trial state. The new firmware must reach a healthy point, for example connecting to the server and running its main loop for a while, and then mark itself as valid. If it keeps crashing and the watchdog resets it before that, the bootloader notices the image was never confirmed and rolls back to the previous slot. The ESP-IDF framework for ESP32 offers this app rollback feature, and many other bootloaders have similar logic.

Real life example 1, the Rangpur irrigation controllers: Each controller is an ESP32 with two OTA slots. The company uploads version 1.4 with the pump bug fixed and signs it. Controllers check for updates at night, when pumps are off. Each downloads the image into the inactive slot, verifies the signature, switches, restarts, runs a self-test and connects to the server before marking itself valid. One controller loses power halfway through its download in a storm; it reboots on the old version and retries the next night. No technician travels anywhere.

Real life example 2, a student project with an Uno: You upload a sketch through USB and the Optiboot bootloader handles it. One day you accidentally set fuses wrongly or overwrite the bootloader, and uploads stop working. The fix is a hardware programmer through the ICSP header, which writes flash directly and can restore the bootloader. This shows the layered picture: the bootloader is convenient, but the hardware programming port is the last way in.

Common mistakes: Writing EEPROM or flash in a tight loop and wearing it out. Assuming globals survive a reset. Overwriting the only firmware copy during an update. Using only a CRC and calling it secure. Not having a rollback path, so a buggy update bricks every device at once. Forgetting that flash writes take milliseconds and can disturb timing or need the watchdog fed.

What exams ask: Describe the sequence from reset to main, including the vector table and the copying of .data and zeroing of .bss. Compare flash and EEPROM, including endurance numbers and the once-a-minute worked example. Explain what a bootloader is and how the Arduino upload works. Describe a safe OTA design with A/B slots, verification and rollback. Distinguish a CRC from a digital signature.

Recap: At reset the CPU starts at the reset vector, the startup code copies .data, zeroes .bss and calls main. Flash and EEPROM have limited write cycles, so write rarely and spread writes with wear levelling. Firmware enters a chip through a hardware programmer, a bootloader or OTA. Safe updates use two slots, verify the new image with CRC and signatures, and roll back automatically if the new firmware does not prove itself healthy.
key_points: At reset the CPU starts at the reset vector; on Cortex-M the vector table's first word is the initial stack pointer and the second the reset handler address.
Startup code copies .data from flash to SRAM, zeroes .bss, sets up clocks and only then calls main().
Flash is erased in pages (128 bytes on the ATmega328P) and programming only turns 1s into 0s.
ATmega328P endurance: flash 10,000 cycles, EEPROM 100,000; one write per minute to one EEPROM byte wears it out in about 69 days.
Write less and use wear levelling; rotating over 10 slots stretches 69 days to about 694 days.
Firmware enters a chip via a hardware programmer (ISP, SWD/JTAG), a bootloader (e.g. Optiboot, 512 bytes on the Uno) or OTA.
Safe OTA uses A/B slots: download to the inactive slot, verify, switch, and roll back if the new image never marks itself valid.
A CRC detects accidental corruption; a digital signature checked with a stored public key proves the image is genuine.
lessons.tip: Draw the flash map of every device you build: where the bootloader, the application slots and the settings live, with addresses. When an update goes wrong, that one picture tells you what could have been overwritten.
lessons.task: Your device saves a log entry to EEPROM every 30 seconds and the EEPROM is rated for 100,000 writes. Calculate how long one EEPROM location lasts, then how many slots you need for wear levelling to reach at least 5 years.

quiz.q: What does the startup code do before calling main()?
options: Turns on the watchdog in window mode
Copies .data from flash to RAM and zeroes .bss
quiz.explain: The C runtime setup copies initial values into RAM and clears uninitialised globals, then calls main.

quiz.q: An EEPROM byte rated for 100,000 writes is written once per minute. About how long does it last?
quiz.explain: 100,000 minutes / (60 x 24) is about 69 days.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a bootloader?
options: To start the application or receive and write new firmware into flash
quiz.explain: A bootloader runs first and either jumps to the application or loads a new one.

quiz.q: Why do safe OTA designs use two firmware slots?
options: So a failed or corrupted download never destroys the working firmware
Because flash cannot be read twice
quiz.explain: The new image goes to the inactive slot; the old one keeps working until the new one is verified.

quiz.q: Which check proves that a firmware image really comes from the manufacturer?
options: A digital signature verified with a public key
quiz.explain: Anyone can compute a CRC; only the private-key holder can produce a valid signature.

lessons.title: From Super-Loop to RTOS: Tasks, States and Preemptive Scheduling
lessons.content:
Picture a small tea stall near a bus stand in Dhaka, run by one man. He boils water, pours tea, hands out biscuits, takes money, gives change and washes cups, one after another, round and round, all day. For a quiet morning this works perfectly. Then a bus stops and fifteen passengers shout at once, one of them wants change for a 1,000 taka note, and the kettle starts to boil over. He can only do one thing at a time, and the slow job (counting change) makes everyone else wait. Firmware has exactly the same problem. This lesson is about the two main ways to organise firmware: the simple super-loop that most small devices use, and the real-time operating system (RTOS) that bigger devices use when the super-loop starts to crack.

Where this fits: Operating Systems taught you processes and preemptive scheduling on a PC. Here we shrink that idea to a microcontroller with a few kilobytes of RAM and ask: how should I structure my program so every job gets done on time?

The super-loop: The simplest structure is one endless loop inside main. First you initialise the hardware once, then you repeat the same list of jobs forever. In pseudo-code: init(); while (1) { read_sensor(); update_display(); check_button(); send_log(); }. Arduino hides this behind setup() and loop(), but underneath, the Arduino core calls loop() again and again from main. There is no operating system at all. Your code owns the whole chip.

Foreground and background: Pure super-loops are rarely alone. Urgent events, such as a byte arriving on the UART or a timer tick, are handled by interrupt service routines (ISRs), which you met in lesson 14. So the classic small-device design is called foreground/background: ISRs are the foreground (they run immediately when hardware asks), and the super-loop is the background (it runs whenever no ISR is running). The ISR does the tiny urgent part, such as copying a byte into a ring buffer and setting a volatile flag, and the loop does the slow part later, such as parsing the whole command.

Loop time decides response time: Suppose one pass of the loop takes these times: read_sensor 2 ms, update_display 10 ms, check_button 0.1 ms and send_log 30 ms. One pass is about 42 ms. If the user presses the button just after check_button finished, the program will not look at it again until the next pass, so the button can wait up to about 42 ms. Fine for a button, terrible for a safety cut-off. The rule is simple: in a super-loop, the worst-case reaction time of any job is roughly the time of the whole loop. Every slow job you add makes every other job slower to react.

The delay() trap: Beginners write blink code like: digitalWrite(LED, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(LED, LOW); delay(500);. While delay() runs, the CPU just spins and does nothing useful, so the button, the sensor and the UART are all ignored for a whole second. One blocking delay can ruin a super-loop.

Cooperative multitasking with millis(): The fix is to never wait inside a job. Instead, each job checks the clock and returns at once if it is not yet time. Using the millisecond counter from lesson 11: if (millis() - lastBlink >= 500) { lastBlink += 500; toggle(LED); }. The job takes microseconds, and the loop keeps spinning fast. Notice the subtraction form millis() - last: with unsigned arithmetic it still works correctly when the counter wraps around, which on Arduino happens after about 49.7 days. Each job voluntarily gives the CPU back quickly. That is called cooperative multitasking, because the jobs cooperate by being short.

State machines: Some jobs are naturally long, for example "send an SMS through a GSM module": send a command, wait for a reply, send the text, wait for OK. You cannot wait inside the loop, so you split the job into states: SEND_CMD, WAIT_PROMPT, SEND_TEXT, WAIT_OK, DONE. Each pass of the loop runs one small step: if we are in WAIT_OK and the reply has arrived, move to DONE; if 5 seconds have passed, move to an ERROR state. The state lives in a variable, so the job can be paused and resumed between passes. With millis() and state machines, a skilled engineer can run a surprising amount of work on an 8-bit chip with no operating system.

When the super-loop breaks: The super-loop starts to hurt in four situations. First, one job is long and cannot easily be split, for example a Wi-Fi library that blocks for two seconds while connecting, or a big flash write. Second, jobs have very different urgencies, and the loop cannot say "this one matters more": every job waits its turn. Third, the code fills up with flags, counters and states, and adding one feature changes the timing of all the others. Fourth, many timing requirements must be proven, not just hoped for. When you see these signs, it is time for an RTOS.

What an RTOS is: A real-time operating system is a small kernel, often just a few kilobytes of code, that lets you split firmware into independent tasks and switches the CPU between them according to clear rules. "Real-time" does not mean fast. It means predictable: the kernel's own operations take bounded time, and the scheduling rules let you reason about whether every task will meet its deadline (the next lessons make this precise). It is not a mini Windows: usually no files, no users, often no memory protection, just a library linked into your firmware.

Tasks: In an RTOS, each job becomes a task (FreeRTOS calls them tasks, some systems call them threads). A task is just a C function with its own endless loop, for example: void sensorTask(void *p) { for (;;) { read_sensor(); wait 100 ms; } }. You write each task as if it owned the CPU alone. It may even wait (block) in the middle, and that is fine, because while it waits the kernel runs someone else. This is the big mental shift: in a super-loop you must never wait; in an RTOS task, waiting is normal and polite.

Task states: Every task is in one of a few states. Running: it is using the CPU right now (on a single-core MCU only one task can be Running). Ready: it could run but a higher-priority task is using the CPU. Blocked: it is waiting for something, such as a time delay to finish, data to arrive in a queue or a semaphore to be given, and it uses no CPU at all. Suspended: it has been switched off explicitly and is ignored until resumed. Most tasks spend most of their life Blocked, which is exactly what we want.

The tick: How does the kernel know when 100 ms have passed? A hardware timer generates a periodic interrupt called the tick, commonly every 1 ms (a tick rate of 1,000 Hz). On ARM Cortex-M chips the SysTick timer is built into the core for exactly this job. On each tick the kernel updates its time count, checks whether any Blocked task's delay has expired and moves it to Ready, and, if tasks of equal priority share the CPU, it may switch between them (time slicing). Delays are therefore measured in ticks: with a 1 ms tick, a 100-tick delay is 100 ms.

Preemptive priority scheduling: Each task gets a priority number. The rule used by most RTOSes, including FreeRTOS, is: the highest-priority task that is Ready always runs. If a high-priority task becomes Ready (because its delay ended, or an ISR gave it data), it immediately preempts, that is interrupts, whatever lower-priority task was running. Example: a motor-safety task has priority 3, a display task priority 2, a logging task priority 1. Logging is busy writing to an SD card when the safety sensor trips. The ISR signals the safety task, the kernel switches to it within microseconds, it stops the motor, then blocks again, and logging continues where it left off. Compare this with the super-loop, where the safety check would wait for the 30 ms log job to finish.

The context switch: To switch tasks, the kernel saves the current task's CPU registers (including the program counter and status) onto that task's stack, stores its stack pointer, picks the next task, restores its stack pointer and pops its registers. The next task continues exactly where it was paused, unaware anything happened. On Cortex-M, a special low-priority exception called PendSV is typically used to do the switch. A context switch costs only a few microseconds on a modern 32-bit MCU, but it is not free, so switching thousands of times per second has a cost.

Every task needs its own stack: Because each task is paused in the middle of its own function calls, each needs a private stack. This is the hidden price of an RTOS. Four tasks with 512-byte stacks need 2 KB just for stacks, which is the entire SRAM of an ATmega328P. That is why RTOSes are much more common on 32-bit chips like STM32 (tens to hundreds of KB of SRAM) or ESP32 (520 KB of SRAM) than on small AVRs. Sizing stacks is a real engineering job: too small and a task silently overwrites another task's memory; too big and you run out of RAM.

FreeRTOS flavour: FreeRTOS is the most widely used open-source RTOS for microcontrollers, under the MIT licence and maintained by Amazon. A task is created with xTaskCreate(sensorTask, "sensor", 256, NULL, 2, NULL): the function, a name for debugging, the stack depth (in FreeRTOS this is counted in words, not bytes), a parameter, the priority and an optional handle. Inside the task, vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)) blocks it for 100 ms. Then vTaskStartScheduler() starts the kernel and never returns. When every task is Blocked, the kernel runs a lowest-priority idle task, a good place to sleep the CPU (lesson 18). If you program an ESP32 with the Arduino tools or Espressif's ESP-IDF, you are already using FreeRTOS underneath, and your loop() actually runs inside a FreeRTOS task. Zephyr and VxWorks are other well-known RTOSes.

RTOS versus embedded Linux: A Raspberry Pi runs Linux; an STM32 runs FreeRTOS. Linux needs a processor with a memory management unit, many megabytes of RAM, storage for a file system, and takes seconds to boot. In return you get networking stacks, file systems, Python and thousands of programs. Standard Linux is not hard real-time by default (there is a PREEMPT_RT variant that improves this). An RTOS fits in kilobytes, boots in milliseconds and gives tight timing, but you write almost everything yourself. Big products often use both: Linux for the user interface, an MCU with an RTOS for time-critical control.

Real life example 1, a prepaid electricity meter: Many homes in Bangladesh now use prepaid meters where you load credit with a token. Inside, firmware has several jobs with very different needs: measuring energy continuously (must never stop), cutting the relay when credit runs out, reading the keypad when someone types a token, updating the LCD, and talking to the utility over a communication module. Written as tasks, the metering task gets a high priority, the keypad and relay tasks medium, and the display and communication tasks low. A slow network reply can no longer delay energy measurement, because the scheduler always lets the metering task run first.

Real life example 2, a rice cooker: A rice cooker has to read one temperature sensor, switch one heater and light one LED. All jobs are short and none blocks. A super-loop with a timer interrupt is perfect here: less RAM, less code, nothing to configure and easy to test. Choosing an RTOS here would be over-engineering. Pick the simplest structure that meets the timing.

Common mistakes: Thinking an RTOS makes code faster; it does not, it makes timing more manageable and costs some CPU and RAM. Using busy-wait loops inside tasks, which starves every lower-priority task; always block with a delay or by waiting on an object instead. Giving every task the same priority, which throws away the main benefit. Making stacks too small, and calling blocking RTOS functions from an ISR.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the super-loop and foreground/background structure. Compute worst-case response time of a super-loop from job times. Explain cooperative versus preemptive multitasking. Draw the task state diagram (Running, Ready, Blocked, Suspended) and explain each transition. Explain what happens during a context switch and why each task needs its own stack. Short notes on the tick and the idle task are common.

Recap: A super-loop runs every job in turn forever, with ISRs in the foreground for urgent work. Its worst-case reaction time is roughly one loop time, so never block inside it; use millis() and state machines. When jobs are long, urgencies differ or timing must be guaranteed, an RTOS splits firmware into tasks with priorities. The highest-priority Ready task runs, the tick drives delays, the context switch saves and restores registers on per-task stacks, and Blocked tasks cost no CPU. Next we see how tasks talk to each other safely.
key_points: A super-loop initialises once and then runs every job in turn forever; Arduino's loop() is a super-loop.
Foreground/background design: ISRs handle the urgent part, the loop handles the slow part later.
In a super-loop the worst-case reaction time is roughly one full loop time, so never block with delay().
Cooperative multitasking uses millis() checks and state machines so every job returns quickly.
An RTOS is a small kernel that runs independent tasks; real-time means predictable, not fast.
Task states: Running, Ready, Blocked (waiting, uses no CPU) and Suspended.
Preemptive priority scheduling: the highest-priority Ready task always runs; the tick (often 1 ms) drives delays.
Each task needs its own stack and context switches cost time, so RTOSes suit 32-bit MCUs with more SRAM.
lessons.tip: Before choosing an RTOS, write the list of jobs with how long each takes and how fast each must react. If a simple loop meets every number, keep the loop.
lessons.task: On paper, list the jobs of a digital wall clock with an alarm (keep time, update display, read buttons, ring buzzer). Write them once as a super-loop with millis() checks and once as RTOS tasks with priorities, and note the worst-case button reaction time for the super-loop.

quiz.q: A super-loop runs jobs taking 2 ms, 10 ms, 0.1 ms (button check) and 30 ms. What is the worst-case wait before a button press is noticed?
quiz.explain: The button is checked once per pass, so a press just after the check waits a whole pass: 2 + 10 + 0.1 + 30 = about 42 ms.

quiz.q: A task waiting for a queue item or for a delay to finish is in which state?
quiz.explain: Blocked tasks are waiting for time or an event and use no CPU until it happens.

quiz.q: In preemptive priority scheduling, which task uses the CPU?
options: The highest-priority task that is Ready
The task that was created first
The task with the biggest stack
Each task in turn for exactly one tick, regardless of priority
quiz.explain: The scheduler always runs the highest-priority Ready task and preempts lower ones when it becomes Ready.

quiz.q: What does vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100)) do in FreeRTOS?
options: Spins the CPU in a busy loop for 100 ms
Blocks the calling task for about 100 ms so other tasks can run
quiz.explain: The task moves to Blocked for that many ticks; the CPU runs other tasks or the idle task meanwhile.

quiz.q: Why is an RTOS rarely used on an ATmega328P?
options: It has no timer for a tick
It is too fast for an RTOS
Each task needs its own stack and the chip has only 2 KB of SRAM
quiz.explain: Per-task stacks eat RAM quickly; four 512-byte stacks would already use all 2 KB.

lessons.title: RTOS Communication: Queues, Semaphores, Mutexes and Priority Inversion
lessons.content:
Think of a student mess in Dhaka with eight boys and one bathroom. There is one key hanging on a nail. Whoever wants the bathroom takes the key, and returns it when done. Nobody walks in on anybody, because nobody can enter without the key. Now imagine there were no key and everyone just tried the door. Sometimes it works, sometimes two people collide, and the result depends on pure luck of timing. Tasks in an RTOS are exactly like these boys: several of them want the same thing (a variable, the UART, an I2C bus), and the kernel can switch between them at any moment. This lesson is about the keys, notice boards and doorbells that let tasks share safely.

Where this fits: Operating Systems already taught you race conditions, critical sections, semaphores with wait and signal, mutexes and the classic problems. We will not repeat the theory. Here we look at the RTOS versions of these tools, how they are used between tasks and interrupt routines on a microcontroller, and the famous bug they can cause on a real spacecraft.

The shared data problem: Suppose a sensor task writes a reading into a global structure with two fields, temperature and humidity, and a display task reads it. The sensor task writes temperature, then the tick fires and the scheduler switches to the higher-priority display task before humidity is written. The display now shows the new temperature with the old humidity, a mix that never existed. This is called a torn read. Even count++ is not safe: it is a read, an add and a write, and a switch between the read and the write loses an update. On an 8-bit AVR, even reading one 16-bit or 32-bit variable takes several instructions, so it can be torn too (recall lesson 14).

The bluntest tool, critical sections: You can stop all switching by disabling interrupts around the risky lines. In FreeRTOS this is taskENTER_CRITICAL() and taskEXIT_CRITICAL(). It works, but while interrupts are off, nothing else can respond, not even urgent hardware. So critical sections must be only a few instructions long, such as copying a small structure. For anything longer, use the kernel objects below, which block only the tasks involved and leave the rest of the system running.

Queues, the notice board: The most useful RTOS object is the queue: a first-in, first-out buffer of fixed-size items that the kernel protects for you. One task sends, another receives. Data is copied into the queue, so the sender can reuse its own variable immediately. If the queue is empty, a receiving task can block (with a timeout) until something arrives, using zero CPU while it waits. If the queue is full, a sender can block until there is space. In FreeRTOS: q = xQueueCreate(5, sizeof(int32_t)) makes a queue of 5 items of 4 bytes each, which needs 20 bytes of storage for the items (plus a small control block). Then xQueueSend(q, &reading, timeout) and xQueueReceive(q, &value, portMAX_DELAY).

Why queues remove so many bugs: With a queue, the sensor task never touches the display task's variables. It just posts complete readings, and the display task takes complete readings. No torn data, no global flags, and the two tasks are decoupled: you can change one without breaking the other. A good rule of thumb in RTOS design is to share data by sending messages rather than by sharing variables wherever you can.

Binary semaphore, the doorbell: A binary semaphore has only two values, empty and full (given). One side gives it, the other side takes it. Taking an empty semaphore blocks the taker until someone gives. It does not carry data, it carries the news that something happened. A typical use: a button ISR gives a semaphore, and a button-handling task, which sits blocked on take, wakes up and does the work.

Deferred interrupt processing: This is the most important pattern in RTOS firmware. Lesson 14 said ISRs must be short. So the ISR does the minimum: clear the hardware flag, maybe grab the data byte, and give a semaphore or send to a queue. A task then does the long part, such as parsing, computing or printing. The task runs at a priority you choose, can block, can use the full RTOS API, and can be debugged like normal code. In FreeRTOS, from inside an ISR you must use the special versions ending in FromISR, for example xSemaphoreGiveFromISR(sem, &woken), because the normal versions may try to block, and an ISR must never block. If giving the semaphore woke a task with higher priority than the one that was interrupted, the ISR ends with portYIELD_FROM_ISR(woken), so that task runs immediately after the interrupt instead of waiting for the next tick.

Counting semaphores: A counting semaphore holds a number instead of just empty or full. Two uses. Counting events: an ISR gives once per event, and the task takes once per event, so if three pulses arrive while the task is busy, none is lost; the count simply goes to 3. Managing a pool of resources: if a system has 3 DMA buffers, a semaphore created with count 3 lets three tasks hold one each, and the fourth task blocks until one is returned. Think of a parking lot with 3 spaces and a counter at the gate.

Mutex, the bathroom key: A mutex (mutual exclusion) protects a shared resource such as the UART, an SD card or an I2C bus that many tasks use. Pattern: xSemaphoreTake(i2cMutex, timeout); talk to the sensor; xSemaphoreGive(i2cMutex);. Only one task can hold the mutex at a time. If another task tries to take it, it blocks until the holder gives it back. The protected section is as short as possible, and you must give the mutex back on every path out of it, including error paths.

Mutex versus binary semaphore: They look similar, but they are not the same thing. A mutex has an owner: the task that took it is the only one that should give it back. A binary semaphore has no owner: the ISR gives, a task takes. Because a mutex knows its owner, the kernel can apply priority inheritance (explained below); in FreeRTOS, mutexes have priority inheritance and binary semaphores do not. Mutexes are also not meant to be used from ISRs. Simple rule: use a mutex to protect a resource, use a binary semaphore to signal an event.

Priority inversion: Here is the trap. Take three tasks: H (high priority), M (medium) and L (low). L takes the I2C mutex and starts a transfer. H wakes up, preempts L, and tries to take the same mutex. It must block, because L holds it. That is fine, as long as L finishes quickly. But now M wakes up. M does not need the mutex at all, and it has higher priority than L, so it preempts L and runs. While M runs, L cannot finish, so L cannot give the mutex, so H cannot run. A medium-priority task is now blocking a high-priority task, for as long as M likes. The priorities have been turned upside down, which is why it is called priority inversion, and the delay is unbounded.

A worked timeline: At time 0 ms, L takes the mutex; its locked work needs 2 ms. At 1 ms, H wakes and blocks on the mutex. At 1.5 ms, M wakes and runs for 50 ms. L only resumes at 51.5 ms, gives the mutex at 52 ms, and H finally runs. H, which expected to wait at most about 1 ms (the rest of L's locked work), waited about 51 ms. If H had a 10 ms deadline, it missed it, and nothing in H's own code was wrong.

The Mars Pathfinder story: This is not just theory. In 1997 NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander, running the VxWorks RTOS, started resetting itself repeatedly on Mars. A high-priority task managing the information bus waited on a mutex held by a low-priority weather-data task, while medium-priority communication work kept running. The high-priority task missed its deadline, a watchdog-like check noticed that, and the system reset. Engineers reproduced the problem on a copy on Earth, found that priority inheritance was switched off for that mutex, and fixed it by uploading a change that turned it on.

Priority inheritance, the fix: While a low-priority task holds a mutex that a higher-priority task is waiting for, the kernel temporarily raises the holder's priority to the waiting task's priority. In our timeline, as soon as H blocks on the mutex at 1 ms, L is raised to H's priority. Now M cannot preempt L. L finishes its locked work at 2 ms, gives the mutex, drops back to its normal priority, and H runs at once. H waited about 1 ms instead of 51 ms. A related method, the priority ceiling protocol, gives the mutex a fixed ceiling priority equal to the highest priority of any task that uses it. Either way, keep locked sections short; inheritance limits the damage but does not make long locks free.

Deadlock: Two tasks, two mutexes. Task A takes the UART mutex, then wants the SD mutex. Task B takes the SD mutex, then wants the UART mutex. Each holds what the other wants, and both wait forever. As you learned in OS, the simplest cure is a lock order: every task always takes the mutexes in the same order (say UART before SD). Using timeouts on take, instead of waiting forever, also turns a silent freeze into an error you can log and recover from.

Lighter tools: Many RTOSes offer more objects. FreeRTOS has event groups (a task can wait for several bits, such as "Wi-Fi up AND time synced") and direct-to-task notifications, a lightweight built-in signal that can often replace a binary semaphore with less RAM and faster operation. The ideas are the same: signal, wait, do not share raw variables carelessly.

Common RTOS bugs: Stack overflow, when a task's stack is too small, corrupts nearby memory and causes random crashes; FreeRTOS can check for it with a hook function during development. Starvation, when a high-priority task never blocks (for example a busy polling loop), so lower tasks never run. Calling a normal blocking API from an ISR instead of the FromISR version. Forgetting to give a mutex on an error path, which freezes every task that later wants it. Holding a mutex while calling vTaskDelay. And using a mutex where a queue would have removed the shared variable completely.

Real life example 1, a school weather station in Rajshahi: A sensor task reads temperature, humidity and pressure over I2C every 10 seconds and sends each reading to a queue. A logger task receives from the queue and writes to an SD card. An upload task sends averages over GSM every hour. A light sensor on the same I2C bus is read by another task. Both I2C users take an I2C mutex, so their transfers never mix. The SD card and GSM can be slow or fail without stopping the readings, because the queue absorbs the delay.

Real life example 2, a garment factory piece counter in Gazipur: Each finished piece on a conveyor breaks an infrared beam, which fires an interrupt. The ISR only gives a counting semaphore. A counting task takes it once per piece and updates the total, and a display task shows the hourly count on a big LED board. When the display task is busy redrawing, pieces still arrive, but the semaphore count just rises and no piece is lost. The ISR stays a few microseconds long, so the beam is never missed.

What exams ask: Explain the shared data problem with an example. Compare queue, binary semaphore, counting semaphore and mutex, and say when to use each. Describe deferred interrupt processing. Explain priority inversion with a three-task timeline, the Mars Pathfinder case, and priority inheritance or ceiling. Show a deadlock between two tasks and how lock ordering prevents it.

Recap: Tasks can be switched at any instruction, so shared data must be protected. Use very short critical sections only for tiny copies. Queues move copied data safely and decouple tasks. Binary semaphores signal events, especially from ISRs using FromISR calls; counting semaphores count events or resources. Mutexes protect shared resources and have owners, which allows priority inheritance against priority inversion. Keep locks short, take them in a fixed order, and use timeouts. Next we measure whether all these tasks can actually meet their deadlines.
key_points: Tasks can be switched between any two instructions, so shared variables can be torn or lose updates.
Critical sections (interrupts off) must be only a few instructions long.
A queue copies fixed-size items FIFO, lets tasks block when empty or full, and decouples producer and consumer.
A binary semaphore signals an event; ISRs give it with FromISR calls so a task does the long work (deferred interrupt processing).
A counting semaphore counts events or a pool of resources.
A mutex protects a shared resource, has an owner and supports priority inheritance; do not use it from an ISR.
Priority inversion: a medium task preempts a low task holding a mutex that a high task needs; Mars Pathfinder 1997 hit this.
Deadlock with two mutexes is prevented by always taking locks in the same order and using timeouts.
lessons.tip: When two tasks need the same data, first ask: can one simply send it to the other through a queue? Most of the time the answer is yes, and the bug disappears before it is written.
lessons.task: Draw a time line (0 to 60 ms) for tasks H, M and L from this lesson, first without and then with priority inheritance. Mark when the mutex is taken and given, and write how long H waited in each case.

quiz.q: What is the best tool to pass sensor readings from one task to another?
options: Disabling interrupts for the whole program
quiz.explain: A queue copies complete items safely between tasks and lets the receiver block until data arrives.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
options: A mutex has an owner and supports priority inheritance
A mutex can hold data, a semaphore cannot
A binary semaphore is always faster than a queue
A mutex can only be used inside ISRs
quiz.explain: Only the owner gives a mutex back, which lets the kernel apply priority inheritance; semaphores have no owner.

quiz.q: In priority inversion with tasks H, M and L, what actually keeps H waiting for a long time?
options: Task M preempting L while L holds the mutex H needs
quiz.explain: M does not need the mutex but outranks L, so L cannot finish and release it, and H stays blocked.

quiz.q: What does priority inheritance do?
options: Temporarily raises the mutex holder's priority to that of the highest waiting task
Turns the mutex into a queue
quiz.explain: While holding the mutex, L runs at H's priority, so M cannot preempt it; afterwards it drops back.

quiz.q: What is the correct way for an ISR to wake a task that will do the long processing?
options: Take a mutex inside the ISR
Give a binary semaphore with the FromISR version that the task is waiting on
quiz.explain: ISRs must never block; FromISR give is non-blocking and wakes the waiting task (deferred interrupt processing).

lessons.title: Real-Time Systems: Deadlines, Rate-Monotonic Scheduling and Response Time Analysis
lessons.content:
A car hits a wall. Inside, a small computer reads an acceleration sensor, decides this is a real crash and not a pothole, and fires the airbag, all within a few tens of milliseconds. If it fires correctly but 300 ms late, the passenger has already hit the steering wheel. The answer was right, but it came too late, so it was wrong. Now think of a YouTube video on a slow mobile connection that buffers for a second. Annoying, but nobody is hurt. Both are computers reacting to the world, but the cost of being late is completely different. This lesson is about systems where time is part of correctness, and the maths that tells us, before we ship, whether every deadline will be met.

What real-time means: A real-time system is one whose correctness depends not only on the logical result but also on the time at which the result is produced. Real-time does not mean fast. A system that must answer within one hour and always does is real-time; a very fast system that is usually quick but sometimes freezes for two seconds is not. The key word is guaranteed: we want a bound on the worst case, not a good average.

Hard, firm and soft: In a hard real-time system, missing a deadline is a failure that can cause damage or injury: airbags, anti-lock brakes, pacemakers, flight control, a factory emergency stop. In a firm real-time system, a late result is useless and is thrown away, but an occasional miss is not a disaster: a video conferencing frame that arrives after its display time, or one missed sensor sample in a monitoring system. In a soft real-time system, a late result still has some value, it just becomes less useful the later it is: a phone's touch response, music streaming, a ticketing website. Most real products mix all three: one ECU in a car might run hard brake tasks and soft diagnostics tasks side by side.

The periodic task model: To reason about timing we describe each task with a few numbers. The period T is how often the task is released (a temperature task released every 100 ms has T = 100 ms). The worst-case execution time C, or WCET, is the longest the task can ever take to run once, on its own, with no interruptions. The relative deadline D is how long after release the job must finish; in the simplest model D = T, meaning each job must finish before the next one is released. Release jitter is the variation in when the job actually starts. Tasks that are triggered by events, like a button, are called sporadic if we know a minimum time between triggers, and aperiodic if we do not.

Why worst case, not average: Suppose a task usually takes 2 ms but takes 7 ms when a cache miss, a long branch path and a slow flash read happen together. If we plan with 2 ms, the system works on the bench and fails in the field on the one bad day. Hard real-time analysis always uses WCET. Finding a true WCET is hard: caches, pipelines and data-dependent loops all change execution time. That is one reason small MCUs with simple pipelines and no cache are loved in hard real-time work: their timing is easy to predict.

Utilization: The fraction of CPU time one task needs is C/T. Total utilization is U = C1/T1 + C2/T2 + ... + Cn/Tn. Example, task set A: task 1 has C = 1, T = 4; task 2 has C = 2, T = 8; task 3 has C = 1, T = 10 (all in ms). U = 1/4 + 2/8 + 1/10 = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.1 = 0.6. The CPU is busy 60% of the time. One rule is absolute: if U > 1 on a single CPU, no scheduler on earth can meet all deadlines, because the work simply does not fit in the time. U <= 1 is necessary, but as we will see, for fixed priorities it is not always enough.

Rate-monotonic scheduling: Last lesson's RTOS uses fixed priorities, so how should we assign them? Rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling has a simple rule: the shorter the period, the higher the priority. A 4 ms task beats an 8 ms task, which beats a 10 ms task. Importance does not enter into it; rate does. In 1973 Liu and Layland proved that, for independent periodic tasks with D = T on one preemptive CPU, RM is optimal among fixed-priority schemes: if any fixed-priority order can schedule the set, RM can too.

The Liu-Layland bound: They also proved a simple test. A set of n tasks is guaranteed schedulable under RM if U <= n(2^(1/n) - 1). The values: for n = 1 the bound is 1.0; for n = 2 it is 0.828; for n = 3 it is 0.780; for n = 4 it is 0.757; for n = 10 it is about 0.718; and as n grows very large it approaches ln 2, about 0.693. So a quick rule of thumb: if your tasks use less than about 69% of the CPU, RM will meet every deadline, whatever the number of tasks.

Worked check, set A: Three tasks, U = 0.6. The bound for n = 3 is 0.780. Since 0.6 <= 0.780, set A is schedulable under RM. Done, no timeline needed. That is the beauty of the bound: one line of arithmetic.

The catch, sufficient but not necessary: The bound is a sufficient test. If U is below it, you are safe. If U is above it but still at most 1, the test says nothing: the set may be schedulable or may not. Many students wrongly write "U is above the bound, so it is not schedulable". That is a classic exam trap. When the bound fails, we need an exact test.

Response time analysis: The exact test for fixed priorities computes each task's worst-case response time R, the longest time from release to finish. The worst case happens when a task is released at the same instant as all higher-priority tasks (the critical instant). Then R_i = C_i + sum over higher-priority tasks j of ceiling(R_i / T_j) x C_j. The ceiling term counts how many times each higher-priority task can be released and preempt task i during a window of length R_i. Because R_i appears on both sides, we iterate: start with R = C_i, plug it into the right side, get a new R, and repeat until the value stops changing (schedulable if R_i <= D_i) or exceeds the deadline (not schedulable).

Worked example, set B: Task 1: C = 2, T = 5. Task 2: C = 2, T = 7. Task 3: C = 1, T = 10. RM priorities follow the periods: task 1 highest, task 3 lowest. U = 2/5 + 2/7 + 1/10 = 0.4 + 0.286 + 0.1 = 0.786. The bound for 3 tasks is 0.780, and 0.786 is just above it, so the quick test is inconclusive. Let us compute R for each task.

Task 1 has nothing above it, so R1 = 2 <= 5. Task 2: start R = 2. Next R = 2 + ceiling(2/5) x 2 = 2 + 2 = 4. Again: 2 + ceiling(4/5) x 2 = 4. It stopped changing, so R2 = 4 <= 7. Task 3: start R = 1. Next R = 1 + ceiling(1/5) x 2 + ceiling(1/7) x 2 = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Again: 1 + ceiling(5/5) x 2 + ceiling(5/7) x 2 = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Stable, so R3 = 5 <= 10. Every response time is within its deadline, so set B is schedulable under RM even though it failed the bound.

A harder one, set C: Task 1: C = 2, T = 4. Task 2: C = 2, T = 6. Task 3: C = 1, T = 12. U = 0.5 + 0.333 + 0.083 = 0.917, far above 0.780. R1 = 2. For task 2: 2, then 2 + ceiling(2/4) x 2 = 4, then 2 + ceiling(4/4) x 2 = 4, so R2 = 4 <= 6. For task 3 the iteration goes 1, 5, 7, 9, 11, 11: for example at R = 9 we get 1 + ceiling(9/4) x 2 + ceiling(9/6) x 2 = 1 + 6 + 4 = 11, and at R = 11 we get 1 + 6 + 4 = 11 again. R3 = 11 <= 12, so even at about 92% load this set just makes it. The lesson: never reject a design because of the bound alone.

Earliest deadline first: RM keeps priorities fixed. Earliest deadline first (EDF) is dynamic: at every moment, the ready job with the nearest absolute deadline runs. For independent periodic tasks with D = T on one preemptive CPU, EDF meets all deadlines if and only if U <= 1. So EDF can use the whole CPU, while RM is only guaranteed up to the bound (and often more, as RTA shows). Sets A, B and C are all fine under EDF since their U is below 1.

RM or EDF in practice: Most commercial RTOSes, FreeRTOS included, give you fixed priorities, so RM-style assignment is what engineers actually use. RM is also easier to reason about under overload: when the CPU is overloaded, the lowest-priority tasks miss first and the important short-period tasks keep running. Under EDF, an overload can make many tasks miss in a chain. EDF needs the kernel to track deadlines, which costs a little more work at run time.

Real-world extras: The clean model ignores some things. If a task can block on a mutex held by a lower task, add a blocking term B_i to the response-time equation; priority inheritance from the last lesson is what keeps B_i small and bounded. Interrupts behave like very high-priority tasks and must be counted. Context switches and the tick cost a little CPU each time. Jitter means a task does not always start exactly at its release. Engineers keep a safety margin, often aiming for clearly less than the computed limit, so the system survives code growth and surprises.

Measuring WCET in the lab: A cheap trick is to set a GPIO pin high at the start of a task and low at the end, then watch the pin on an oscilloscope or logic analyzer (lesson 24) for hours and record the longest pulse. On ARM Cortex-M3 and M4 chips, the DWT cycle counter can count CPU cycles between two points in code. Professional teams also use static analysis tools that compute a bound from the machine code. Measured maximums are not proven worst cases, so add margin.

Real life example 1, a drone flight controller: A small quadcopter reads its gyroscope and adjusts motor PWM in a control loop that commonly runs hundreds to thousands of times per second. That loop is hard real-time: if it misses a few periods the drone wobbles or flips. Lower-rate tasks such as reading the battery voltage, the radio receiver or a GPS run at lower priority. With RM priorities, the fast control loop automatically gets the highest priority, which is exactly what we want.

Real life example 2, a cutting machine in a Narayanganj factory: A fabric cutting machine has a light curtain; if a worker's hand crosses it, the blade must stop within a fixed time. That task is hard real-time with a short deadline. The same controller updates a display of pieces cut and sends daily totals to the office computer, soft tasks that can be late without harm. Engineers compute U, check RTA for the safety task with interrupts included, and keep the safety path as short as possible.

Common mistakes: Thinking real-time means fast. Using average execution time instead of WCET. Saying a set is unschedulable because U is above the Liu-Layland bound. Assigning priorities by importance rather than by rate, which can make a short-period task miss its deadline. Forgetting interrupt load and blocking time. Thinking U <= 1 is enough for fixed priorities.

What exams ask: Define hard, firm and soft real-time with examples. Define period, WCET, deadline and jitter. Compute U and apply the Liu-Layland bound for a given n. Run response time analysis on a three-task set. Compare RM and EDF, and state the EDF condition U <= 1.

Recap: In real-time systems a late answer is a wrong answer. Model each task with T, C and D, and use worst-case times. U = sum of C/T must be at most 1. Rate-monotonic gives shorter periods higher priority and is optimal among fixed priorities. If U <= n(2^(1/n) - 1), the set is safe; if not, run response time analysis before deciding. EDF reaches U <= 1. Next we learn the tools that let us see what our firmware is actually doing.
key_points: Real-time means the result must be correct and on time; it means guaranteed worst case, not fast.
Hard: a miss is a failure (airbag, brakes); firm: a late result is useless; soft: a late result loses value.
Each periodic task has period T, worst-case execution time C (WCET) and deadline D, often D = T.
Utilization U = sum of C/T; U > 1 on one CPU can never be scheduled.
Rate-monotonic: shorter period means higher priority; optimal among fixed-priority schemes (Liu and Layland, 1973).
Liu-Layland bound n(2^(1/n) - 1): 0.828 for 2 tasks, 0.780 for 3, about 0.693 for large n; it is sufficient, not necessary.
Response time analysis R = C + sum ceiling(R/Tj) x Cj gives the exact answer; set B (U = 0.786) gives R = 2, 4, 5 and is schedulable.
EDF meets all deadlines if and only if U <= 1 (D = T, one preemptive CPU).
lessons.tip: In every scheduling problem, first write U and the bound side by side. If U is below the bound, stop; if not, do response time analysis task by task, writing every iteration.
lessons.task: Make your own three-task set (pick C and T), compute U, compare it with 0.780, then run response time analysis by hand. Change one C until the lowest-priority task just misses its deadline and note the U where that happens.

quiz.q: What is the Liu-Layland rate-monotonic bound for 3 tasks, approximately?
quiz.explain: 3 x (2^(1/3) - 1) is about 0.780; 0.828 is for two tasks and 0.693 is the limit for very many tasks.

quiz.q: A three-task set has U = 0.786, just above the bound 0.780. What can you conclude?
options: The bound is inconclusive, so do response time analysis
quiz.explain: The bound is only sufficient; set B in this lesson has U = 0.786 and RTA shows R = 2, 4, 5, all within deadlines.

quiz.q: Under rate-monotonic scheduling, which task gets the highest priority?
options: The one with the longest WCET
The one with the shortest period
The one with the longest deadline
quiz.explain: RM assigns priority by rate: shorter period, higher priority.

quiz.q: An airbag controller where a late deployment can injure someone is an example of:
quiz.explain: Missing the deadline is a failure that can cause harm, which defines hard real-time.

quiz.q: For independent periodic tasks with D = T on one preemptive CPU, when does EDF meet all deadlines?
options: Only when all periods are equal
quiz.explain: EDF is optimal on one CPU: U <= 1 is both necessary and sufficient under these assumptions.

lessons.title: Debugging, Testing and the Embedded Design Process
lessons.content:
Imagine your little brother's toy car stops working. On a laptop program you would just read the error message on the screen. But the toy car has no screen, no keyboard, and the program inside it lives on a chip smaller than your fingernail. When it misbehaves, it simply sits there, silent. Embedded debugging is the art of making a silent machine tell you what it is thinking. In this lesson we also zoom out and look at how a whole embedded product is designed and tested, from an idea on paper to a box on a shop shelf in Elephant Road.

Why embedded debugging is harder: On a PC, your program and your debugger run on the same powerful machine, with gigabytes of memory and a big screen. In an embedded system, the code runs on the target (the MCU), while you sit at the host (your laptop). The target may have 2 KB of SRAM, no display, and it is busy talking to real hardware with real timing. If you pause it, a motor keeps spinning and a UART byte keeps arriving. Bugs also come from three places at once: your code, the hardware (a loose wire, a missing pull-up, a wrong resistor) and timing (an interrupt arriving at the worst moment). A good embedded engineer always asks first: is this a software bug, a hardware bug, or a timing bug?

Tool 1, the humble LED: The very first debugging tool is an LED on a GPIO pin. Turn it on when the code reaches a certain line, blink it twice when an error happens, or toggle it every time the main loop runs. If the LED stops blinking, the loop is stuck. It sounds childish, but it costs one instruction and almost no time, so it does not disturb timing. Many boards ship with an LED on a pin for exactly this reason, like the LED on pin 13 of the Arduino Uno.

Tool 2, printf over UART: The next step is to print messages through the UART to a serial terminal on your laptop, using a USB-to-serial adapter. You write something like printf("temp=%d\n", t) and watch the values scroll by. This is called printf debugging or logging, and it is the most used technique in the world, because it needs nothing but a spare TX pin. You learned the UART frame in lesson 15, so let us now count its cost.

The hidden cost of printf: At 9600 baud with 8N1 framing, each character needs 10 bits, so one character takes about 1.04 ms. A 40-character debug line therefore takes about 41.7 ms to leave the chip. If your loop must run every 10 ms, a single printf just broke your timing, and the bug you were chasing may disappear or a new one may appear. At 115200 baud one character takes about 86.8 microseconds, and the same 40 characters need about 3.5 ms, which is much better but still not free. On top of that, printf with formatting can add several kilobytes of flash, which hurts on a 32 KB chip. Rules of thumb: use a high baud rate, keep messages short, never print inside an ISR, and if possible put the text into a buffer and send it with interrupts or DMA in the background.

Heisenbugs: A bug that changes or vanishes when you add debugging code is jokingly called a Heisenbug. It usually means a timing problem, an uninitialized variable, a stack overflow or a missing volatile. If adding a printf makes the bug go away, the bug is still there; you just moved the timing.

Tool 3, the GPIO toggle for timing: To measure how long a function takes, set a spare pin high at the start and low at the end, then look at the pin with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. The width of the pulse is the execution time, measured with almost zero disturbance. This is the best way to measure the worst-case execution time (WCET) you needed in the real-time lesson. You can also toggle a pin inside an ISR to see how often the interrupt fires and how long it lasts.

Tool 4, the debug probe, JTAG and SWD: Real debuggers talk to the chip through a special hardware port. JTAG was standardised as IEEE 1149.1, first for boundary scan, which tests the solder joints of a board by controlling the pins of chips from outside.
