Later it became the common way to debug and program processors. It uses signals called TCK (clock), TMS (mode select), TDI (data in), TDO (data out) and often a reset line. ARM Cortex-M chips also offer SWD, Serial Wire Debug, which needs only two signal pins: SWDIO (data) and SWCLK (clock), plus ground. A small debug probe, such as an ST-LINK for STM32 boards or a J-Link, connects these pins to your laptop's USB port.

What a debug probe lets you do: With a probe and a debugger program (often GDB, or the one built into an IDE such as STM32CubeIDE), you can flash new firmware, halt the CPU, set breakpoints (stop when this line is reached), step one line at a time, look at and change variables and registers, and see the call stack. Cortex-M cores have hardware breakpoint units, so breakpoints work even though the code is in flash. You can also set a watchpoint: stop when this memory address is written. Watchpoints are magic for finding who corrupts a variable. The classic 8-bit Arduino Uno does not have this kind of easy debug port through its USB cable, which is one reason many professionals move to ARM boards.

A warning about halting: When you stop at a breakpoint, the CPU freezes but the world does not. A UART may overflow, a PWM may keep driving a motor, and the watchdog may reset the chip. Many MCUs can freeze timers and the watchdog while halted; switch that on. For timing bugs, use pin toggles instead.

Tool 5, the logic analyzer: A logic analyzer records many digital signals at once over time and shows them as square waves on your laptop. Cheap USB analyzers with 8 channels are popular with students. The magic feature is protocol decoding: the software reads the waveform on your SPI, I2C or UART lines and writes the bytes on top, such as 'Address 0x48 write, ACK, data 0x00'. If your I2C sensor does not answer, the analyzer shows immediately whether the start condition, the address and the ACK bit are really on the wire. Rule: sample several times faster than the fastest signal; for a 400 kHz I2C clock, a few MHz of sample rate is the minimum, and more is safer.

Tool 6, the oscilloscope and multimeter: A logic analyzer only shows 0 and 1. An oscilloscope shows the real voltage over time, so you can see slow rising edges caused by weak pull-ups, ringing, noise on an ADC input, or a power rail that dips when a motor starts. A multimeter answers simpler questions: is the supply really 3.3 V, is this wire connected, how much current does the board draw in sleep? Many 'software bugs' turn out to be a supply dipping below the brown-out level.

A step-by-step debugging method: First, reproduce the bug reliably. Second, check the boring things: power, ground, clock, wiring, the right pin numbers, the right baud rate. Third, divide and conquer: cut the system in half (does the sensor work alone? does the UART work alone?) until the faulty part is small. Fourth, form a hypothesis and test it with one change at a time. Fifth, after fixing, write down the cause, so the team does not repeat it. This is the same scientific method you use in a physics lab, applied to firmware.

Testing, unit tests on the PC: Much firmware logic does not need hardware at all: the moisture-to-percent conversion, the debounce state machine, a ring buffer, a command parser. Write this logic as plain C functions that do not touch registers, and compile them for your laptop with a normal compiler. Then write small tests: assert(percent(455) == 50). Frameworks such as Unity and Ceedling are popular for embedded C. Tests run in a second, every time you change code. The trick is a thin hardware abstraction layer: only a few small functions touch registers, and everything else is pure logic you can test anywhere.

Testing on the target and hardware-in-the-loop: Some things can only be tested on the real chip: timing, interrupts, peripherals. Integration tests run on the target and report results over UART. In bigger companies, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing connects the real controller board to a computer that pretends to be the outside world. For a car engine controller, the HIL rig simulates engine speed sensors and checks the injector signals the board produces. That way you can test dangerous situations, like a sensor failure at full speed, safely on a desk.

Other kinds of testing: Stress tests run the device for days to catch rare bugs. Boundary tests feed extreme values. Power tests cut the supply in the middle of a flash write. Environmental tests matter in Bangladesh, where a pump-house device may face 40 degrees Celsius and monsoon humidity.

The design process, big picture: An embedded product usually goes through these steps. Requirements: what must it do, how fast, at what cost, on what power, in what environment? Specification: turn wishes into numbers, like 'read moisture every 10 minutes, run 6 months on battery, cost under 3,500 taka'. Architecture: pick the MCU, sensors, communication and power, and draw a block diagram. HW/SW partitioning: decide which jobs go to hardware (a dedicated chip or peripheral) and which to software. Then prototype, design the custom board, write firmware, test, and finally manufacture and maintain.

HW/SW partitioning in one example: To generate a 20 kHz signal, software toggling a pin in a loop wastes the CPU and jitters when interrupts arrive, while a timer's PWM hardware does it perfectly with zero CPU time. Fast, regular jobs go to hardware; flexible logic goes to software.

Prototype to product: Most projects start on a development board like an Arduino, an STM32 Nucleo or an ESP32 DevKit, with sensors on a breadboard. Once it works, engineers design a custom printed circuit board (PCB) that is cheaper, smaller and more reliable than breadboard wires. Then come certification where needed, pilot production, field trials and mass production.

Version control for firmware: Keep all firmware in Git and tag every version you flash to real devices, so when a farmer reports a bug from version 1.3, you can rebuild exactly that code. Printing the firmware version over UART at boot costs one line and saves hours.

Real life example 1, a bKash-style POS terminal: Imagine a team in Dhaka building a small payment terminal. The card reader works on the bench but fails randomly in a shop. With a logic analyzer they see the SPI clock to the reader has glitches whenever the thermal printer runs. An oscilloscope shows the 3.3 V supply dropping when the printer motor starts. The fix is hardware: a bigger capacitor and a separate supply path for the printer. No amount of code changes would have found it.

Real life example 2, a garments factory counter: A sensor counts pieces on a production line in Gazipur, but the count is sometimes too high. A printf shows nothing strange, and adding it makes the bug rarer: a Heisenbug. Toggling a pin in the interrupt and watching it on the scope reveals that the input bounces, firing the ISR two or three times per piece. A debounce step in the input handling, which you met in lesson 10, fixes it, and a unit test on the PC locks in the fix.

Common mistakes: Debugging only with printf and ruining the timing. Leaving the watchdog running at a breakpoint. Forgetting a common ground between the logic analyzer and the board. Mixing register access into all code so nothing can be tested on a PC. Skipping numeric requirements and discovering too late that the battery lasts a week.

What exams ask: Compare JTAG and SWD and name their signals. Explain breakpoints and watchpoints. Show with a UART calculation why printf can change behaviour. Compare a logic analyzer and an oscilloscope. Explain unit testing and HIL, and the design steps with HW/SW partitioning.

Recap: Embedded debugging means making a silent target show its inner state: LEDs and pin toggles cost almost nothing, printf is easy but slow, a JTAG or SWD probe gives breakpoints and watchpoints, and logic analyzers and oscilloscopes show what really happens on the wires. Good firmware is designed to be tested: pure logic tested on the PC, timing and peripherals tested on the target, and whole systems tested in the loop. All of it lives inside a design process that starts with clear, numeric requirements.
key_points: Embedded bugs come from software, hardware or timing; always check power, ground, clock and wiring first.
LED and GPIO pin toggles are almost free and do not disturb timing; a toggled pin plus a scope measures execution time.
printf over UART is easy but slow: at 9600 baud a 40-character line takes about 41.7 ms, at 115200 about 3.5 ms.
JTAG (IEEE 1149.1: TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO) and ARM's two-wire SWD (SWDIO, SWCLK) let a debug probe flash, halt, step, and set breakpoints and watchpoints.
A logic analyzer records many digital lines and decodes UART, SPI and I2C; an oscilloscope shows real voltages, noise and supply dips.
Keep hardware access in a thin layer so pure logic can be unit tested on a PC; use target tests and hardware-in-the-loop for the rest.
The design process: requirements, numeric specification, architecture, HW/SW partitioning, prototype, custom PCB, testing, certification, production and updates.
Keep firmware in version control and print the firmware version at boot.
lessons.tip: Before touching the code, say out loud: is this software, hardware or timing? Then pick the tool that fits: unit test for logic, scope for voltages, logic analyzer for protocols, pin toggle for timing.
lessons.task: On paper, calculate how long a 25-character debug message takes at 9600 and at 115200 baud (8N1). Then write two plain C functions from an earlier lesson (for example, ADC reading to volts) and three assert-style test lines for each that you could run on a PC.

quiz.q: How many signal pins does ARM's Serial Wire Debug (SWD) need, besides ground?
quiz.explain: SWD uses SWDIO for data and SWCLK for clock, two signal pins plus ground.

quiz.q: At 9600 baud with 8N1 framing, about how long does a 40-character debug message take to send?
quiz.explain: Each character is 10 bits, about 1.04 ms, so 40 characters take about 41.7 ms.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for seeing the decoded bytes of an I2C transaction that a sensor does not answer?
options: An LED on a spare pin
A logic analyzer with protocol decoding
quiz.explain: A logic analyzer records SDA and SCL and decodes start, address, ACK and data bytes.

quiz.q: A bug disappears when you add a printf. What does this most likely suggest?
options: A timing, race or memory problem that the extra code shifted
The bug is fixed for good
quiz.explain: Such Heisenbugs usually come from timing, races, uninitialised variables or stack issues; printf only moved them.

quiz.q: Why is a thin hardware abstraction layer useful for testing?
options: It makes the code run faster on the MCU
It removes the need for a debugger
Logic that does not touch registers can be compiled and unit tested on a PC
It lets the watchdog be disabled
quiz.explain: With register access isolated in a few functions, pure logic like conversions and parsers can be tested on a laptop.

lessons.title: IoT Connectivity, Safety and Security
lessons.content:
Think of a fish farmer in Mymensingh. At 3 a.m., on a hot, still night, the oxygen in his pond starts dropping. If nobody switches on the aerator, by sunrise thousands of fish may be floating. A small box in the pond with an oxygen sensor could notice the drop and send him an alert, or even switch on the aerator by itself. The moment an embedded system can talk to phones and servers, it becomes part of the Internet of Things, IoT. That power comes with a price: anything that can be reached from the Internet can also be attacked from the Internet. This lesson covers how embedded devices connect, how they stay secure, and how they stay safe.

What IoT means: The Internet of Things is the idea of connecting everyday physical objects, such as meters, pumps, locks, cameras, cars and wearables, so they can send data and receive commands. A typical IoT system has three parts. The device (or node) at the edge is an embedded system with sensors and actuators. A gateway or network carries its data, for example a Wi-Fi router, a LoRa gateway or a mobile network. And a server or cloud stores the data, shows dashboards, and sends commands or alerts to people's phones.

Why connect at all: Connection gives remote monitoring (read the pond from Dhaka), remote control (switch a pump from your phone), alerts (SMS when the cold storage gets warm), data over time (which field dries fastest), and firmware updates over the air, which you met in lesson 20. But every connection costs energy, money, and security effort, so the first design question is always: what really needs to be sent, and how often?

The connectivity trade-off: Every wireless technology trades three things against each other: range, data rate and power. You cannot get long range, high speed and tiny battery use all at once. Fast links like Wi-Fi burn power; long-range low-power links like LoRa send only small amounts of data. Choose by the job: a security camera needs a fast link, a soil sensor sending one number every ten minutes does not.

Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi gives high data rates and uses the router most homes and offices already have, with a range of tens of metres indoors. Chips like the ESP32 make it cheap and easy. The cost is power: Wi-Fi radios draw much more current than an MCU, and joining a network takes time. Wi-Fi suits mains-powered devices like smart plugs and cameras, or battery devices that wake rarely and send quickly.

Bluetooth Low Energy: BLE is designed for very low power and short range, typically within a room or a house. Its big advantage is that every smartphone already has it, so a fitness band or a medical thermometer can talk directly to a phone app without any router. The phone then acts as the gateway to the Internet. BLE is ideal for wearables and devices you set up from a phone nearby.

Zigbee and mesh networks: Zigbee is built on the IEEE 802.15.4 radio standard and forms a mesh, where devices pass messages for each other, so a network can cover a whole building even though each radio has short range. It is common in smart lighting and home automation. Mesh is handy, but it needs a coordinator or hub to connect to the Internet.

LoRa and LoRaWAN: LoRa is a long-range, low-power radio that can reach several kilometres in open areas, which suits farms, rivers and villages. The price is a very low data rate, so it can send small messages like 'moisture 42 percent', not photos. LoRaWAN is the network protocol on top: many nodes talk to one gateway, and the gateway forwards their data to a server over the Internet. Radio frequencies are regulated, so in Bangladesh you must use a band allowed by the regulator, BTRC.

Cellular, from SMS to NB-IoT: Mobile networks cover almost all of Bangladesh, including remote char areas where there is no Wi-Fi. A simple GSM module can send SMS alerts, which every phone can receive with no app and no internet package, a big advantage for farmers. Newer cellular IoT standards such as NB-IoT and LTE-M are designed for low-power devices sending small data, but whether they are available depends on the operator, so check before you design around them. Cellular needs a SIM and a monthly cost, and the modules draw large current bursts when transmitting.

A quick comparison in words: For short range and high speed with mains power, pick Wi-Fi. For a device talking to a phone nearby, pick BLE. For many devices in one building, consider a Zigbee mesh. For small data over kilometres with batteries, pick LoRa. For anywhere-coverage and SMS to plain phones, pick cellular. Many real products combine two, for example BLE for setup from a phone and LoRa or cellular for daily reports.

How devices talk to the cloud, MQTT: Sending data needs an application protocol. HTTP works, but it is heavy for a tiny device. A very popular choice in IoT is MQTT, a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol. Devices connect to a central server called a broker. A sensor publishes a message on a topic, like farm/field3/moisture, with the value 42. Any phone app or server that subscribed to that topic receives it from the broker. The sensor does not need to know who is listening. MQTT's fixed header can be as small as 2 bytes, and it offers three quality of service levels: QoS 0 (at most once), QoS 1 (at least once) and QoS 2 (exactly once). The standard port is 1883, and 8883 is used for MQTT over TLS.

Edge versus cloud decisions: Should the pump decision be made on the device or in the cloud? If the cloud decides, a network outage, very common in rural areas during storms, leaves the field without water or the pump running forever. A good rule: safety-critical and time-critical decisions are made locally on the device, at the edge. The cloud is used for logs, dashboards, alerts and changing settings. The device must keep working sensibly when the link is down.

Why security matters: In 2016 the Mirai malware infected huge numbers of IoT devices such as IP cameras and home routers, mostly by trying their factory default usernames and passwords. It then used them to launch some of the largest denial-of-service attacks seen at that time, knocking major websites offline. The devices worked perfectly for their owners, who never knew. Cheap, connected and forgotten devices are a perfect army for attackers.

Common weaknesses: Default or hard-coded passwords that are the same on every unit. Debug ports such as JTAG or SWD left open, letting anyone with a probe read out the firmware and its secret keys. Firmware updates that are not signed, so an attacker can install their own code. Data sent in plain text, so anyone on the network can read it or fake it. The same secret key in every device, so cracking one opens all of them. And devices that never get security updates.

Defences, part 1, identity and transport: Give every device its own unique credentials or key, never one shared password. Force the user to change any default password at setup. Use TLS (the same protection behind https) for connections to servers: TLS encrypts the data so eavesdroppers cannot read it, checks integrity so it cannot be changed on the way, and uses certificates so the device knows it is talking to the real server and not an impostor. Many 32-bit MCUs such as the ESP32 have hardware accelerators for the cryptography this needs.

Defences, part 2, secure boot and signed updates: Secure boot builds a chain of trust. Code in the chip's boot ROM, which cannot be changed, checks the digital signature of the bootloader using a public key stored in the chip. The bootloader then checks the signature of the application. If any signature is wrong, the code does not run. Signed OTA updates use the same idea: the company signs the new firmware with a private key kept safely in the office, and the device only accepts images whose signature verifies. Add flash encryption or readout protection, and lock or disable the debug port in production units, so the firmware and keys cannot simply be copied out.

Defences, part 3, design habits: Turn off services you do not need. Validate every message from outside: check lengths, ranges and formats before using them, so a malformed packet cannot overflow a buffer. Use least privilege: a device that only reports temperature should not accept commands to change its firmware server. Plan for updates from day one, because a device that cannot be patched stays vulnerable forever.

Safety is different from security: Security protects the system from people who want to harm it. Safety protects people and property from harm that the system itself can cause, through faults or bugs, even with nobody attacking. A classic warning is the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine in the 1980s: software errors, including a race condition, let it give several patients massive radiation overdoses, and earlier hardware safety interlocks had been removed because engineers trusted the software. The lesson: never rely on software alone where lives are at stake.

How safety is designed in: Fail-safe defaults mean that when something fails, outputs go to the safe state: a heater turns off, a pump stops after a maximum run time, a door lock follows the rules for fire escape. Independent checks, like a hardware thermal cut-out next to a software temperature limit. Watchdogs and brown-out resets, from lesson 19. Industries have functional safety standards that demand this discipline, such as IEC 61508 in general, ISO 26262 for cars and IEC 62304 for medical device software. You do not need their details now, only that they exist and require evidence, testing and documentation.

Privacy: IoT devices collect data about people: when a family is home, what they buy, where a delivery bike goes. Collect only what you need, keep it only as long as needed, protect it in transit and storage, and tell users what you collect. A smart meter that reports usage every few seconds can reveal when a house is empty; a daily total may be enough for billing.

Real life example 1, the Mymensingh fish pond: A node with a dissolved oxygen sensor and a temperature sensor reads every five minutes. It sends readings over LoRa to a gateway at the farm office, which forwards them by MQTT to a server. If oxygen drops below a set limit, the node itself switches on the aerator through a relay, without waiting for the cloud, and the server sends an SMS to the farmer. The gateway's MQTT connection uses TLS, and the node only accepts signed firmware.

Real life example 2, a cold storage in Bogura: Potatoes in cold storage must stay within a narrow temperature range. A Wi-Fi temperature logger in each chamber publishes readings every minute. When load shedding hits and the generator fails to start, the readings rise and the owner gets an alert on his phone. The logger also stores readings in flash during Internet outages and uploads them later, so the record has no gaps.

Common mistakes: Choosing Wi-Fi for a battery device far from any router. Making the cloud responsible for safety decisions. Shipping with a default password like admin/admin. Leaving the SWD port open on production boards. Accepting OTA images without a signature check. Confusing safety with security in exam answers.

What exams ask: Define IoT and its layers. Compare Wi-Fi, BLE, Zigbee, LoRa and cellular by range, data rate and power. Explain MQTT publish/subscribe, broker and QoS levels. List IoT security threats and defences, explain secure boot and signed updates. Distinguish safety from security with examples, and name functional safety standards.

Recap: IoT connects embedded devices to people and servers through gateways and the cloud. Every radio trades range, rate and power; choose by the job. MQTT gives lightweight publish/subscribe messaging through a broker. Security needs unique credentials, TLS, secure boot, signed updates and closed debug ports. Safety needs fail-safe defaults, independent checks and local decisions that keep working when the network is down.
key_points: An IoT system has devices at the edge, a gateway or network, and a server or cloud for storage, dashboards and alerts.
Wireless links trade range, data rate and power: Wi-Fi is fast but power-hungry, BLE is short-range and low-power, LoRa is long-range with tiny data rates, cellular covers almost everywhere.
MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol: devices publish to topics on a broker, subscribers receive; QoS 0, 1 and 2; port 1883, or 8883 with TLS.
Safety-critical decisions should be made locally on the device so it works when the network is down.
Mirai (2016) showed how default passwords turn IoT devices into attack armies.
Defences: unique credentials, TLS, secure boot chain of trust, signed OTA updates, readout protection and locked debug ports, input validation.
Safety protects people from the system's own faults; standards include IEC 61508, ISO 26262 and IEC 62304; Therac-25 shows the danger of trusting software alone.
lessons.tip: For every IoT design, write three lines: what goes wrong if the network dies, what goes wrong if someone steals one device, and what goes wrong if someone sends a fake command. If you cannot answer all three, the design is not finished.
lessons.task: Pick three connected devices around you (a router, a smart TV, a prepaid meter, a phone-controlled bulb). For each, write which link it uses, roughly how much data it sends, whether it runs on battery or mains, and one security risk with one defence.

quiz.q: A soil sensor on a farm, far from any router, must run on batteries and send one small number every 10 minutes over a few kilometres. Which link fits best?
quiz.explain: LoRa trades data rate for long range and low power, which suits small, infrequent messages over kilometres.

quiz.q: In MQTT, what does the broker do?
options: Receives published messages and delivers them to subscribers of the topic
quiz.explain: Devices publish to topics on the broker, and the broker forwards each message to clients subscribed to that topic.

quiz.q: How did the Mirai malware mainly take over IoT devices?
options: By trying factory default usernames and passwords
quiz.explain: Mirai scanned for devices and logged in with well-known default credentials.

quiz.q: What does secure boot do?
options: Erases the firmware at every reset
Checks the digital signature of each boot stage and refuses to run unsigned code
quiz.explain: Secure boot builds a chain of trust from the boot ROM, verifying signatures before running the next stage.

quiz.q: Which statement best separates safety from security?
options: Safety protects people from harm caused by the system's own faults; security protects the system from attackers
Security is only about passwords; safety is only about batteries
Safety is needed only for cloud servers
quiz.explain: Safety deals with harm from faults even with no attacker; security deals with deliberate attacks.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Smart Irrigation Controller for a Bangladesh Farm
lessons.content:
Rahim chacha grows tomatoes and brinjal on a small plot near Rajshahi. In the dry season he walks to the field twice a day, feels the soil with his fingers and decides whether to run his small solar pump. Some days he waters too much and wastes groundwater; other days he is at the bazar, the soil cracks and the plants wilt. His nephew, a CSE student, says: 'Chacha, let me build you a little box that watches the soil and runs the pump for you.' This final lesson builds that box, step by step, using almost everything from this course.

Step 1, requirements in plain words: Before touching a chip, write what the box must do. Measure soil moisture regularly. Switch the pump on when the soil is dry and off when it is wet enough. Never run the pump endlessly, even if a sensor breaks. Send an SMS to chacha's ordinary phone when the pump starts, when something goes wrong, and when the battery is low. Run without mains electricity, because there is none in the field. Survive heat, dust and monsoon rain. Cost as little as possible, and be easy to fix.

Step 2, turn wishes into numbers: A specification makes requirements testable. Read moisture every 10 minutes. Pump on below 30 percent moisture, off above 70 percent. Maximum pump run of 45 minutes, then stop and alert. Controller battery life of at least two months with no sun at all, as a safety margin for cloudy weeks. At most about 4 SMS per normal day. Parts cost around 3,500 taka. These numbers are design choices for this example, and every later decision is checked against them.

Step 3, choose the connectivity: The field is far from any Wi-Fi router, so Wi-Fi is out. LoRa would need a gateway somewhere with Internet, and chacha does not use apps. Mobile coverage exists, and every phone receives SMS with no internet package. So the design uses a GSM module for SMS. This is the lesson 25 trade-off in action: we need tiny data, wide coverage and an ordinary phone at the other end, and cellular SMS fits.

Step 4, choose the microcontroller: The job is simple: read one analog sensor, drive one relay, talk UART to the GSM module, sleep most of the time. An 8-bit AVR such as the ATmega328P has a 10-bit ADC, UART, timers, a watchdog and good sleep modes, which is plenty. An ESP32 would be overkill without Wi-Fi, and its radio is not needed. An important detail: a ready-made Arduino Uno board draws far too much current even when its chip sleeps, because of its regulator, USB chip and power LED. For a battery product we use the bare chip on a small custom board, prototyped first on an Uno.

Step 5, the block diagram: In words, the diagram is: a solar panel charges a Li-ion battery through a charger module; the battery feeds a low-dropout regulator that powers the MCU. A capacitive soil moisture sensor connects to an ADC pin and gets its power from a GPIO pin, so it is only on while measuring. A transistor driver on a GPIO pin switches the relay coil, with a flyback diode across the coil. The relay contacts switch the pump, which has its own bigger solar supply. The GSM module connects to the UART, and its power is cut by a MOSFET switch when not in use. A voltage divider lets an ADC pin read the battery voltage.

Step 6, the pin map: Writing the pin map early prevents wiring mistakes. For example: ADC channel 0 for the soil sensor, ADC channel 1 for the battery divider, pin 8 to power the sensor, pin 7 to the relay driver, pin 6 to the GSM power switch, the UART pins to the GSM module, and one spare pin for a status LED.

Why a capacitive sensor: Cheap resistive probes pass current through bare metal legs in wet soil and corrode within weeks, so their readings drift. Capacitive sensors keep the metal covered and last much longer. Powering the sensor only while reading also saves energy.

Step 7, calibration: The ADC gives a raw number from 0 to 1023, not a moisture percentage, and every sensor and every soil type is a bit different. So we do a two-point calibration, as in lesson 17. Put the sensor in completely dry soil from the field: suppose it reads 620. Put it in fully soaked soil: suppose it reads 290. For this sensor, a higher reading means drier soil. Then moisture percent = (620 - raw) x 100 / (620 - 290). Check: raw 455 gives (620 - 455) x 100 / 330 = 165 x 100 / 330 = 50 percent. Raw 521 gives 30 percent and raw 389 gives 70 percent. The two calibration numbers are stored in EEPROM so they can be changed in the field without new firmware.

Step 8, sampling and filtering: One reading can be disturbed by noise, especially when the GSM module or relay switches. So each measurement powers the sensor, waits a short moment for it to settle, takes 8 ADC readings a few milliseconds apart, and takes the median or the average. A median ignores a single wild spike, which you saw in the moving-average example of lesson 17. Readings outside the possible range, such as below 200 or above 900, are treated as a sensor fault, not as soil moisture.

Step 9, control with hysteresis: A naive rule says 'pump on below 50 percent, off above 50 percent'. With noise, a reading that wobbles between 49 and 51 would click the relay on and off every few minutes, wearing out the relay and the pump. Hysteresis uses two thresholds: on below 30 percent (raw above 521), off above 70 percent (raw below 389). Between them, the pump keeps whatever state it already has. This is exactly how a fridge thermostat works, and it is cheap and robust.

Step 10, the state machine: The firmware is a super-loop with a small state machine, no RTOS needed. SLEEP: the MCU is in power-down, woken by the watchdog timer. MEASURE: power the sensor, read, filter, decide. PUMPING: relay on, re-measure every minute, track run time. ALERT: power up the GSM module, send an SMS, power it down. FAULT: pump off, alert sent, keep retrying measurement slowly. Each state does a small piece of work and returns, so nothing blocks, as you saw in lesson 21.

The safety rules inside the states: If the pump has run 45 minutes and moisture has not passed 70 percent, the firmware turns the pump off and enters FAULT, because something is wrong: a dry tube well, a broken pipe, or a sensor lying on a dry spot. If the sensor reading is impossible, the pump is switched off rather than on. If the battery is low, the box sends one last alert and stops using the GSM module. When in doubt, the pump goes off; a few dry hours are better than a burned pump or a flooded field.

Step 11, the watchdog and long sleeps: The ATmega328P watchdog can time out after up to about 8 seconds. Here it plays two roles. In sleep, its interrupt wakes the MCU, which counts wake-ups and goes back to sleep until about 10 minutes have passed. In normal work, it is a real watchdog: the code feeds it only at the end of each successful pass through the main loop, so a hang in the GSM code or a stuck UART resets the chip. After any reset, the firmware reads the reset-cause register, makes sure the relay output starts off, and reports watchdog resets in the next SMS.

Step 12, the power budget: Each wake-up for measuring keeps the board active for about 2 seconds at about 40 mA, including the sensor. Sleep current for the whole custom board is assumed to be about 50 microamps. Over one 10-minute cycle of 600 seconds, the average is (40 x 2 + 0.05 x 598) / 600, which is about 0.183 mA, or about 4.4 mAh per day.

SMS energy: A GSM module draws large current bursts while transmitting, so its supply needs a strong battery and a big capacitor. Assume each SMS needs the module on for about 10 seconds at an average of about 300 mA, including registering on the network. Four SMS per day is 4 x 10 x 300 / 3600, about 3.3 mAh per day. Total: about 7.7 mAh per day.

Battery and solar check: A 2,000 mAh battery divided by 7.7 mAh per day gives about 259 days with no sunlight at all, far above the two-month requirement, even if real batteries lose some capacity to heat, age and self-discharge. A small 1 W solar panel with about 4 hours of good sun and, say, 50 percent overall charging efficiency gives about 1 x 4 x 0.5 / 3.7 V, about 540 mAh per day, much more than we use. So the design has a big margin, which is what you want in a field where dust covers the panel. If the GSM module were left on all the time instead of being switched off, this budget would collapse, which is why the MOSFET switch matters.

Step 13, firmware updates and settings: SMS-based firmware download is impractical, so this design keeps a serial bootloader, as in lesson 20. A technician can update it in the field with a laptop and a USB-serial cable. Settings that change more often, like thresholds or the phone number, can be changed by a specially formatted SMS from an allowed number, which the firmware checks carefully before accepting. A version string is included in every daily status SMS.

Step 14, security, scaled to the risk: A field irrigation box is not a bank, but an attacker who can send fake SMS commands could switch off watering for weeks. So the box only accepts commands from a stored list of numbers, requires a short PIN inside the message, checks every value against safe limits, and never lets a command disable the 45-minute safety cut-off. The debug and programming pins are inside a sealed box, not on the outside.

Step 15, testing: Pure logic gets unit tests on a laptop: the percent formula (raw 455 must give 50), the hysteresis rule and the state machine with fake sensor values, including impossible readings and a sensor stuck dry. On the bench, a pot of soil, a cup of water and a small 5 V pump replace the field. Then a pilot: one box on one plot for two weeks, with the old manual routine running alongside, comparing its decisions with chacha's own judgement. Heat, dust and rain test the enclosure; the box sits in the shade with a sloped lid and the cable glands face down.

Step 16, cost estimate: Rough prices that change from shop to shop: MCU and board parts about 500 taka, capacitive sensor 250, relay module 150, GSM module 600, battery with charger 600, solar panel 800, enclosure and wires 500. About 3,400 taka, inside the target; the existing pump is not counted.

What this capstone used: Characteristics and design metrics (lesson 2), MCU choice and anatomy (lessons 3 to 5), embedded C and registers (6 to 8), GPIO (9), timers and the watchdog (11 and 19), ADC (13), UART (15), sensors, actuators and drivers (17), power management (18), the boot and update path (20), the super-loop and state machine (21), debugging and testing (24), and connectivity and security (25). That is the real point of embedded systems: no single topic is hard, but a good product needs all of them working together.

Common mistakes in projects like this: Running an Arduino Uno board on a battery. One threshold instead of hysteresis. Letting an SMS or the cloud decide safety. Leaving the GSM module always on. Forgetting the relay flyback diode. Using the raw reading as a percentage.

What exams ask: Design a system for a given application: block diagram, justified MCU choice, control logic or state machine, power budget and battery life, and how reliability and safety are handled.

Recap of the course and what next: You started with what an embedded system is and why its constraints matter, went inside the microcontroller, learned to control its registers in C, used GPIO, timers, PWM, ADC, interrupts and serial buses, then added power, reliability, boot, RTOS, real-time analysis, debugging, IoT and security, and finally built a complete product. Good next steps are PCB design, an RTOS such as FreeRTOS on an STM32 or ESP32, embedded Linux on boards like the Raspberry Pi, control systems, and machine learning on tiny devices. Pick a real problem near you, a pond, a shop, a classroom, and build it.
key_points: Start from plain requirements, then turn them into numbers: 10-minute reading, 30/70 percent thresholds, 45-minute pump limit, battery and cost targets.
Connectivity follows the job: no Wi-Fi in the field and an ordinary phone at the other end make GSM SMS the right choice.
Use a bare low-power MCU on a custom board; a full Arduino Uno board wastes too much current while sleeping.
Two-point calibration: percent = (dry - raw) x 100 / (dry - wet); with 620 and 290, raw 455 gives 50 percent.
Hysteresis (on below 30, off above 70) stops relay chatter; a maximum run time and fault states make the pump fail safe.
Power budget: about 0.183 mA average for measuring plus about 3.3 mAh/day for SMS, about 7.7 mAh/day, so 2,000 mAh lasts about 259 days without sun.
The watchdog both wakes the MCU from sleep and resets it on a hang; the reset cause is checked and the relay starts off.
Test pure logic on a PC, then on the bench, then in a field pilot; the capstone joins almost every topic of the course.
lessons.tip: For any project, write the numeric specification and the power budget on one page before buying parts. Most failed student projects die from a missing number, not from a missing feature.
lessons.task: Redo the power budget on paper for a version that measures every 5 minutes instead of 10, with the same 2 s at 40 mA, 50 uA sleep and 4 SMS a day. How many days does a 2,000 mAh battery last without sun? Then draw the state machine with its five states and label every arrow with its condition.

quiz.q: With a dry reading of 620 and a wet reading of 290, what moisture percent does a raw reading of 455 give?
Why does the controller use two thresholds (on below 30, off above 70) instead of one?
options: Because the ADC has two channels
Hysteresis stops the relay from switching on and off rapidly when readings wobble
quiz.explain: With one threshold, noise near it would chatter the relay; hysteresis keeps the current state between the two limits.

quiz.q: The pump has run for 45 minutes and moisture is still below 70 percent. What should the firmware do?
options: Keep pumping until moisture reaches 70 percent
Turn the pump off, enter a fault state and send an alert
quiz.explain: A maximum run time is a fail-safe: something is wrong (dry well, broken pipe, bad sensor), so the pump goes off and the farmer is told.

quiz.q: Why is the GSM module powered through a MOSFET switch?
options: So it can be fully switched off between messages, which keeps the power budget small
To protect it from the soil sensor
quiz.explain: A GSM module left on would draw far more than the whole sleeping controller; switching it off makes the battery last months.

quiz.q: Why was a capacitive soil sensor chosen over a cheap resistive probe?
options: Resistive probes pass current through bare metal in wet soil and corrode, drifting over time
quiz.explain: Resistive probes corrode within weeks; capacitive sensors keep the metal covered and last longer.
